2HDM+S and the Madala hypothesis

In the above section we have described the particle modelling scenarios that are usually considered
in indirect detection literature. Here, we briefly outline the phenomenology of a relatively new
model, which also provides a DM candidate particle. The model is based on a generic extension to
the SM, known as the two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) (proposed in Lee (1973), see also Branco
et al. (2012)), which simply introduces the possibility of a second doublet of the Higgs field. This
type of model is well-motivated by some theoretical deficiencies of the SM, and an extra Higgs
doublet is necessary in some models of supersymmetry or models that contain axions. A specific
type of 2HDM model, which is known as a Type-II 2HDM (the most similar to supersymmetric
models, and popular in the literature) that also permits the existence of a new Higgs-like particle,
𝑆, and a DM candidate particle, 𝜒, was originally proposed in von Buddenbrock et al. (2015),
and then later expanded upon in von Buddenbrock et al. (2016). The addition of 𝑆 to the generic
2HDM has motivated the naming convention of ‘2HDM+S’ for this model, which we adopt for
this thesis. The model has also been referred to as the Madala hypothesis in the literature, which is
a word in the isiZulu language that translates to ‘old person’. This name is a reference to the extra
Higgs scalar (denoted 𝐻, the Madala boson) that is introduced by the second Higgs doublet, since
𝐻 is conventionally heavier (due to being ‘older’) than the SM Higgs (von Buddenbrock 2017).

An observable signature of the 2HDM+S model is the production of a number of leptons in
particle colliders that would be considered anomalous, or in excess, of SM theories. In this regard,
the authors of von Buddenbrock et al. (2016) found that the relevant parameters of the 2HDM+S
model were compatible with data gathered from Run 1 of the CMS and ATLAS experiments in
the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) (The CMS Collaboration et al. 2008; Aad et al. 2008). Then,
after analysis of further Run 2 data, the model parameters were constrained, but still viable (von
Buddenbrock et al. 2019) (see also von Buddenbrock et al. (2017), von Buddenbrock (2017), and
von Buddenbrock et al. (2018)). Of these constraints, we only focus on a few that are most relevant
to this work. In particular, we follow the general analyses of Beck et al. (2023b) and Beck et al.
(2017), which were the first to investigate the possibility of using this new model in indirect DM
searches. In these works, a fixed mass of the Madala boson of 𝑚𝐻 = 270GeV and the scalar S of
𝑚𝑆 = 150GeV are used. Since the 𝜒 particle is still unconstrained by LHC data, results were found
for a range of possible masses. However, as the particle 𝜒 is assumed to couple directly to 𝑆, there
are still some theoretical limits on its mass which are determined by the associated interaction
chains. In the cases of the 𝜒 particle having spin of 0, 1/2, or 1, the Lagrangians that define these
interactions are given by (Beck et al. 2023b, eqs. 7-9):

3.1.2 Halo models
With the characteristics and behaviour of the individual DM particles set, we then need to model
the distribution of these particles in the regions we are interested in. There is substantial evidence
to suggest that DM particles have a tendency to clump together and form gravitationally-bound
halos, coming from both analytical arguments (see for instance Silk et al. (1993)) and from a host
of large 𝑁-body simulations (see Kuhlen et al. (2012) or Vogelsberger et al. (2020) for excellent
reviews). Since the properties of these halos – including their formation histories, inner structures
and mass distributions – have been the topic of several dedicated studies in recent years, the
current paradigm of DM halo modelling has become quite robust. In this Section we will provide
a brief outline of some pertinent aspects of DM halo modelling, and present the specific equations
that are used in this work. For more comprehensive summaries or reviews on this topic, we refer
the reader to the following works: Navarro et al. (2010), Bertone (2010, ch. 2), Kuhlen et al. (2012),
Zavala et al. (2019), and Vogelsberger et al. (2020).

In this work, only the formation of Cold, non-relativistic DM (CDM) halos is considered, as
the particle models used here all behave like CDM. We note that although other DM scenarios, like
WarmDM(WDM)or Self-InteractingDM(SIDM), can also lead to the formation of halos, there can
be significant departures from CDM halo characteristics (especially in the case of SIDM) (Kuhlen
et al. 2012; Zavala et al. 2019). The majority of these halo characteristics have been sourced from
analyses of modern 𝑁-body simulations, which are run on high-performance supercomputers

utilising thousands of CPU cores and taking millions of CPU hours. These simulations usually
track an ensemble of 𝑁 particles (consisting of dark or baryonic matter, or both) from the very
beginnings of structure formation, seeded by tiny density perturbations that grow with inflation
and produce large self-gravitating halos of DM, up to the current epoch. Treating the evolution of
these particles in a numerical fashion also allows the non-linear regimes of standard structure
formation theories to bemore accurately probed, avoidingmany of the assumptions and limitations
of analytical methods. Many such simulations have been performed over the past three decades,
and a complete review of them could be the subject of an entire thesis. Since we are only focused
on a few very particular outcomes from these simulations, we provide just a brief list of some of
the more notable projects, which can serve as a starting point for further reading in this subject.

The most long-standing of these simulation projects is the Millennium project, which, in its
various forms, has been running since 2005. The inaugural simulation, now known as Millennium
I (Springel et al. 2005), tracked the evolution of 10 billion DM particles in a (685Mpc)3 volume.
Since then, the Millennium II, XXL and most recent MillenniumTNG simulations (Boylan-Kolchin
et al. 2009; Angulo et al. 2012; Hernández-Aguayo et al. 2023) have all improved either the number
of simulated particles (up to over a trillion with the inclusion of neutrinos) or the simulated
volume (up to (3000Mpc)3). The DEUS FUR (Dark Energy Universe Simulation Full Universe
Run) (Alimi et al. 2012) is another notable project, with 550 billion simulated particles and three
different dark energy models in an enormous (29Gpc)3 volume that spans the entire observable
universe. Finally, the PKDGRAV3 code (Potter et al. 2017) has performed a 2 trillion particle
cosmological simulation that makes use of extremely fast and efficient computational techniques
that should scale with improvements to particle number, ensuring the viability of larger and more
detailed simulations in the future.

The results of these CDM simulations on cosmological scales also agree well with observational
surveys of large-scale structure in the universe (Springel et al. 2006), which reinforces the notion
that the large-scale dynamics of structure in the universe behaves in a manner consistent with our
standard ΛCDM cosmology. However, a major limitation of older, large-scale 𝑁-body simulations
is that they lacked the spatial resolution to probe the small-scale structure of individual DM
halos. Though, this problem has diminished in recent years with larger simulations and more
dedicated studies. In this work, the structure of individual halos is vital to the accurate modelling
of expected DM-related emissions, and the DM halo density (which appears in Equation (3.4))
plays a particularly important role. Throughout the rest of the thesis a large emphasis is placed
on the very inner regions of DM halos, since these regions contain the largest density of DM and
thus produce the strongest observable emissions.

Before describing the modelling of halo density profiles, we note that descriptions of the
physical properties of DM halos – their spatial boundaries and points of interest, enclosed mass,
etc. – depend entirely on the mathematical definitions of these properties. Real halos would be
clumps of virialised particles with no distinct border and potentially complex three-dimensional
geometry. In this work, wemake use of very common definitions in the literature, the first of which
is an assumption that the halos are spherically symmetric and can be described by a single radial
parameter. Evidence from some 𝑁-body simulations suggest that halos would very likely have
triaxial shapes (Dubinski et al. 1991; Bett et al. 2007), with prolate central regions and oblate outer
regions. However, since spherical density profiles still approximate the simulations quite well
(discussed more below), a spherical approximation should not affect the final results significantly
(although, adaptations of the numerical modelling schemes used in this work could be a potential
area for future work). The second definition we make use of is that of the virial radius, 𝑅vir, and
mass, 𝑀vir. These are defined in terms of the spherical collapse model, whereby the virial radius
is chosen at the point where the enclosed (collapsed) halo has a mean density that matches some

3.2.1 Diffusion
Finding an exact form of the diffusion coefficient 𝐷(x, 𝐸) can often be challenging, due largely to
the uncertainties in the structures of the host magnetic fields. Due to the Lorentz force, we know
that the charged, high-energy electrons should spiral around the magnetic field lines, however the
particles can scatter or deviate from these field lines if there are irregularities in the magnetic field.
Since we expect real magnetic fields in large structures to have some level of irregularity, and if
we assume the scatterings are random, the resulting movement of electrons can be approximated
as isotropic diffusion away from areas of high density (the approximation of isotropic diffusion
also helps in reducing the dimensionality of the problem, as the diffusion coefficient should be
considered as a tensor otherwise). Since the vast majority of studies in the literature make use of
this approximation, we likewise adopt it in this work.

The magnitude of the aforementioned scattering effect is dependent on the scale of the irregu-
larities when compared to the gyro-radius of the particle’s orbit; the scattering is only appreciable
when these two scales are similar, whereas relatively small irregularities are ignored by the gyrat-
ing electron. However, irregularities can also be generated by the streaming of the high energy
particles in the field through the production of Alfvén and hydromagnetic waves (Longair 2011),
which adds an extra layer of complexity to their analytical description.

Due to the theoretical complexity and the observational uncertaintieswhen describing diffusion
in these scenarios, it is common for studies to use simple expressions for the diffusion coefficient
that use various approximations. The simplest of these would be the case of Bohm diffusion (see,
for example, Günter 2016), which is considered as a lower limit for the diffusion coefficient as it is
just related to the gyro-radius 𝑟𝑔 of the particle in the magnetic field, i.e.

3.2.3 Magnetic fields and gas densities

3.3 Observable emissions from DM
The emissions from the electrons that are produced by DM annihilation are dominated by syn-
chrotron radiation, which is detectable primarily in the radio frequency band. The accurate
modelling of this radiation is one of the integral components of a good indirect DM search, and is
a well-studied area of radiative astrophysics. In the following Sections we describe (briefly) some
features of synchrotron radiation emitted by ultra-relativistic electrons, drawing mainly from the
analysis in Longair (2011), which has become a standard source in the literature.

3.3.1 Synchrotron emission
When considering the case of a single electron in a simple, static magnetic field, its movement is
helical with a constant pitch angle (𝛼), representing the angle between the electron velocity (v)
and magnetic field (B) vectors. This helical motion is caused by the Lorentz force F = 𝑞(v×B) of a
charge 𝑞 in a magnetic field, which results in a constant velocity that is parallel to the magnetic field
lines (the ‘guiding centre’ of the motion) and an acceleration that is exactly perpendicular to this
guiding centre. The accelerated motion of the electron is what, through standard electromagnetic
theory, generates the synchrotron radiation.

The characteristic frequency spectrum of synchrotron radiation from a single electron is shown
in Figure 3.6. This spectrum is determined by the synchrotron kernel function, which is usually

CHAPTER 4

Solving the Diffusion-Loss Equation

The nature of Equation (3.19), that of being a second-order partial differential equation, means
it cannot trivially be solved by analytical methods. However, since the problem of cosmic ray
propagation is a rather well-studied one, there have been a variety of techniques used to find
solutions to this equation in the literature. Eachmethod ismore or less computationally performant
depending on the user’s desired level of accuracy in the result, and in the amount of time and
effort given to setting up the algorithms. In the following Chapter we will outline each of the
variations found in the literature, and then focus in particular on the method we have developed
and used in this project. A visual comparison of the results of each method can be found at the
end of this Chapter, in Section 4.4.

4.1 Overview of solution methods

Semi-analytical solutions
The most commonly cited technique for solving Equation (3.19) in the literature was introduced
by Colafrancesco et al. (2006), although a similar technique, tailored specifically for the MW halo,
was used before that in Baltz et al. (1998). This method has since appeared in a multitude of radio
indirect detection studies and is the method of choice in the software package RX-DMFIT (Mc-
Daniel et al. 2017), which has in turn been used in a variety of studies (this package will be
discussed in detail at the end of this Chapter). Here we outline the fundamental parts of the
method and comment on its applicability to different astrophysical modelling scenarios; for a de-
tailed analysis and derivation of the formulae we refer the reader to the appendix in Colafrancesco
et al. (2006).

To work with Equation (3.19) in a way that provides an analytical solution, there are several
assumptions about the physical environment – which lead to simplifying approximations – that are
required. Themost significant of these approximations is that the diffusion function, 𝐷, and energy-
loss function, 𝑏, depend only on the energy of the electrons and not on any spatial coordinate, i.e.
𝐷(x, 𝐸) ≈ 𝐷(𝐸) and 𝑏(x, 𝐸) ≈ 𝑏(𝐸). Because of the noted uncertainty in the magnetic field and gas
density profiles in certain astrophysical objects, this approximation may be unimportant in certain
cases. However, as will be further discussed in later Sections, high-resolution radio data that is
able to resolve the inner regions of these objects makes this approximation a significant hindrance
to finding reliable results when that information is available. The other approximation necessary
for this method is that the relevant physical quantities obey spherical symmetry, such that spatial
effects are described only in terms of the radius 𝑟 from the centre of the halo. The validity of this
assumption depends entirely on the geometry of the relevant astrophysical target; cool-core galaxy
clusters or dSphs should easily qualify, whereas highly elliptical or spiral galaxies would benefit
from a more detailed spatial analysis (for an example of a solution that incorporates more than
one spatial dimension, see Egorov (2022)).

Numerical solutions
The majority of the use cases for numerical solutions to the diffusion-loss equation are in the
field of galactic cosmic-ray physics. There are two prominent pieces of software that perform this
function: the seminal GALPROP package1 (Strong et al. 1998; Porter et al. 2022) (also used with
extensions in Egorov (2022)) and the DRAGON(2) package2 (Evoli et al. 2017). The other notable
use of a numerical solution is by the authors of the series Regis et al. (2014), Regis et al. (2015b),
Regis et al. (2015a), Regis et al. (2017), and Regis et al. (2021). Their use case is relevant here,
because the method presented within those papers is motivated by the same thing as this project –
to solve the propagation of charged DM annihilation products in astrophysical objects (and not
necessarily within the MW).

In each of the above-mentioned sources, a similar technique has been used to solve Equa-
tion (3.19), originally inspired by GALPROP. This method is based on a finite-differencing method
known as the Crank-Nicolson scheme, which discretises Equation (3.19) in the spatial and energy
(momentum) dimensions. Once it is discretised, the operators of each dimension are solved
alternatively through a technique known generally as ‘operator splitting’, a technique which
drastically simplifies the computational complexity of the problem, as will be discussed further
in detail below. While there are a significant number of numerical effects that need to be consid-
ered and potentially tweaked for different use-cases, the outcome of this method is a noticeable
computational speed-up over the semi-analytical method described in Section 4.1.

The other important benefit to using numerical solutions is the ability to consider the full spatial
dependance of the relevant magnetic field and gas density profiles throughout the modelling
process. In various cases, such as for dSphs, the spatial profiles of these properties are still highly
uncertain. Thus, in the past they have often been estimated or had their spatial dependance
completely averaged out (with the exceptions of Storm et al. (2013) and Beck (2019b), which
use a more physically motivated approach to the averaging of these quantities, see also Sarkis
et al. (2022) for details of this approach). As the data from astronomical observatories become
more precise in the future and we have higher resolution images to hunt for DM in though, our
understanding of the physical properties of these objects will also improve. This makes having a
solution to Equation (3.19) that contains an accurate spatial treatment of these properties vital in
any future searches for DM that use these new data sets.

In the following Sections, the numerical technique that we have developed to solve the diffusion-
loss equation is described in detail. This technique addresses some of the issues present in other
solution methods, and will hopefully occupy a niche that exists in the DM indirect-detection
hunting space: as a computational tool that is efficient, general and accurate.

4.3 Algorithm details
As stated, the generalised CN scheme in Equation (4.23) is sufficient to solve simple diffusion
problems in one dimension. In the case of the diffusion-loss equation considered in this work
however, the electron distribution and diffusion function are not onlymultivariate, but the equation
also has a term associated with energy losses. To effectively make use of the scheme and benefit
from its stability, we have thus developed various extensions to the general version presented
above. These extensions include a generalisation of the scheme to more than one dimension,
techniques that reduce the computational cost of the algorithm, and a method to ensure that the
solution is accurate on various relevant physical scales.

Before proceeding, wemake note of a point of ambiguity that has existed in the literature around
the naming of this solutionmethod. In Regis et al. (2015b, app. A) and all versions of the GALPROP
Explanatory Supplement (sec. 5.3.3) available at the time of writing, there is a description of
a solution method that is referred to as the Alternating-Direction-Implicit (ADI) method. The
details of this method are similar to those of the operator splitting technique presented above,
except for one subtle, but distinct, technical difference. In the ADI method, during each ‘half’-step
in Equation (4.38), the implicit part of the CN method is applied to each operator, while the other
is treated explicitly (ensuring that the full operator is used during every half-step). Since the
outline of the method in Regis et al. (2015b) specifies “the implicit updating scheme is alternately
applied to the r- and E-operators in turn, keeping the other coordinate fixed”, it seems (albeit without
full knowledge of the algorithms actually used by these authors) as though the use of the term
ADI is in error, since this scheme would not use the full operator at every half-step. The most
recent publication associated with the development of the GALPROP package (Porter et al. 2022,
sec. 3.3.1) refers to the method used only as operator splitting, and makes no mention of the ADI
method. We thus refer to the solution shown above likewise, and note that results appearing
in previous publications of this work might erroneously refer to it as the ADI method. In all
circumstances, the underlying method is identical, and the difference is in name only.

4.3.7 Stability and convergence
The continuation or termination of the algorithm is managed by several conditions relating to
how the electron distribution 𝜓 is changing between iterations. These conditions are split into two
categories: stability and convergence, as described below.

Stability
At each step of the operator splitting method (Equation (4.38)), the 𝜓 distribution is updated
according to the CN scheme. The changes to 𝜓 during the initial few iterations are large, and then
gradually decrease until it nears the equilibrium solution, which should then be independant
of time. The condition of stability we require in this method is that the relative change in the
distribution from time step 𝑛 − 1 to 𝑛 is small – i.e. the changes in 𝜓 have begun to reduce and the
function approaches a constant value over all grid points in ̃𝑟 and 𝐸̃. The precise condition enforced
in the code depends on the method used in the algorithm, either the ‘accelerated’ method (ACC)
or the ‘constant-step-size’ (CSS) method. Both of these methods are inspired by the GALPROP
package (the relevant methods are described in the Explanatory Supplement, sec. 5.3.3 or in Strong
et al. (1998, app. B)).

ACC method In the ACC method, the initial timestep (Δ𝑡𝑖) is chosen to be large compared to the
timescales of all relevant physical effects. This value can be chosen manually in the code,
and defaults to 1 × 109 years, but should always follow the condition

Δ𝑡𝑖 > max{𝜏𝐸, 𝜏𝐷} . (4.56)

The timestep Δ𝑡 is then, from this initial value, reduced by a certain factor (the default value
in the code is 0.5) after a minimum number of iterations (𝑛min) have passed. The value
of 𝑛min can be chosen manually, and would usually benefit from some insights about the
performance of the algorithm that are gained after running benchmark tests. In the ACC
method, iterations above the cap of 𝑛min are considered to be stable. The reduction in the
value of Δ𝑡 continues until some minimum value Δ𝑡min, which defaults to 100 years in the
code.

CSS method In this method there are no hard caps on the number of iterations. Instead, we
calculate the relative difference between the 𝜓 distributions at subsequent iterations, and set
a certain tolerance threshold for this value (say, 0.1%). If the relative difference, calculated
as follows, is less than this tolerance then we consider the algorithm to be stable:

∣1 − 𝜓𝑛−1

𝜓𝑛 ∣ < tolerance . (4.57)

The ACC method is generally preferred for the majority of calculations. The primary reason
for this is that in most relevant astrophysical scenarios, there are a wide range of timescales which
affect the electron distribution. In the CSS method, using step sizes that are low enough to actually
capture the effects of shorter timescales leads to the algorithm needing a huge number of iterations
to converge on the equilibrium solution. Conversely, while needing only relatively few iterations,
large timesteps can lead to inaccurate final solutions as the impact from short-timescale processes
are lost during each iteration. The ACC method addresses both of these drawbacks, since the
timestep is changed dynamically and covers all relevant timescales (provided that Δ𝑡𝑖 and Δ𝑡min
are chosen appropriately). When dealing with various astrophysical scenarios, it could be of
benefit to tweak the parameters discussed above to find a set that leads to a convergent and
accurate final solution in the most computationally efficient way.

Convergence

4.4 Method comparisons and testing
There are two main considerations when describing the accuracy of the OS method. The first is
the accuracy of the final equilibrium distribution of electrons on all relevant scales, i.e., have all
of the physical effects had the correct impact on the distribution throughout the algorithm? The
second is, how closely do the results of this numerical method compare to other solution methods,
particularly the widely-used semi-analytical methods described in Section 4.1? While aspects of
these two points have already been mentioned throughout this Chapter, we discuss them in more
detail below.

4.4.1 Accuracy and benchmarking
The accuracy of the final solution on different physical scales is directly related to the size of the
timestep Δ𝑡 and how it compares to the timescales of the diffusion and energy loss processes,

In practice, the benchmarking test described above requires a considerable number of iterations
to achieve, which takes a lot of computing time on a personal computer. While it does ensure the
most accurate solution possible when using the OS method, it is inefficient to use when there are
many computations needed (in the case of survey data being compared to many DM models, for
instance). Further, the relative difference in the electron distribution between iterations tends to
rapidly diminish at higher iteration numbers. This suggests that cutting out the final iterations that
seek the above computer-precision convergence condition can, in general, result in significantly
better computation times while having little risk of inaccuracies, which can be valuable in practical
settings. To test the accuracy of solutions found with the much more efficient ACC method, we
thus use the CSS method with the convergence condition Equation (4.59) as a benchmark test case
for a set of results. We then compare the results to those found using the ACC method, and if they
are compatible within a certain tolerance, we proceed to use the ACC method for testing various
parameter variations. The choices of either method (CSS or ACC) and whether the convergence is
based on the benchmark case are all controlled by flags in the code which allow for conveniently
switching between methods.

4.4.2 Comparisons to semi-analytical method
The second measure of accuracy we consider is how closely the solution compares to other,
independent methods. We have thus performed some basic tests of our algorithm using identical
parameters to calculations with the semi-analytical method described in Section 4.1 (referred to
from here as the Green’s Function method or GF). We first perform these calculations by using
the same GF used in Colafrancesco et al. (2015a), Beck (2019b), and Sarkis et al. (2022), and then
use a dedicated software package RX-DMFIT. The pertinent parameters used during the tests are
shown in Table 4.1, and any relevant parameters not shown therein or mentioned explicitly are
taken to be the standard values referred to at their descriptions in this thesis.

Calculations of the surface brightness for a set of targets and parameters were carried out
in Sarkis et al. (2023a), using both the OS and GF methods. We have reproduced a subset of
those results here, highlighting the most relevant comparison between methods in a galaxy cluster
scenario. In this case we observe very close agreement between the two methods, with a large
overlap in the surface brightness values for the full range of WIMP masses. The most notable
trend in these results is that for lower mass WIMPs (which produce stronger emissions, due to
the inverse mass relationship in the electron source function), there is a universal discrepancy
in the surface brightness in the inner regions of the halo. In the case of low mass WIMPs the OS
method produces slightly higher surface brightness values than the GF method in these regions,
but in all cases the OS method seems to produce relatively brighter values compared to the outer
regions of the halo. In the outer regions, there is negligible difference between the methods for
low mass WIMPs. These results seem to indicate that the most significant differences between
the two solution methods emerge from the centre of the halo. This is expected behaviour, as the
spatial dependance of the diffusive environment is retained in the OS method, but not in the GF
method.

4.4.3 RX-DMFIT
We have performed a set of simple calculations with the Radio and X-ray DMFIT (RX-DMFIT)
package, for the purpose of comparing the results to the ones obtained with the method developed
in this project. The code was originally written to extend the DMFIT package (Jeltema et al. 2008)
with radio and X-ray calculations, particularly the emissivity and flux outputs from synchrotron
and Inverse Compton (IC) processes. The code, written in C++, was obtained through an online
GitHub repository 5, which also hosts the package documentation. The information presented
in this section has been taken from either the documentation or the publication associated with
the package release (McDaniel et al. 2017). RX-DMFIT also necessarily makes use of two main
external libraries: the DarkSUSY package (Gondolo et al. 2004; Bringmann et al. 2018) and the
GNU Scientific Library (GSL) (Galassi 2009). These external tools provide the particle spectra
for the annihilation of WIMPs (necessary for the source term 𝑄) and the numerical integration
routines used for various calculations in the solution method, respectively.

Because of the nature of the calculations we have performed with this software, (i.e., for com-

primary capabilities. Many of the concepts and methods used have already been described in this
thesis, so we will often refer to previous equations and solution techniques. The defining feature
of RX-DMFIT is that it uses the GF solution method to the diffusion-loss equation, and the method

which are designed for fast numerical computations, also noticeably improve the performance

RX-DMFIT and GALPROP).

4.5 Summary
In this Chapter we began by providing a high-level overview of some of the methods used to
solve the diffusion-loss equation found in the literature. The most common technique in DM
indirect detection studies involves the use of Green’s function approximations that are solved semi-
analytically to yield the equilibrium distribution of electrons produced duringWIMP annihilations.
One requirement of these approximations is the removal of any spatial dependance in functions
that describe physical quantities, like the magnetic field and thermal gas density profiles that
appear in the diffusion and energy-loss functions. This is usually done by averaging the relevant
profiles, and substituting the spatially-dependant functions for scalar averages in the diffusion-loss
equation.

An alternative approach to these semi-analytical methods makes use of the Crank-Nicolson
finite-difference scheme to discretise the quantities involved in the diffusion-loss equation, and then
solve it iteratively and numerically. The primary benefits of this approach are that it is significantly
faster computationally, and that the full spatial dependance of the relevant quantities can be
kept during the entire calculation. Outside a single other research team that have implemented
a numerical technique for radio DM studies, these methods are typically used in the field of
galactic cosmic-ray physics. This field has been shaped around the popular and publicly available
GALPROP code package, which has pioneered many aspects of the accurate modelling of cosmic-
ray propagation. However, the central focus of this package is on galactic cosmic-ray propagation,
and not on extragalactic DM radio studies, which is the central focus of this work. We have
therefore developed an algorithm that implements and extends the core numerical method that is
used in GALPROP, and embedded it into a general code base that contains a comprehensive suite
of DM-related calculations and models.

In this Chapter we have discussed, in detail, all relevant aspects of the developed algorithm, in-
cluding: the variable transformations used, themultidimensional extensions to the Crank-Nicolson
scheme, the specific linear algebraic techniques used to solve the related matrix equations, the
initial and boundary conditions and several important considerations relating to stability, com-
putational performance, convergence and accuracy. We have also produced a set of benchmarks
and tests of the algorithm, to ensure that the results it produces are reliable and accurate. As
part of these tests, we have carried out a simple set of comparisons to the publicly available code
package RX-DMFIT, which utilises the semi-analytical Green’s function solution method. The
overall trend in these comparisons is that there is a general agreement in the results, with certain
notable exceptions. In the centre of small structures like dSphs there can be a significant difference
in the radio emissivity output of both methods, which can in turn lead to an equally significant
difference in the total flux from these objects. As an example, we calculated the expected radio
emissivity from the Reticulum II dSph, and found a relative difference of nearly 75% between the
two methods near the centre of the halo, which led to a difference of 45% in the integrated flux
at the MeerKAT reference frequency of 1280 MHz. In the much larger Coma galaxy cluster, the
relative difference in output from the methods never went above 30%.

The differences in the predicted emissions from each method can be attributed to the mathe-
matical treatment of various modelling parameters. In particular, the substitution of the radial
magnetic field profile with a scalar average results in electrons losing less energy to synchrotron
radiation, which allows the electrons modelled by the Green’s functionmethod to diffuse outwards
from the centre of the halo a relatively further distance than equivalent electrons modelled with
the numerical method. Since this effect leads to a lower electron number density, the total radio
emissivity output from these regions is subsequently reduced. In the case of Reticulum II, the
output emissivity from the Green’s function method behaves similarly to the effect of using a
larger diffusion constant with the numerical method.

We place a large emphasis on the accuracy of the predicted emissions in the centre of DM
halos, as these are the regions where the strongest radio emissions are expected. With the recent
availability of observational data from sophisticated radio interferometers that boast extremely
high resolution and sensitivity (which is the topic of the next Chapter), accurate modelling of
radio emissions from DM on small spatial scales is essential to maximise the scientific potential
of the data. Since we use also make use of new survey data from the MeerKAT telescope in
this work, a solution method that can produce these results in a reliable and efficient way is

CHAPTER 5

Observational Data

A focus point of the theoretical aspects mentioned in the above Chapters is the need for robust
modelling of the DM halo and its emissions, particularly in the dense central regions of the halo.
Correspondingly, the need for high resolution and high sensitivity radio data with which to
compare the models to is just as important. Because of the large wavelengths of the radiation in
radio studies, the spatial resolution achievable with a single radio dish is severely limited by its
physical size (which leads to giant radio dishes that are hundreds of metres wide, like the 305 m
Arecibo 1 or 500 m FAST 2 instruments). In contrast, the recent advent of radio interferometry
observatories has allowed for much higher resolutions and sensitivities to length scales not feasible
with single radio dishes. The capability of these telescopes to image the sky in such detail presents
us with a fortunate opportunity to hunt for signs of DM emission using the modelling tools already
described (a detailed study of radio instruments and their design principles is outside the scope
of this work, so we refer the reader to reference textbooks like Thompson et al. (2017) and Condon
et al. (2016) for more information regarding instrumentation). As such, we make use of recent
observations performed with the MeerKAT interferometer (Jonas et al. 2018) in this project, which
makes it the first analysis of MeerKAT data in the context of DM searches.

The MeerKAT instrument is currently composed of 64 radio dishes arranged in an array with
a dense 1 km-diameter core and a maximum baseline between individual dishes of 7.7 km. It
is located in the Northern Cape in South Africa, and released first-light images on the 16th July
2016 with the full array being completed in 2018. The pertinent observations to this project were
released as part of the first public Data Release (DR1) of the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy
Survey (MGCLS, (Knowles et al. 2022)), released on 11th November 2021. The following Chapter
provides an overview of the data from the MGCLS, how it is accessed and processed, and how
the models are concurrently prepared for a robust and statistical search within the data.

5.1 Data from MGCLS

The MGCLS is a radio survey observation programme performed between June 24th, 2018 and
June 16th, 2019 with MeerKAT’s L-band (900-1670 MHz) receiver. It consists of 115 galaxy clusters,
positioned between 0° and −85° Declination (DEC) and at a median redshift of 0.14. Each target
was observed for 5.5 - 9.5 hours with a minimum of 59 of MeerKAT’s 64 total radio dishes, for a
total observing time of ∼ 1000 hours. A comprehensive list of details for these observations can be
found in Knowles et al. (2022); in this work we focus on the enhanced data products for a small
selection of targets from this survey, which will be described as necessary later in this Chapter.

The full sample of clusters observed with MGCLS is made up of two general groups, the
so-called radio-selected and X-ray-selected clusters. The radio-selected group consists of 41 clusters
that have been observed in previous radio searches, and are likely to contain large diffuse radio
emissions in the form of radio halos or relics. Because of this selection criterion, the radio-selected
clusters also have relatively large masses. Since the total mass of these clusters is dominated by
DM, a large mass leads (in general) to a higher central DM density and thus stronger indirect
emissions. The remaining X-ray selected sample on the other hand is based only on clusters found
in the Meta-Catalogue of X-ray-detected Clusters (MCXC, Piffaretti et al. (2011)). This selection
has no bias to any radio emission properties.

The selection of targets to use for our analysis is based on several factors, foremost of which
is the lack of bright radio halos in the images. Since the expected synchrotron emission from
the DM halo (see Section 3.3.1) is diffuse and relatively faint, a bright source of non-thermal

5.2 Data processing

All the data used in this project is accessed from an online repository through a DOI 3 in the form
of archived FITS files for each source, Stokes parameter and resolution. We consider only the
enhanced data products, which include primary beam corrected images of the central 1.2° × 1.2°
map. The relevant files for our targets have been downloaded from this repository and extracted.
Each file contains multiple planes (datasets), consisting of: the intensity of the surface brightness
at the reference frequency (1280 MHz), the spectral index, the uncertainty associated with each of
these quantities, and the 𝜒2 values of a combined least-squares fit of the data. We note that the
uncertainty planes are measures of the statistical noise in the image, and not of the systematic
effects involved in the processing of the interferometric data. Then, the relevant planes for this
work are the intensity and its associated uncertainty, which are extracted from the cubes for further
processing. The full resolution data for the unpolarised intensity (Stokes-I) images are used in
this work. These all have synthesised beam sizes (represented by the FWHM - Full Width at Half
Maximum) of ∼ 7.5 − 8″ and RMS noise levels of ∼ 3 − 5 𝜇Jy beam−1.

Figure 5.1 is a visual representation of the first plane of each FITS data file, as downloaded
from the repository. These show the image intensities before any regions of interest are extracted
and the compact sources are subtracted. We note in these images the presence of various artefacts
(particularly in RXCJ0225, and around various bright compact emissions). These artefacts result
from the processing of the interferometric data, through various stages of the highly complex
calibration and imaging phases. We make no attempt to categorise these here, and refer the reader
to Knowles et al. (2022) for further details.

5.2.1 Selection of RoI
The enhanced product images are of an area of only 1.2° × 1.2° around the pointing coordinates,
as this is the region within which the applied primary beam corrections are reliable. However, the
good spatial resolution of the images (of the order of the beamwidth FWHM, 7.5 − 8″) means that
they still contain many pixels. This is an important factor for the statistical analysis performed in
this work, which will be discussed further below and in Chapter 6. To illustrate the effects of the
size of the region on the analysis, we consider the source RXCJ0757 as an example. The image of
this target contains ∼ 12×106 pixels in the 1.2°×1.2° region, which is a huge amount of image data.
However, since DM searches find the most benefit from observations in the high-density inner
regions of halos (where the strongest emission is expected), the pixels in the outer edges of the
image are less useful than those in the centre. Therefore, we crop each target’s image to a smaller
region that is focused on the centre of the DM halo, usually within a square of size 2.5′ × 2.5′. For
RXCJ0757, this results in a 120 × 120 pixel image, for a total number of 14.4 × 103 pixels. Whether
this size is reasonable or even optimal for each source depends on several factors, described below.

Firstly, there is an issue of correlation between individual pixels in any radio flux density image.
This is due to the nature of radio telescope observations, which have non-negligible beamwidths
within which the radiation is detected. This correlation can be complex to account for in general,
involving calculations of matrices that describe the covariance between each pixel. In this project,
following Regis et al. (2015b) and Regis et al. (2021), we make the approximation that all the
pixels within a single beamwidth (of the synthesised beam) are fully correlated with each other,
while those outside of the beamwidth are completely uncorrelated. This approximation will be
described quantitatively in Chapter 6. The effect of correlated pixels, and the above approximation,
on the size of the image is that it reduces the effective number of pixels (resolution elements)
considered statistically independent, which is a requirement of the statistical analysis we adopt.
Therefore, in all cases we consider the number of resolution elements in an image to be the total
number of distinct beamwidths, i.e. the total number of pixels divided by the number of pixels in
a single beamwidth. This calculation is then performed for each image. For the reduced image
size of 2.5′ × 2.5′ for RXCJ0757 mentioned above, the approximation leads to ∼ 377 resolution
elements, with 38 pixels per beamwidth.

important for the statistical analysis performed on each image. On one hand, smaller regions
will lead to better constraints on DM parameters, as they will more directly probe the inner, high-
density region of the DM halo. However, smaller regions also contain fewer data points, too few
of which results in unreliable statistics. We implement this consideration as a soft lower-limit on
the size of the image – keeping the number of resolution elements large enough for us to reliably
use the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and Wilks’ Theorem (WT) (collectively referred to as the
Statistical Tests or ST) in the analysis. On the other hand, larger regions have enough data points
with which to reliably do any statistical analysis. They, however, produce less stringent constraints
on the DM halo emissions, as the faint outer regions of the halo are lost in the data and do not
contribute significantly to the overall search.

When finding a RoI that satisfies the above considerations, one also needs to account for
any pixels that are deemed unusable. After the source-subtraction procedure (described in the
following Section), there may be some pixels that have negative values that are not a feature of the
interferometric data itself, but rather as artefacts resulting from extremely bright point sources.
Following the analysis performed in Regis et al. (2021), we mask any pixels that have an absolute
value that is larger than 3 times the total uncertainty of the data. In the majority of the cases
investigated here, we find that this masking criterion has no impact on the results, with most RoI’s
containing no pixels that meet the condition. In some clusters there are a non-zero number of
pixels that are masked, however the impact on the results is negligible.

An alternative method to choose the RoI’s of the images is to dynamically scale the size of the
RoI according to some physical property associated with the target cluster, instead of setting a
constant angular size of say, 2.5′ × 2.5′. In Table 5.2 we show one example of this, with RoI’s found
using the scale radius of the DM halo as the characteristic angular size. In these cases, the physical
size of the cluster would determine the amount of data that enters into the analysis. Since the
resolution of the telescope is finite however, this could cause the RoI’s of some clusters to be either
too large or too small to be optimal in regard to the point made about the number of available
resolution elements made above. We have therefore investigated two strategies for choosing a RoI
in this thesis: one using a constant angular size of 2.5′ × 2.5′, and one using a dynamic RoI based
on half the value of the scale radius of the DM halo (equivalent to half the values in Table 5.2).
This choice should represent a reasonable physical scale in most modelling scenarios, although
choices based on other physical characteristics may be made. In each case however, we stress that
the RoI should necessarily have more than 50 resolution elements in order for the results to be
considered valid. The choice of RoI, and its impact on the final results of the analysis, will be
discussed further in Chapter 6.

The surface brightness images obtained through the MGCLS data repository still contain compact
point sources and extended emissions, resulting from bright radio galaxies or extended structures
like jets. As mentioned in the beginning of this Chapter, these elements hamper the search for DM
signatures in the image, as the expected synchrotron emissions from DM are faint and diffuse. We

Once the data images from the MGCLS have been processed according to the above methods, the

halo environment (corresponding to each target in Table 5.1) are shown in Table 5.3. Additionally,
the following modelling configurations, which have been discussed in detail in previous Chapters,
are used in each simulation:

• WIMP masses in the range 10 - 1000 GeV

• Annihilation channels in the set (𝑏𝑏, 𝜇−𝜇+, 𝜏−𝜏+, 2HDM+S)

• Two DM halo density profiles, corresponding to the gNFW profile with 𝛼 = 1 and 𝛼 = 0.5

• Use of the full form of Equation (3.19) (i.e. both diffusion and energy loss effects are always

• Kolmogorov-type turbulence with a diffusion coefficient of 𝐷0 = 3.1 × 1028 cm2 s

• Use of the OS solution method

5.3.1 Position of DM halo centre
The pointing coordinates used in the MeerKAT observations of the cluster sample have been given
in Table 5.1. These values do not necessarily point to the centre of mass of the cluster though,
where the centre of the DM halo should be located. The exact location of this central coordinate
can be determined in several ways: via lensing measurements, chosen as the peak brightness value
in X-ray observations of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) gas, or as the central coordinates of the
Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) in optical observations. However, as discussed at length in Seppi
et al. (2023), these independent measures of the cluster centre may be offset from each other, and
are expected to be offset for clusters that are not dynamically relaxed (due to late-time formation or
recent merger activity). The results of Seppi et al. (2023) show that the offset between the BCG and
the peak of the X-ray emissions, in a sample of galaxy clusters observed by the eROSITA telescope,
can be tens or hundreds of kpc. Since this offset can also be affected bymergers and AGN feedback,
the determination of the true centre of a cluster is a complicated endeavour that requires precise
observations and dedicated multi-wavelength studies, complemented by large-scale simulations
of the DM halo.

In the case of cool-core clusters – or more specifically, those which have dynamically relaxed
cores – we can be rather certain that either commonly-used measure, the X-ray brightness peak
or the BCG, is a good estimate for the centre of the DM halo. Unfortunately, when there is an
offset in these measures as described above, the high-resolution nature of the MeerKAT images
causes the RoI around these points to be entirely different (we note that in the lucky event that
neither region has artefacts or large extended emissions, there could be a negligible effect on the
final results, however this would have to be investigated on a case-by-case basis). Further, the
RoI’s around the MGCLS pointing coordinates are often completely distinct from these central
coordinate estimates, an example of which is shown for the Abell 4038 cluster in Figure 5.5. In
this case, the images display extremely different behaviour in the two regions, with one (at the
location of the peak X-ray brightness) showing bright extended emissions throughout the region,
while the other displays much a much fainter overall surface brightness. Such a large discrepancy
in the RoI’s would quite clearly lead to large differences in the final results (especially given
the imperfect nature of the current implementation of our source-subtraction procedure). This
example illustrates the general difficulty in selecting a location for the centre of the DM halo in
high-resolution images of galaxy clusters.

5.3.2 Model reprojection
The generated DM emission model, with proper central sky coordinates, is now mapped onto a
FITS image. This mapping procedure transforms the radial surface brightness values (calculated
with Equation (3.50)) into a two-dimensional space under the assumption of spherical symmetry.
The target pixel density of the output image can be set manually, and is chosen to be at least better
than the one found in the MGCLS images, i.e. ∼ 1″ per pixel. Due to the high resolution of these
images, the full model (which is calculated up to the diffusion radius of the halo) contains a huge
amount of data which is mostly made up of the outer regions of the halo. Since these regions are
useless in the analysis, we discard them and keep only pixels within a ‘cut-off’ radius from the
halo centre that is chosen to encapsulate each RoI. An example of an image generated in this way
is shown in Figure 5.6a, which shows a model calculated for 100 GeV mass WIMPs in an NFW-like
halo that is centred on the coordinates for the Abell 4038 cluster.

The form of the model in Figure 5.6a, while being a complete model of the DM emission, is
not yet ready for a full statistical comparison to the MGCLS data. The final step in this process
is to ensure that every pixel in the model image corresponds exactly to its counterpart in the
MGLCS image, including the pixel sizes and locations (in sky coordinates) and physical units.

CHAPTER 6

Dark Matter Hunting

In the previous Chapters, we described both the theoretical modelling of the expected DM
signal, and the processing of the observational data from various astronomical targets. In this
Chapter, we combine the results of each of these (generally referred to from here as just the model
and data respectively) in a robust statistical analysis that searches for any DM emissions in each
data image. The primary outcome of this analysis is a set of annihilation cross-section magnitudes,
calculated over a range of DM particle masses, that are excluded by non-detection of emission in
the data. These ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 curves are the standard way of constraining the DM parameter space in
DM indirect detection studies, and were discussed in terms of the current state of the literature in
Chapter 2 (seen in Figures 2.4 and 2.6). The following Sections provide an outline of the relevant
theoretical aspects involved in the statistical analysis, demonstrate how it is performed, and then
present the main results of the analysis with a concluding discussion.

6.1 Statistical framework
To directly compare the data to the models, we adopt a standard framework for hypothesis testing
that includes the use of 𝜒2 statistics and likelihood ratio tests. The methodology roughly follows
the one used in Regis et al. (2015b, sec. 5) and Regis et al. (2021, sec. 4) for the same purpose,
which is also discussed in a general context in Wall et al. (2003, ch. 6). The details of the specific
implementation used here will be described as follows.

6.1.1 Likelihood ratio tests
Firstly, we define the likelihood function ℒ𝑖, which defines the probability of the obtained data
given a certain set of model parameters (represented by the subscript 𝑖). In our analysis, since
the annihilation cross-section is treated as a free parameter, we use a simple range of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ values
to define each model while keeping all other modelling parameters constant. By comparing the
likelihoods of these models, we then find a value of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ that either best explains the data, or
conforms to some statistical constraint. One standard way to perform this comparison is through
a likelihood-ratio-test (LRT), which produces a test statistic 𝜆 as follows:

𝜆 = −2 log [ℒ𝑖/ℒmax] , (6.1)

where the likelihood function ℒmax is the maximum over any model likelihood ℒ𝑖. The form of
the ratio test in Equation (6.1) (i.e. −2 times the logarithm of the likelihood ratio) is written so as
to conform to Wilks’ Theorem (Wilks 1938; Silvey 1991, ch. 7), which states that:

Theorem 6.1 (Wilks’ Theorem) For a sample size 𝑛 that uniformly approaches ∞, and a parameter
spaceΘwhich has a subset Θ0 associated with the null hypothesis𝐻0, then, if𝐻0 is satisfied, the distribution
of 𝜆 = −2 log(Λ), where Λ is the ratio of likelihoods defined over Θ and Θ0, is, up to terms of order 1/√𝑛,
𝜒2-distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in dimensionality of Θ and Θ0.

One of the requirements of Wilks’ Theorem is that the null hypothesis be true. In our analysis,
the null hypothesis represents the case where no DM emission at all is present in the data images,
which is set by the model ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ = 0 (with all alternative models having some non-zero value of
⟨𝜎𝑣⟩). In Regis et al. (2015b), a test for the detection of non-zero DM signals in six Local Group
dSphs is performed by calculating a LRT with the null hypothesis, similarly to Equation (6.1), i.e.

𝜆 = −2 log [ℒ0/ℒmax] . (6.2)

in many types of statistical analyses. In a general form, it can be stated as:

Theorem 6.2 (Central Limit Theorem) Given a sample of 𝑛 random, independent and identically-

6.3 Discussion
In this Section we outline some of the general trends that are observed in the exclusion curves
presented above, and then compare the results to relevant works in the literature. Firstly, we note
that the strength of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits, typically measured by how much of the parameter space below
the expected thermal relic value is probed by the results, can often be explained qualitatively in
terms of the DM modelling parameters and morphology of the image data. For example, we see
significant changes in the ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits when different DM halo density profiles are used. This is
expected behaviour, as higher DM densities leads to more annihilations in the same volume and
thus a larger number of electrons which are able to radiate synchrotron emission. Since the two
profiles examined here, the standard NFW profile and the gNFW profile with an index of 𝛼 = 0.5,
have contrasting DM density at the centre of the halo (see Figure 3.3), the higher relative central
density of the NFWprofile results in universally stronger limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩. This effect is made clear in
Figure 6.7, which compares the results from using both profiles in terms of individual targets and
annihilation channels. We see that RXCJ0225, RXCJ0600 and RXCJ0757 are significantly affected,
whereas A133 and A4038 are more robust to this change. While A133 and A4038 both have slightly
more massive halos than the other targets, they also noticeably have bright extended emissions in
the centre of their data images (caused by bright radio galaxies or extended structures like jets,
see for example Figure 5.5), which are missing in the other targets. These bright non-DM-related
emissions (and the resulting source-subtraction procedure) could be ‘covering’ the central regions
where the difference between the profiles is most stark, thus leaving A133 and A4038 less impacted
by changes to the central density profile.

Although the results produced from all clusters in the sample are relatively clustered, the
two that produce the most stringent upper limits on the annihilation cross-section are A4038 and
RXCJ0600, especially in the case of more shallowly-cusped halo profiles. Both of these clusters
probe a significant portion of the parameter space below the thermal relic cross-section, for any
halo profile index. In the case of RXCJ0600, almost the entire mass range would be ruled out for
annihilation in the 𝑏𝑏 channel and an NFW halo, and up to ∼ 200GeV for a gNFW halo. Given that
themodelling parameters of the DMhalo in RXCJ0225 are relativelymodest compared to the rest of
the sample, we attribute these stringent results to the observational data, which is both the faintest
and most devoid of bright compact sources of the MGCLS images sampled here. In contrast, the
RoI of A4038’s data image has a relatively large amount of bright source emission, however it
also has the most massive halo, strongest magnetic field normalisation, and largest thermal gas
population density of the cluster sample, factors which all contribute to stronger model emissions.
Specifically, the synchrotron energy loss rate of the propagating electrons (which is the dominant
effect at relevant energies, see Figure 3.4) depends on the square of the magnetic field strength,
and the emitted synchrotron power depends directly on the magnetic field strength. While the
explicit effect of the thermal gas population on the output synchrotron emission is not trivial, it
seems that the higher magnetic field strength and mass of A4038 are sufficient to enable such
strong ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits.

On the other hand, the prize for the weakest limits goes to A133 with an NFW halo, and is
shared between RXCJ0225 and RXCJ0757 with gNFW halos. This could again be explained by the
discussion given above, as RXCJ0225 actually produces comparatively strong limits with an NFW
halo, but its substantial depdendance on the shape of the density profile almost encompasses
the differences observed in all other targets. We also note that the RXCJ0225 data has the most
egregious presence of non-physical artefacts due to the interferometric image processing (see
Figure 5.1), although theworst regions in the full mapwere ultimately avoided in the final 2.5′×2.5′

RoI.
The characteristics of each annihilation channel in the results shown here agree well with the

literature. These channels are sometimes separated into so-called hard or soft channels (Gaskins
2016), corresponding to the 𝜇−𝜇+, 𝜏−𝜏+ (hard) and 𝑏𝑏 (soft) channels shown here. This distinc-
tion can clearly be seen in Figure 3.1, with the generally similar spectral behaviour of the quarks
and bosons being quite different to that of the leptons. This is precisely the reason only a small
subset of possible channels are used in the calculations and then considered as representative
of other channels. In the results presented above the leptonic channels (i.e. 𝜏−𝜏+ and 𝜇−𝜇+)

result in much steeper ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 curves than the softer quark channel, with regions below
∼ 60 − 70GeV being dominated by the 𝜇−𝜇+ channel, and above by the 𝑏𝑏 channel. This particular
dividing value depends on the particle interactions and decay pathways that produce the final
state electrons in each channel, which is likely similar for the channels studied here. Compared to
these three channels, the limits from the 2HDM+S model, with spin 0 𝜒’s annihilating through the
channel 𝜒𝜒 → 𝑆 → 𝑒+,−, are relatively weak (although they can be reconciled with predictions for
observations with MeerKAT, see following Section). As low mass WIMPs are being increasingly
constrained with modern observations (see Regis et al. (2021) for example), the most promising
avenue for constraining large WIMP masses thus seems to be through the quark channels.

In Figure 6.8, we draw comparison between results that are found using different RoI’s. In
Figure 6.8a we have used a constant RoI size of 2.5′ × 2.5′ in all clusters, whereas a dynamic RoI
calculated based on half of the scale radius of the DM halo in each cluster was used in Figure 6.8b,
using values presented in Table 5.2. The motivations for using either of these two schemes were
discussed in Chapter 5, and we discuss briefly how the results are affected by these choices here.
Between the results, we observe marginal changes in the example case of annihilation through
the 𝑏𝑏 channel and NFW profile. Because of the nature of this comparison, the limits produced
for each cluster target might increase or decrease based on the physical size and distance of the
cluster. Further, each data image contains a unique morphology that would manifest in different
ways when the RoI is increased or decreased from the constant value of 2.5′ × 2.5′, especially in
the target images that have bright extended emission associated with the BCG. The total average
relative differences (normalised relative to the larger values) between the results using each RoI,
are: 6.4%, 1.4%, 43.3%, 27.2% and 10.4% for the A133, A4038, RXCJ0225, RXCJ0600 and RXCJ0757
clusters, respectively. However, we note that the number of resolution elements available in the
dynamic RoI of the RXCJ0225 cluster was only 21, which is well short of the 50 elements that
we consider to be required for the statistical analysis to be valid. All other clusters had ≥ 100
resolution elements, and can thus be considered statistically valid. We also note that although
this dataset was chosen to be displayed, it represents an instructive example for other results; as
the selection of the RoI only changes the region of the data image that is analysed, changes in
modelling parameters (such as halo profile or annihilation channel) produce results that exhibit
identical behaviour. The conclusion we draw from this comparison is that the use of either scheme,
a static or dynamic determination of the RoI, is less impactful to the results when compared to
some other sources of uncertainty (like halo profile index or magnetic field normalisation). It
could thus be chosen optimally for each target, with the only requirement being that the number of
resolution elements remains statistically valid in all cases. Since the resolution of the model images
can be adjusted freely (with some inevitable uncertainty in the description of the innermost radii
of the halo density profile, see Section 3.1.2), higher resolution data in the future could further
improve the viability of smaller RoI’s, providing stronger ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits.

We observe in Figure 6.9 that the upper limits on the annihilation cross-section are more
sensitive to changes in the magnetic field normalisation strength at lower values of 𝐵0, with less
impact between larger values. As discussed in Chapters 3 and 5, a precise determination of this
value from empirical sources is difficult, which is the reason we have chosen the conservative
estimates of 5 𝜇G and 8 𝜇G for dynamically disturbed (NCC) and dynamically relaxed (CC)
clusters, respectively. Studies of magnetic fields in galaxy clusters (Govoni et al. 2006; Guidetti
et al. 2008; Govoni et al. 2017; Stuardi et al. 2021; Osinga et al. 2022) indicate central magnetic field
strengths (corresponding to the normalisation value of our magnetic field profiles) of larger than
∼ 2 𝜇G, but in extreme cases this rises to 30 𝜇G (Govoni et al. 2004). As with the comparison
between RoI’s, the general behaviour of the upper limits on the cross-section shown in Figure 6.9
translates to other modelling configurations and targets, and the range in limits shown therein
should thus provide a reasonable estimate of the sensitivity of the results to various possible
magnetic field normalisations.

Comparisons to related work
With observations from the full SKA project just on the horizon, a number of studies have predicted
strong prospects for using the SKA or its pathfinders for radio-based DM indirect detection (Co-
lafrancesco et al. 2015a; Colafrancesco et al. 2015b; Beck et al. 2017; Storm et al. 2017; Beck 2019b;

Chen et al. 2021), and indeed the use of the ASKAP instrument has already produced some of
the strongest limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ of any wavelength in the literature (Regis et al. 2021). However, as
discussed before in this thesis, there has been relatively little modern interest in the use of galaxy
cluster search targets, with much attention going to the satellite dSph galaxies of the Milky Way.
Some studies have been performed that test specific models of DM, or investigate the general
morphology of the radio emissions from galaxy clusters (for example in Colafrancesco et al. (2006),
Colafrancesco et al. (2011), Marchegiani et al. (2018), Marchegiani et al. (2019), and Chan et al.
(2020)), but the most direct comparisons to the literature for this work come from studies that
produce ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 exclusion curves, as we have above. Of these works, we find that the results
presented here are almost always more constraining.

In Kiew et al. (2017), the authors studied the predicted DM-induced radio emission from six
galaxy cluster targets, for a very similar range of modelling parameters as those considered here.
The halos were modelled with NFW density profiles and 𝑏𝑏 and 𝜇−𝜇+ channels (the most extreme
channels in our results as well, excluding the 2HDM+Smodel), with a very similar set of magnetic
field and gas density models. However, they use the Green’s function solution method for the
diffusion-loss equation (as described in Section 4.1), a somewhat less sophisticated exclusion
framework, and a set of galaxy cluster targets (using a variety of radio flux observations mostly
at 1.4 GHz) that has no overlap with the one used here. The limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ can be seen in figure
3 of Kiew et al. (2017). These limits are improved by all of our NFW results, and in the case of
our best results (RXCJ0600) the limits are strengthened by more than an order of magnitude.
This improvement can be generally attributed to the quality and general faintness of the radio
data, as the higher resolution of MeerKAT allows the crucial inner regions of the halo to be more
accurately probed with surface brightness measurements.

The above comparison is very similar for the work of Storm et al. (2013), which also notably
used the DMFIT software package for solutions to the diffusion-loss equation, and considered
magnetic field profiles that are weighted by the halo density profile. Again, the results presented
in this thesis significantly strengthen the ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits for compatible cases (i.e. excluding the
estimated effects of substructure) (Storm et al. 2013, figs. 3-6), which can be explained with similar
reasoning as before. A more recent study by the same authors, Storm et al. (2017), investigated the
potential indirect detection capabilities of the (at the time of publication) planned radio surveys
of LOFAR (van Haarlem et al. 2013), ASKAP (Johnston et al. 2008) and APERTIF (Oosterloo
et al. 2009) projects for generic galaxy cluster models at 1.4 GHz. The main projections for these
observations are seen in figure 3 of Storm et al. (2017). Compared to the results shown here, there
is a small but distinct strengthening of the limits in all cases, with larger differences for the ASKAP
and APERTIF projections.

The final set of direct comparisons can be drawn from our own work in Beck et al. (2023a),
which presents a set of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits obtained with radio data from the Coma and Ophiuchus galaxy
clusters. This study uses a wide range of modelling parameters, and also employs the operator
splitting method developed in this thesis (Chapter 4). When compared to the unaltered radio data
results from both clusters, the limits presented in this thesis are significantly stronger (especially
in the case of Ophiuchus, due to the less concentrated halo). However, the limits found using
radio data that was extrapolated to smaller inner radii are much stronger, and probe similar
WIMP masses and cross-sections as the best results shown here. The extrapolation of the data
was motivated by the enhanced ability of high-resolution interferometers to probe these regions
(which was previously unavailable to single-dish radio instruments), and the lack of evidence to
suggest that there is any significant change in behaviour of the diffuse radio emission at smaller
radii in these targets. The most limiting results in Beck et al. (2023a) are also comparable to those
found in Regis et al. (2021), which uses radio data of the Large Magellanic Cloud from the other
SKA pathfinder, ASKAP. While the search target used in that study was not a galaxy cluster, it is
still a notable set of results given how strong the constraints are (visible in figures 4 and 6) and
since the analysis of the data is performed in a very similar way to the one used in this thesis.
These comparisons, coupled with the ones discussed above, suggest that limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ found
using a combination of MeerKAT data and accurate modelling techniques can live up to the high
expectations created by early work in this field.

We also make a brief comparison to work done for the 2HDM+S DM model, as all the previous
points apply only to the usual SM channels. As this particular model is relatively new in the

Finally, we comment briefly on the status of these results compared to other multi-messenger
indirect detection studies in the literature. Our most constraining target case, that of RXCJ0600
with an NFW halo, rules out ≲ 800GeV WIMPs when annihilating through the 𝑏𝑏 channel. This
limit falls within the uncertainty region shown for the same channel in Regis et al. (2021, fig.
4), though is slightly above the most optimistic bound. Given that the limits presented therein
are the most constraining indirect detection limits on WIMPs to date, the results shown here
suggest that the approach taken in this work contains significant value to the field of radio-based
indirect detection. The results for RXCJ0600 are also more constraining than any results found
with gamma-rays, neutrinos or anti-protons thus far (see Figure 2.4 and cited references), and
notably rule out the proposed best-fit WIMP model associated with the Galactic Centre excess
measurements (Cholis et al. 2022). Outside our best case, the clusters A4038 and RXCJ0225
produce limits that are comparable with the strongest results from gamma-ray observations (Hoof
et al. 2020; Armand et al. 2021), with all other cases presented here (which correspond to more
shallow DM halo profiles or weaker magnetic field normalisations) being less stringent than
the current leading-edge results. Notably, many of our results rule out WIMPs with masses
below GeV, and almost all exclude those below 10 GeV. Since this is the mass range that is most
suited for collider-based detection schemes among the alternative search techniques (see ATLAS
Collaboration (2022) and Figure 2.2), improved results from future collider experiments should
provide a complementary view on the results presented here.
