Conclusion

This thesis provides a comprehensive study of state-of-the-art radio-based indirect DM de-
tection searches. It includes detailed descriptions of the necessary physical modelling scenarios,
a rigorous presentation of a newly-developed algorithm to solve the diffusion-loss equation, a
showcase of observational data from the MeerKAT telescope, and a statistical search for DM
signals within radio images. The motivation for this work was based on one of the most pressing
open problems in modern physics, the nature of DM, and the recent emergence of sophisticated
radio telescopes that are able to image the sky in unprecedented detail and thus effectively hunt
for faint signatures of DM. The beginning of this thesis outlined some of the background and
historical aspects of astrophysical DM, the existence of which is suggested from strong observa-
tional evidence and motivated by theoretical extensions to the SM. A resolution to both of these
points could come from generic WIMPs, weakly-interacting particles that have the potential to
create observable signals through self-annihilation processes. The particular process we have
focused on in this work is the emission of synchrotron radiation in the radio band, which occurs
when electrons and positrons that are produced by WIMP annihilations gyrate around magnetic
fields. When there is a sufficient amount of DM, usually in the form of giant halos that encompass
compact astrophysical structures like galaxies or galaxy clusters, this synchrotron emission should
be visible to us as a region of diffuse radio emission. The premise of this work is thus to search for
these emissions by modelling all the necessary physical processes and comparing the predicted
emission to observational data of the region.

A large emphasis has been placed on the accuracy of the calculations of the expected DM-
induced synchrotron emission, as accurate models are needed when using modern, high-quality
radio data. For the modelling of DM parameters, which includes the energy spectra of annihilation
channels and the density profile of the halo, we have used the most up-to-date modelling scenarios
that are available in the literature. We obtained the spectra for all SM annihilation channels
from the most recent version of the PPPC4DMID results (Cirelli et al. 2011) (which also contain
electroweak corrections (Ciafaloni et al. 2011)), and used the spectra in Beck et al. (2023b) for the
annihilation channel in the 2HDM+S model. We have then used two halo density profiles, the
standard NFW profile and a generalised version of the NFW with a more shallow central cusp, in
all sets of results. Although the NFW profile provides excellent overall fits to the results of large
𝑁-body simulations, the small-scale regions around the centres of halos are still not well resolved
by these simulations. Given the uncertainty in the central regions and the lack of precise halo
modelling data in the literature for many galaxy cluster targets, the use of the two considered
profiles should encompass any variation in form of the density profile in these objects. We reiterate
that the density in these central regions is a salient factor in modern DM searches, as the ability
for high-resolution data to spatially resolve and isolate the strong synchrotron emissions they
produce can have a significant impact on the final constraints found, particularly in the case of
faint radio data.

The other modelling aspect we focused on in this thesis is the solution to the diffusion-loss
equation, which is a truncated form of the general cosmic-ray propagation equation that encapsu-
lates the relevant effects of diffusion and energy-loss. The equilibrium solution to this equation is
necessary for the calculation of the expected synchrotron emission from a population of electrons,
however the nature of being a second-order partial differential equation means it requires a set of
non-trivial mathematical techniques to solve. A common approach to finding these solutions in
the literature has been a semi-analytical method that makes use of Green’s functions to find the
equilibrium solution directly. This approach has two significant drawbacks for general use: it can
be computationally expensive, and it requires approximations about the spatial distribution of any
involved physical quantities (like the magnetic field or thermal gas density). In this thesis we have
therefore presented, in rigorous detail, a numerical solution method that has been developed with

Page 89 of 104



7. Conclusion M. Sarkis, PhD Thesis

the primary purpose of addressing these two drawbacks, and solving the diffusion-loss equation
in a computationally performant and accurate way. The method is based on the Crank-Nicolson
finite-differencing scheme (generalised to multiple dimensions with an operator-splitting tech-
nique) that calculates the equilibrium solution iteratively. The implementation of the algorithm
used in the method draws inspiration from the GALPROP package (Strong et al. 1998), which is
a well-developed publicly-availalble software package used extensively in the field of galactic
cosmic-ray physics.

To test the solution method developed in this project, we have provided a set of comparisons
between the results of our code and RX-DMFIT (McDaniel et al. 2017), which is another publicly-
available software package that uses a semi-analytical method to solve the diffusion-loss equation.
The package has been used in the literature to compute the expected synchrotron emissions from
DM halos, and in the results presented here we compare the output DM-induced radio emissivity
and integrated flux for a model galaxy cluster and dSph galaxy. We found general agreement
between the output of each code, with some notable exceptions. Principle among these was a
significant difference in the emissivity function at small radii within the dSph halo, with our code
leading to a maximum of 75% more emission in this region. The difference was attributed to the
mathematical treatment of the physical quantities involved, and in particular the substitution
of the full magnetic field profile with a scalar average. This approximation leads to electrons
at the centre of a DM halo losing relatively less energy to synchrotron radiation, which allows
them to diffuse further through the halo. This effect reduces the electron number density in
the inner regions of the halo, and thus also reduces the total output emission from this region.
Since the high-density central region of a halo is of such importance in searches for DM-related
emission, this lack of spatial accuracy can represent a major hindrance when using these models
in conjunction with high-resolution observational data.

Several studies have shown that the SKA and its precursor instruments, with their high
sensitivity and spatial resolution, are well-suited to produce novel DM search results, and the
first studies to utilise ASKAP and MeerKAT data have already placed stringent constraints on the
DM parameter space. In this work, we selected five nearby galaxy clusters, observed as part of
the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey programme (Knowles et al. 2022), to act as a set of
observation targets within which to hunt for radio signals of DM. These galaxy clusters are all
at a low redshift (𝑧 ≤ 0.06) and were chosen based on several criteria related to their potential
effectiveness in DM searches, such as the overall quality of the data, the amount of bright compact
emission present in the image, and the availability of modelling parameters in the literature. The
data images for the chosen targets were subject to a number of processing techniques to prepare
them for a statistical DM signal search, which included the selection of an optimal region around
the centre of the cluster (to leverage the strong emissions in these regions) and the removal of
any compact emission in a source-subtraction process (as these sources hide the relatively faint
diffuse synchrotron emission from DM). These processed images were compared to the computed
model emissions from the DM halos in each target, which were mapped onto two-dimensional
FITS images and reprojected onto the same coordinate system as the data, ensuring that each pixel
in the model image corresponded to the exact sky location of the data image.

The comparison betweenmodel and data images then followed a standard statistical framework,
using a likelihood ratio test, that resulted in a set of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 exclusion curves calculated at
a confidence level of 95%. Of the targets considered here, the galaxy cluster RXCJ0600.8-535
produced the strongest constraints on the cross-section ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩, regardless of the density profile
used to model the DM halo. This was primarily due to the relative faintness of the region in the
radio data provided by the MGCLS, which allows for more penetrative testing of the DM model
emissions. When using an NFW density profile, there is at least partial coverage of the thermal
relic cross-section limit from all targets, with especially strong constraints on lower mass WIMPs.
When the gNFW profile is used the resulting constraints are (expectedly) weaker, particularly
for targets with faint radio data in the region of interest, although in some cases this modelling
scenario still produces constraints on low-mass WIMP models.

Our results also included a variety of representative annihilation channels that are well-studied
in the literature, like quark or leptonic channels, as well as the comparatively unexplored 2HDM+S
model. The leptonic channels (𝜇−𝜇+ especially) produce steep ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 curves, providing
strong constraints on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ at low masses, whereas the quark channel (𝑏𝑏) has a flatter curve, but

7. Conclusion M. Sarkis, PhD Thesis

probes the thermal relic cross-section at larger masses. The limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ presented here are
almost always more constraining than current results (that use corresponding source targets and
modelling scenarios) in the literature. The results from the 2HDM+S channel produce relatively
weaker constraints than the SM channels, but are in general comparable to the limits found for
this model in the literature. Our exclusion curves agree with the trend in modern radio-based
DM indirect studies that rule out low-mass WIMPs, requiring remaining viable models to have
relatively higher masses, of hundreds of GeV.

Given that most of the galaxy clusters used as search targets in this work have not been used in
indirect detection studies before, these results represent a strong opening move for DM searches
in galaxy clusters with MeerKAT data. Future work in this field, which could include directed
observations from MeerKAT (rather than the survey observations used here), improved source
subtraction procedures, or more advanced analysis techniques (like interferometric data-stacking
or baseline tapering), promises to deliver even better results in the ongoing search for the nature
of DM. With observations from the full SKA on the horizon, we can also look forward to a future
with completely ruled out parameter spaces, or even the detection of a so far elusive DM signal.

”Ihr wollt meinen Schatz? Den könnt ihr haben!
Sucht ihn doch! Irgendwo hab ich den größten

Schatz der Welt versteckt!” - Gol D. Roger





Abstract

Weakly-Interacting-Massive-Particles (WIMP) provide a possible solution to the unanswered
question of the underlying nature of dark matter in the universe. In this thesis, we explore the
WIMP paradigm with different theoretical frameworks in order to get a deeper understanding
of dark matter observables, which can be tested in current and future experiments.

In order to gain further insight into the impact of experimental constraints on parameter
scans and their interplay with each other, we investigate the complex Two-Higgs Doublet
model. Here, we quantify the allowed CP-violation in the fermionic couplings to the Standard
Model-like Higgs boson. To improve our scanning procedure, we furthermore employ modern
machine learning algorithms.

Exploring the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model can
become a tedious task, due to the large number of parameters in the model. We therefore
develop the tool NMSSMScanner, which allows us to explore the parameter space in a convenient
way. As a proof-of-concept, we maximize the production cross section of a resonant non-
Standard Model-like Higgs boson decaying into various final states. Furthermore, we calculate
the dark matter relic density and direct detection cross section in this model to further
constrain the available parameter space with experimental data. To incorporate these features
into our toolchain, the dark matter code RelExt is extended by an implementation of the
calculation of the relic abundance and the direct detection cross section in this theoretical
framework.

In addition, we calculate the dark matter relic density at next-to-leading order including
electroweak and QCD corrections in the framework of the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model. We argue that the inclusion of higher-order calculations is important in
understanding the parameter space in dark matter models. This work is used as a proof-of-
concept, in order to automate the next-to-leading order relic density calculation in RelExt

for arbitrary models in future works.

Zusammenfassung

Schwach wechselwirkende massive Teilchen (engl. weakly interacting massive particles (WIMP))
können eine mögliche Antwort auf die Frage nach der zugrunde liegenden Natur von dunkler
Materie darstellen. In dieser Arbeit werden wir das sogenannte WIMP-Paradigma in ver-
schiedenen theoretischen Modellen untersuchen, um ein tieferes Verständnis der Observablen
des dunklen Materieteilchens zu gewinnen. Diese können in gegenwärtigen und zukünftigen
Experimenten getestet werden.

Um weiterführende Einblicke in die Auswirkungen experimenteller Einschränkungen auf Scans
im Parameterbereich und das Zusammenspiel der Parameter zu erhalten, werden wir das kom-
plexe Zwei-Higgs-Dublett-Modell untersuchen. Hierbei werden wir die theoretisch erlaubte
Ladungs- und Paritätsverletzung in den fermionischen Kopplungen zum Standardmodell-
Higgsteilchen quantifizieren. Dabei werden wir moderne Machine-Learning-Algorithmen zur
Verbesserung unserer Scanverfahren einsetzen.

Die Untersuchung des nichtminimalen supersymmetrischen Standardmodells kann aufgrund
der großen Anzahl an Parametern zu einer mühsamen Aufgabe werden. Wir entwickeln
deshalb ein Tool, mit dem man den Parameterraum bequem untersuchen kann. Als Proof-of-
Concept wird der Wirkungsquerschnitt für die resonante Produktion eines nicht im Standard-
modell enthaltenden Higgsbosons maximiert, welches in verschiedene Endzustände zerfällt.



viii

Des Weiteren berechnen wir in diesem Modell die Reliktdichte der dunklen Materie sowie
den Wirkungsquerschnitt für den direkten Nachweis von dunklen Materieteilchen in Streuex-
perimenten. Hierfür wird der Code RelExt erweitert, indem die Berechnung der Reliktdichte
und des Wirkungsquerschnittes für die dunkle-Materie-Streuung an Nukleonen implementiert
wird.

Darüber hinaus wird die Reliktdichte im Kontext der komplexen Singulett-Erweiterung des
Standardmodells auf nächsthöherer Ordnung berechnet. Dabei wird gezeigt, dass die Hinzu-
nahme von Korrekturen höherer Ordnung wichtig ist, um den Parameterbereich von Dunkle-
Materie-Modellen besser zu verstehen. Diese Arbeit wird als Proof-of-Concept dienen, um
in zukünftigen Arbeiten die Berechnung der Reliktdichte auf nächsthöherer Ordnung für be-
liebige Modelle in RelExt zu automatisieren.

CHAPTER 1

Introduction

The success story the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics has been underlined by the
discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 by the ATLAS [1] and CMS [2] collaborations at the Large
Hadron Collider (LHC). However, even though the SM is able to explain many phenomena,
there are questions that still remain unanswered, which indicates the existence of physics
beyond the SM (BSM).

One of these open questions is the underlying nature of dark matter in the universe. The
Standard Model of Cosmology is able to describe the evolution of the universe, while only
being dependent on some parameters, which can be obtained by the measurement of the
Cosmic Microwave Background [3]. From this measurement, we observe that ∼ 5% of the
energy budget of the universe is baryonic in nature, while ∼ 27% consists of dark matter. It
is assumed, that dark matter is electrically neutral, cold, i.e. moving at non-relativistic veloc-
ities, and collisionless, and has a lifetime longer than the age of the universe. Therefore dark
matter solely interacts through the gravitational force and couples weakly to SM particles.
The SM cannot provide a suitable dark matter candidate, thus we have to investigate BSM
frameworks.

A promising type of candidates for dark matter are Weakly-Interacting-Massive Particles
(WIMPs). The so-called WIMP-paradigm states that the experimentally measured dark
matter relic abundance, which reads [3]

Ωch
2 = 0.1200± 0.0012 , (1.1)

can be obtained with a dark matter particle with a mass and couplings to SM particles of the
order of the electroweak scale. Extensions of the SM scalar sector can provide such WIMPs.
In these Higgs portal models, the dark matter candidate communicates with the SM via a
Higgs mediator. These models have two advantages. The first advantage is that extending
the scalar sector of the SM provides us with a rich phenomenology which can be probed not
only at the LHC, but also in future collider experiments. The second advantage is that the
Higgs portal models can be probed in different and complimentary experiments in order to
discover a possible dark matter signature. In direct detection experiments, one can use the
Higgs boson as a mediator in dark matter-nucleus scattering [4]. At the time of writing this
thesis, no signal in direct detection experiments has been measured. Nonetheless, these null
results provide exclusion limits that constrain the parameter space of a given model.



2 1. Introduction

Calculating the dark matter relic abundance can become tedious when dealing with models
that include not one but multiple dark sector particles. To circumvent this issue, we have
developed a tool that computes the relic density for an arbitrary dark matter model with
a single dark matter candidate stabilized by a discrete symmetry. Additionally, we imple-
mented algorithms to explore the parameter space in which the dark matter relic abundance
agrees with the experimental measurement. In the literature, the dark matter relic density
is, in most models, calculated only with leading-order diagrams. However, as experimental
precision improves, theoretical predictions must also become more precise. Therefore, we
will investigate in this thesis the impact of next-to-leading order electroweak and quantum
chromodynamics (QCD) corrections on the dark matter relic abundance.

This thesis consists of five main parts. In Part I, we will first give an short overview of the SM
(Sec. 2.1) and proceed with establishing the different BSM frameworks, which are the Complex
Singlet Extension of the Standard Model (CxSM) (Sec. 2.2), the complex Two-Higgs Dou-
blet Model (C2HDM) (Sec. 2.3) and the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model
(Sec. 2.4). Afterwards, we will provide a short introduction into the Standard Model of Cos-
mology in Ch. 3, and thereby develop the mathematical framework to calculate the dark
matter relic abundance in Sec. 3.5 and the direct detection cross section in Sec. 3.6.

To give precise theoretical predictions, we need to understand the impact of experimental
constraints on the parameter space in a given BSM theory. Therefore in Part II, we will in-
vestigate the interplay between collider constraints and the constraints of the electric dipole
moment on the parameter space, by quantifying the allowed size of charge-parity (CP) vi-
olation in the fermionic couplings to the SM-like Higgs boson. We will first provide the
expressions in order to calculate the electric dipole moment in Sec. 4.1. Afterwards, we will
present the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and also the scan ranges of our
input parameters in Ch. 5. In order to obtain our results, we will use two different approaches.
In the first strategy, we will use a guided scan, while in the second strategy we will use ma-
chine learning algorithms in order to explore the parameter space. The results for the former
case will be presented in Ch. 6. In Ch. 7, we will give a short overview on the used machine
learning algorithm, which is succeeded by results using this technique. Finally, Ch. 8 will
conclude this part.

In Part III, we will consider the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM),
where we developed the tool NMSSMScanner.As a proof-of-concept of our new tool, we max-
imize the cross section values for the production of a Higgs boson X, which subsequently
decays into a pair consisting of a SM-like H plus non-SM-like Higgs boson Y , X → HY using
a Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo algorithm. Furthermore, the NMSSM provides a possible dark
matter candidate, which is the lightest supersymmetric particle. Therefore we provide in
Sec. 9.1, the framework how to calculate the dark matter relic abundance in the NMSSM.
Furthermore, in Sec 9.2 we provide also an overview on how the direct detection cross section
is obtained in the NMSSM. In Ch. 10, we present our dark matter tool RelExt, which is
able to compute the dark matter relic abundance, assuming the freeze-out mechanism, for an
arbitrary dark matter model where the dark matter particle is stabilized by a discrete symme-
try. We furthermore extend the code by implementing the relic density and direct detection
calculation for the NMSSM. In Ch. 11, we will present an overview of the tool NMSSMScanner,
the additional observables tested and the computer codes used in the analysis. The results
of our analysis will be presented in Ch. 12. Finally, in Ch. 13 will conclude this part.

In Part IV, we will investigate the impact of higher-order corrections on the dark matter relic
density in the framework of the CxSM. We will first present how to obtain the dark matter
relic density at next-to-leading order in Sec. 14.1. Here, ultraviolet and infrared divergences
can arise. We will present in Ch. 15 how we treat these and show how to obtain ultraviolet-
and infrared-finite annihilation cross sections. In Ch. 16, we present all relevant theoretical

we will present the results of our analysis. Finally, we will conclude this part with a summary
and outlook in Ch. 18. Part V is the final part and consists of a summary and conclusion of
this thesis.

Theories Beyond the Standard Model

As mentioned in the introduction, the SM has many unanswered questions, such as the
hierarchy problem or the nature of dark matter. To address these problems, BSM theories
are needed. In what follows, we first provide a brief overview of the SM. This is followed by
the introduction of the BSM theories investigated in this thesis. Further, we will provide the
necessary notation and conventions used throughout this thesis. For further information on
the various models, references will be provided.

2.1. Standard Model of Particle Physics

The SM is a quantum field theory [5] that describes the fundamental particles and their inter-
actions. Unifying the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces into a single theory describes
these interactions in terms of local gauge groups. The Lagrangian of the SM is invariant
under local symmetry transformations of the gauge groups

SU(3)C × SU(2)L × U(1)Y . (2.1)

the weak and electromagnetic interactions and is described by the Glashow-Weinberg-Salam
theory [6–8], whose underlying symmetry group is SU(2)L × U(1)Y ; the associated gauge

2.4. Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model

In this section, we will briefly introduce the NMSSM. Here, we will follow the reviews [45,46]
and the works of [9, 47].

The NMSSM goes beyond the minimal supersymmetric extension of the SM, the MSSM.
While in the MSSM the SM scalar sector is extended by an additional scalar doublet, the
NMSSM adds an additional scalar singlet field. Further, each field is promoted ot a superfield,
which contains both SM (and the additional scalar doublet and singlet) degrees of freedom
and the ones of their supersymmetric partner, the superpartner. These superpartner differ
from the SM particles only in their spin quantum number by 1/2. This leads to the following
particle content

• The fermions of the SM, obtain spin-0 superpartners, the sfermions. Accordingly, the
superpartners of quarks leptons are therefore called squarks and sleptons, respectively.

Brief Overview of the Standard Model of Cosmology

One of the most sought-after problems in modern physics is the existence of dark matter.
Little is known about the nature and properties of dark matter. However, there is multiple
evidence (cf. Refs. [3,50,51]). To compute and study dark matter observables, it is necessary to
first establish the theoretical framework in which these quantities can be consistently defined
and evaluated. This framework is the so-called Standard Model of Cosmology. Note that
explaining it in its full complexity is beyond the scope of this thesis. We therefore refer to
Refs. [52–54] for a more comprehensive overview. In this work, we will focus only on aspects
relevant to understanding the thermal history of the universe and to calculating dark matter
observables, in particular, the relic density. Here, we follow the description given in Ref. [53].

3.1. General Relativity

We start our description with Einstein‘s field equations (EFEs), which read

Gµν + Λgµν = 8πGTµν . (3.1)

Here, Gµν ≡ Rµν − 1

space-time, Rµν is the Ricci tensor, R the Ricci scalar, G is the gravitational constant, gµν
is the metric tensor and Λ is the cosmological constant. Further, Tµν denotes the energy
momentum tensor, which reads

Tµν = (ρ+ p)uµuν + pgµν + qµuν + uµqν + πµν , (3.2)

where uµ is the velocity four-vector, ρ the energy density, p denotes the isotropic pressure, qµ

fluid behaves as a perfect fluid, i.e., qµ = 0 and πµν = 0, corresponding to a large-scale
homogeneous and isotropic description of the universe. The energy-momentum tensor then
reduces to

Tµν = (p̄+ ρ̄)uµuν + p̄gµν . (3.3)

In Fig. 3.1, the power spectrum measurement of the PLANCK experiment over the dipole
parameter is shown. The peaks shown in this figure arise from acoustic oscillations in the
baryon-photon fluid as the photons decoupled from the thermal bath. During this period,
gravitational wells formed from large amounts of dark matter. These gravitational wells pull
the baryon-photon fluid inward, thereby compressing it. This process is counteracted by
the pressure exerted by the photons, which leads to a rarefaction of the fluid. The tem-
perature fluctuations of the CMB are then induced as the photons travel through different
regions with varying gravitational potentials. Through the compression and rarefaction of

the baryon-photon fluid, oscillations are created. These oscillations are embedded in the
power spectrum of the CMB, where the even-numbered peaks correspond to acoustic modes
undergoing compression at the time of photon decoupling, while the odd-numbered peaks
correspond to acoustic modes in a rarefaction phase. Through the amplitudes and positions
of the peaks, we can now extract the cosmological parameters of the ΛCDM. The position of
the first peak, which corresponds to the time of last scattering, allows us to infer the curvature
of the universe. Further, the baryon content of the universe can be examined by taking the
ratio of the amplitudes of the first and second peaks in the CMB power spectrum. This is
motivated by the fact that if a higher baryon content exists in the baryon-photon fluid, this
would result in a stronger compression and a weaker rarefaction. Vice versa, a smaller baryon
density results in weaker compression and stronger rarefaction of the fluid. Analyzing, there-
fore, the amplitude ratios of the first two peaks allows us to obtain information on the baryon
content in the universe. Furthermore, because dark matter does not interact with photons,
it would only affect the amplitudes of the compression peaks. Therefore, a large third peak

Thermal Freeze-Out

In this production mechanism, we assume that in the early Universe every particle, including
the dark matter particle, is in thermal equilibrium with the thermal bath. This implies
that the production and annihilation rates are equal. However, due to the expansion of the
Universe, two effects occur, which we briefly explain below.



28 3. Brief Overview of the Standard Model of Cosmology

1. As the Universe expands, the temperature T decreases. Consequently, light particles
no longer have enough energy to efficiently produce heavy particles. The annihilation
process then becomes dominant, and the heavy particle number density decreases.

2. Due to the expansion of the Universe, it also becomes less likely for two particles to
interact. As a result, the annihilation rate Γann decreases. When the annihilation rate
becomes comparable to the expansion rate of the Universe, i.e. Γann = H, annihilations
cease to be efficient. This point in time is referred to as freeze-out point.

CHAPTER 4

Introduction

To make predictions across different BSM models, it is important to understand how con-
straints affect the parameter space. In this part, we will investigate how collider constraints
and the electron electric dipole moment (eEDM) constraint interplay in the C2HDM frame-
work, which we introduced in Sec. 2.3.

We work in a CP-violating 2HDM with a softly broken Z2 symmetry that allows CP violation
both in the scalar potential and the Higgs Yukawa interaction. The model naturally eliminates
FCNC at tree level while still accommodating CP violation, thereby generating EDMs for
fundamental particles. The dominant contributions of the EDM are given by the two-loop
Barr-Zee diagrams [67]. Further, it has been seen in Ref. [41] that a new type of two-loop
diagrams, dubbed as ”kite diagrams”, are necessary to obtain a gauge-independent result.
In recent developments [68], it has also been shown that one-loop diagrams are relevant
to the calculation of the eEDM. There are two reasons why it is important to keep track
of the relevant diagrams when calculating the eEDM. First, the experimental sensitivity is
steadily improving: the current 90% confidence-level limit given by the ACME collaboration
is 1.1× 10−29e.cm [69–71], while the JILA collaboration sets a limit of 4.1× 10−30e.cm [71].
However, the individual contributions to the eEDM are of order 10−27. This means that
there must be a large cancellation among the eEDM diagrams to obtain a significant CP
violation, while still accommodating the eEDM constraints. In prospect of the expected
future sensitivity of O(10−33) [72–74], formerly neglected diagrams become more and more
relevant. We also show that virtual charm quarks must be considered in the Barr-Zee diagrams
to obey the expected sensitivity.

Our approach will be as follows. We will perform an extensive parameter scan in the Type
II of the C2HDM with h2 = h125, where h125 represents the SM-like Higgs boson. Here, we
apply all theoretical and experimental constraints to obtain a valid parameter set. We will
use two scan methods in our analysis, the guided scan and a scan using Machine Learning
(ML) algorithms. These scans are then used to quantify the allowed size of CP violation in
the fermionic couplings to the SM-like Higgs boson, in light of additional contributions to the
EDM calculation and the most recent experimental data.

In this chapter, we present the formulas used to compute the electron EDM. Then we will
provide the list of theoretical and experimental constraints applied, along with the scan ranges
for the input parameters.

Fermion Masses used in the EDM Calculation

An additional question, aside from which diagrams to include, arises regarding the choice of
the renormalization scheme. Explicitly, two different schemes can be employed regarding the
fermion mass renormalization. The most common renormalization schemes used for the top
and bottom masses are the MS masses evaluated at the scale µ = MZ (mt(MZ),mb(MZ))
[41, 78, 80] or the pole mass used for the top quark and the running MS bottom quark mass
evaluated at the scale µ = mb, i.e., (mt,mb(mb)) [39,81–83]. For the third generation lepton
τ , we always use the pole mass mτ . For brevity, we will refer to the first choice as MZ-
masses scheme and to the second choice as ”pole masses” scheme. In previous work [84], that
did not include the full two-loop calculation including the kite contribution in the eEDM,
it has been shown that the choice of the used renormalization scheme has an impact on the
phenomenological results. Here, in the Type-II of the C2HDM, with h2 = h125 has been
investigated. By evaluating the fermions at the MZ scale, it has been found that a sizeable
CP-odd component in hSMbb̄ is excluded by the combined experimental constraints from the
upper limit on the eEDM and from the cross-section limits searches for BSM scalars. On the
other hand, by using the pole mass scheme, the possibility of sizeable CP-odd components
remained possible. We will investigate these statements in this work in light of the updated
eEDM calculation with the additional kite contributions.

5.1. Experimental and Theoretical Constraints

5.1.1. Theoretical Constraints

In principle, one can choose the input parameters given in Eq. (2.61) freely. However, not
every combination of parameters will constitute a valid parameter point, as these parameters
must still satisfy theoretical and experimental constraints. To obtain a point, which is con-
sistent by theory, it has to fulfill the condition that the potential is bounded from below and

model is stable and consistent with phenomenology. Furthermore, the chosen input param-

discuss the conditions associated with these constraints to ensure that the parameter points
are theoretically consistent. In our analysis, these conditions are implemented and checked
for each parameter point.

5.2. Experimental Constraints

Electroweak Precision Measurements

Measurements of electroweak observables are sensitive to loop-induced effects from new
physics. If the BSM effects are captured completely by the self-energy corrections to the
gauge boson propagators, one can parametrize these effects through the oblique parameters
S, T , and U [97, 98]. To obtain a valid parameter point, we require that these agree at the
2σ level with the global fit of Ref. [99], which is given by

S = 0.04± 0.11, T = 0.09± 0.14, U = 0.02± 0.11 . (5.5)

Flavour Constraints

From the rare B-meson decays, in particular the process b→ sγ, we obtain constraints for the
charged scalar mass mH± . We incorporate this constraint using the formula from Ref. [100].
Here, we require that the result agrees with the experimental measurement at 3σ [101]. It
has been shown [102–106] that this implies a lower bound of mH± ≥ 580 GeV at 95% CL for
the Type II C2HDM. Additionally, the global fit of Ref. [99] confirms this lower bound and
also shows that this also holds for the Lepton flipped type.

CHAPTER 7

Phenomenology with Machine Learning Algorithms

In the previous chapter, we used a guided-scan method to obtain the parameters. However,
Ref. [119] shows that when using machine learning (ML) algorithms to scan the parameter
space, the traditional method often misses a large portion of the valid parameter space,
with significant consequences for phenomenological interpretations. This motivated us to use
these ML algorithms within the C2HDM framework. In general, ML has become essential for
particle physics analysis [120–124]. In particular, it has become essential for data analysis in
experiments like the LHC, as the data obtained has become more complex and the sample sizes
have grown larger. We are interested in exploring the parameter space of BSM theories. Given
the goal of discovering the unknown physical implications in a highly constrained parameter
space, we employ scan techniques that do not rely on an initial set of sampled data. We
use the CMA-ES algorithm first developed in Ref. [125], with an additional histogram-based

a sketch of an approach to obtain valid parameter points with ML techniques. We first
initialize a multivariate normal distribution with a randomly chosen mean value, and the

7.1. Covariant Matrix Adaptation Evolutionary Strategy

Evolutionary strategies (ES) use an iterative process in which possible solutions to a given
problem are tested, and the best are used to generate new ones. In BSM physics, the solution
to the problem is to find valid parameter points that minimize Eq. (7.2). In contrast to
Genetic Algorithms, ES does not use a previously sampled data set to generate new points.
Instead, the new solutions are generated from a distribution called the generation. The points
for each generation are sampled from the parameter distributions based on the best candi-
dates from the previous iteration. In CMA-ES, the distribution is a multivariate normal
distribution N i(mi, Ci), where mi denotes the mean value and Ci is the covariance matrix
of the i-th generation. As stated before, we initialize the normal distribution with a random
point as its mean, and set the covariance matrix to the identity matrix multiplied by a global
factor σ. From this distribution, λ candidates are generated, and their suitability is checked
with Eq. (7.2). Afterwards, the best µ candidates are sorted and from these a new distri-
bution N i+1(mi+1, Ci+1) are generated, with a new mean mi+1 and a new covariant matrix
Ci+1. This procedure is expected to behave similarly to first- and second-order optimization
methods. The mean is updated along the direction of steepest descent of the loss function,
while the covariance matrix provides an approximation to its Hessian. However, CMA-ES
does not calculate the derivatives of the loss function, which in fact means that one can use
it on nonconvex, ill-conditioned, and non-continuous loss functions. This has the advantage
that the algorithm converges quickly and can be applied to various applications. For further
information on this strategy, we refer to Ref [125].

algorithms. The caveat of this algorithm is that the explored parameter space is highly
localized. In our approach, which was also applied in Ref. [126], we add a novelty reward
to the loss function. Here, we calculate the point density and add it to the loss function as

CHAPTER 8

Conclusion

In this part of the thesis, we investigated the impact of the collider and eEDM constraints
on the parameter space of the C2HDM, which we introduced in Sec. 2.3.

We first introduced the formulas used for the full two-loop eEDM calculation, including a
new class of diagrams, the so-called kite diagrams. Furthermore, we investigated the depen-
dence on the renormalization scheme used for the fermion masses in the eEDM calculation.
Afterwards, we gave an overview of the theoretical and experimental constraints applied in
our study. In the case of constraints arising from measurements of the CP properties of the
SM-like Higgs boson, we distinguished how to apply these constraints. Here, we studied the
impact of applying the constraints on the CP-violating coupling of HSMτ τ̄ , either with the
public tool HiggsTools or with Eq. (5.8).

In Chapter 6, we then performed a guided parameter scan, which we dubbed Strategy 1,
for the Type II C2HDM with h2 = h125. We have shown that with this scan method, one
obtains valid parameter points that scatter around the SM-like solution. Furthermore, we
investigated the impact of the kite diagrams on the parameter space. Here, we have confirmed
that the kite diagrams are of the same order as the Barr-Zee diagrams, and therefore need to
be included in the analysis of the eEDM.

In Chapter 7, we introduced the ML algorithms we used in our second scan method, dubbed
Strategy 2. Here, we used the CMA-ES algorithm with an additional anomaly-detection
component as a novelty reward. Using these ML algorithms, we then performed an extensive
parameter scan. First, we analyzed the impact of the renormalization scheme choice for the
fermion masses. We saw that with the inclusion of the kite diagrams, one obtains qualitatively
the same results. This is in contrast to the previously obtained results in Ref. [84], where
the kite diagrams were not included in the eEDM calculation. In addition, we showed that
using ML algorithms can reveal previously overlooked valid parameter regions. Next, we
discussed the impact of including the charm quark in the eEDM calculation. Here, we saw
that the charm quark contribution to the eEDM is of order 10−29e.cm, which is larger than
the experimental limits. Therefore, including this contribution is necessary to obtain a correct
estimate of the eEDM in the C2HDM. It does not change qualitatively the phenomenology
on the CP-odd coupling cob , however. Lastly, we briefly commented on the other cases of the
C2HDM and provided an update on the possibility of sizeable CP-odd couplings in other
types of the model.



60 8. Conclusion

In summary, we performed a complete analysis of the C2HDM, using ML to explore the full
parameter space and the observables that comply with current theoretical and experimental
constraints. The ML method shown can be applied to any sampling in constrained scenarios,
such as BSM models with a large number of parameters.



Part III.

Dark Matter Analysis in the NMSSM





CHAPTER 9

Introduction

As the SM leaves open questions like the nature of DM or why there is more matter than
antimatter in the universe, we have to consider models beyond the SM. Among the many
BSM theories, supersymmetry (SUSY) answers many of the open questions. Furthermore, it
provides a relation between bosons and fermions through SUSY transformations. The scalar
sector of the Minimal Supersymmetric extension of the SM (MSSM) contains two complex
Higgs doublets, which are further extended in the NMSSM (c.f. Sec. 2.4) by a complex singlet
superfield. This introduction solves the so-called µ-problem of the MSSM, but adds additional
input parameters to the model. In SUSY, the tree-level mass of the lightest doublet-like CP-
even Higgs boson has an upper limit, such that higher-order corrections are needed in order
to comply with the measured Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV . Therefore, the mass of the Higgs
boson is now a derived parameter. This, along with the large number of input parameters,
makes parameter scans in the NMSSM difficult. Searching for benchmark scenarios that
comply with all relevant theoretical and experimental constraints is particularly difficult due
to the complexity of the parameter space.

To solve this problem, we developed NMSSMScanner [128], a framework that enables efficient
scans of the NMSSM parameter space. To obtain valid parameter points, we include all
relevant collider and low-energy constraints, as well as DM constraints. The framework is
implemented using code that computes relevant NMSSM observables and compares them
against theoretical and experimental constraints. One of these observables is the DM relic
density and the direct-detection cross section of the potential DM candidate, here, the lightest
neutralino χ̃0. To calculate these observables, we used the public code RelExt and, as part
of this project, added the NMSSM as a new model to the toolchain.

In this chapter, we provide an overview of the formulas used to calculate the DM observables.
This is followed in Ch. 10 by a brief description of the public code RelExt [129]. In Ch. 11,
we will discuss the additional observables considered in NMSSMScanner. Afterwards, we will
present our results in Ch. 12.

CHAPTER 10

RelExt - A Dark Matter Tool for Efficient Scans

Calculating DM observables such as the relic density and the direct-detection cross section
can be tedious in a BSM model like the NMSSM. Over the years, many codes like MadDM

[136–138], DarkSUSY [139], SuperISO [140] and MicrOMEGAs [66,141–145] have been developed
to calculate DM observables. However, finding the appropriate input parameter configuration
to achieve the relic abundance given in Eq. (3.22) for an arbitrary model becomes harder as
the model grows more complex. To overcome this problem, we developed the public code
RelExt, which calculates the relic density and includes a scanning tool that efficiently searches
for parameter values that yield the correct relic density. Furthermore, we have extended the
code to implement direct-detection in the NMSSM. Also, it is possible to evaluate the relic
density calculation not only at tree level but also at next-to-leading order (NLO), which we
will showcase in Part IV for the CxSM. The code can be downloaded at

https://github.com/jplotnikov99/RelExt.

RelExt is a C++ code, which calculates the relic density for DM particles that undergo the
freeze-out mechanism described in Sec. 3.5 for any model with a Z2 symmetry, which stabilizes
the DM particle. In order to run the code, the user only needs to provide a FeynRules [146]
model file. RelExt then calculates all (co-)annihilation amplitudes of the DM candidate of
the given model, generates the corresponding cross sections, and calculates with that the
thermally averaged cross section given in Eq. (9.30). The relic density is then obtained by
solving the Boltzmann equation given in Eq. (3.66). For a more detailed description of the
implementation of the C++ code, we refer to Ref. [129]. Note that in the current version of
RelExt, it is only possible to work with models that have one DM candidate. Furthermore,
BSM theories with DM annihilation processes that are CP-violating and enter the relic density
calculation, cannot be described by the derivation given in Sec. 3.5, and hence, cannot be
treated in RelExt. In this work, we provide a brief overview of the structure of the code.
Afterwards, we show how we implement the calculation of the direct-detection cross section
in RelExt.

In Figure 10.1, we show the flowchart of the code. RelExt can be divided into two parts. We
denote the first part as New Model Implementation and the second part as DM Observables

and Parameter Search. We will start our description with the former.

10.1. New Model Implementation

If the user wants to implement a new model in RelExt, they have to provide a FeynRules

and the computer codes used. Further, we will provide the ranges of our parameter scan.

11.1. Organization of the Scan

To perform our analysis, we use a modified version of the Python code BSMArt [161]. This
code allows us to connect all relevant programs and pass the necessary information of a given
BSM model through the program chain. In BSMArt, it is possible to use different scanning
techniques, such as Active Learning [162], Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), random
scans, or user-defined algorithms to scan the parameter space. Since BSMArt was initially
developed as a complementary framework to SARAH/SPheno [163,164], it has proven effective
across many BSM frameworks [162,165–173].

Higgs and SUSY Spectra and Decays

In order to calculate the Higgs and SUSY mass spectra, we link the Fortran code NMSSMCALC
[174] to BSMArt. The code computes the SUSY mass spectrum at leading order and evaluates
the Higgs boson mass spectrum in the CP-violating NMSSM (CNMSSM), including full one-
loop corrections [175, 176] as well as important two-loop QCD and electroweak corrections
of order O(αtαs) [177], O(α2

t ) [178] and O((αt + αλ + ακ)
2) [179]. NMSSMCALC additionally

provides predictions for the leptonic anomalous magnetic moments and the EDM at one- and
two-loop level [180, 181]. Furthermore, NMSSMCALC computes the Higgs boson decay widths
and branching ratios. These calculations have been adopted from the Fortran code HDECAY.
Also, NMSSMCALC is used to calculate the SUSY particle decays, including tree-level two-
and three-body decays, loop-induced decays, and NLO SUSY-QCD corrections for processes
involving color-charged particles [182].

Single and di-Higgs Production

In order to comply with the single Higgs boson production constraints regarding the LHC
SM-like Higgs boson data and the exclusion limits from BSM Higgs boson searches at the

To calculate the non-resonant di-Higgs production cross section, we use the Fortran code
HPair [185].17 The resonant di-Higgs constraints are checked by HiggsTools. We multiply
the production cross section of a non-SM-like single boson, which is obtained with the code

is then checked against the experimental measurements.

SUSY Searches

In our analysis, we use the code SModelS [191–194] to check the constraints from SUSY
searches. SModelS computes the leading-order squark and gluino pair production cross section
via PYTHIA [195]. Additionally, it applies a K-Factor for the QCD corrections from NLL-

Fast [196–203] at next-to-leading logarithmic order matched to next-to-leading order. The
electroweakino pair-production cross sections are obtained using an in-house code. Here,
we apply for the NLO electroweak corrections an approximate K-factor of 1.3, which can
be used when the electroweakinos are lighter than the squarks [204, 205]. At leading order,
the mixed squark-electroweakino pair production is computed by SModelS. The total cross
section of multi-particle final states in the SUSY scenario is then obtained by combining the
production cross sections with the SUSY particle branching ratios obtained by SDECAY [206],
which includes the SUSY particle decays in the NMSSM [182] . The total cross section is
then compared with the experimental analyse.

DM Observables

As stated in the previous chapters 10 and 9, we compute the relic density and the direct-
detection cross section of the lightest neutralino using RelExt, which was extended to include
also the NMSSM as a model. The relic density is compared with the experimental limit
given in Eq. (3.22). We use Eq. (9.37) to compare with the latest exclusion bounds of the
Lux-Zeplin experiment [4].

11.3. Scan Procedure

We generate a parameter sample using the tool NMSSMScanner, optimizing an MCMC scan
with likelihood functions for each individual final state considered. This means that at first,
we perform a random scan over the ranges provided in Tab. 11.1 and use these points as
seeds for the MCMC scan. As a proof-of concept of the new tool NMSSMScanner, we try to
obtain the maximum cross section values for the resonant production of a Higgs boson X,
which subsequently decays into a SM-like plus non-SM-like Higgs boson pair X → HY , we
optimize the MCMC scan with likelihood functions L. For example 18, for the maximation
of the scalar resonance, we chose the following likelihood function

Lsmax = exp{(s0(σ × BR)/µ)} , (11.7)

where σ denotes the production cross section of HY and BR denotes the product of the
branching ratio of H and Y decaying into the considered finale state. The normalization
µ = σseed ×BRseed is calculated at the seed point. In our analysis, we set s0 = 2, as this was
found to be the optimal value for convergence.

CHAPTER 13

Conclusion

In this part of the thesis, we presented the program package NMSSMScanner, which is built to
efficiently scan the complex parameter space of the NMSSM. Within the scope of this project,
we implemented the NMSSM relic density and the direct-detection cross section calculation in
the public code RelExt. We have presented the necessary framework for calculating the relic
density and the direct-detection cross section in the NMSSM. Afterward, we gave an overview
of the public code RelExt in Ch. 10 and described how we automate the implementation
of an arbitrary model in RelExt. In Ch. 11, we presented how we organize the program
chain in the program package NMSSMScanner. Here, we discuss the various experimental
constraints included in our analysis. In Chapter 12, we presented as a proof of concept
benchmark points, which maximize the cross section of a SM-like and non-SM-like Higgs
boson pair, which is produced by a resonant scalar or pseudoscalar Higgs boson, in various
decay channels. Further, we extended the investigation compared to Ref. [128] by providing,
for each benchmark point, information on the DM observables, i.e., the DM relic density and
the direct-detection cross section. Also, we investigated the possibility of obtaining the correct
relic density in the NMSSM while still complying with the exclusion limit of LUX-Zeplin.
We have shown that there is still a parameter region that saturates the relic density, complies
with the exclusion limits of the Lux-Zeplin collaboration, and lies above the neutrino floor.
In summary, we provided a proof of concept for our new package NMSSMScanner and the

CHAPTER 14

Introduction

The SM has unsolved problems, one of which is the nature of dark matter. As described
in Ch. 3, it is possible to extract from the CMB the current energy budget of dark matter
in the universe. The dark matter relic abundance has been measured by the PLANCK
collaboration to be Ωch

2 = 0.1200 ± 0.0012 [3]. This value acts as a constraining factor on
the parameter space of models with dark matter candidates. Calculating the relic abundance
from a theoretical point of view, for any model, involves computing the (co-)annihilation
cross sections of dark matter into SM particles. In practice, this calculation is generally
done at leading-order. However, as experiments become more and more precise, theoretical
predictions also need to be precise. In Refs. [226–229], the electroweak next-to-leading order
effects on the relic density have been investigated in the framework of the inert-doublet
2HDM. In this work we computed the full electroweak and QCD higher-order effects in the
framework of the CxSM, described in Sec. 2.2. As described in Ch. 10, it is possible to
choose between a variety of codes to calculate the relic abundance at leading-order for an
arbitrary model. However, at next-to-leading order, this calculation becomes more difficult.
In MicrOMEGAs [141,142,144,145] it is possible to include next-to-leading order corrections via
predefined functions. Furthermore, the code DM@NLO [230] provides the next-to-leading order
(SUSY) QCD corrections for dark matter (co-)annihilation in the Minimal Supersymmetric
Standard Model. In this work, we use our code RelExt, which we introduced in Ch. 10,
and extended the already implemented relic density at leading-order in the context of the
CxSM by the calculation of next-to-leading order electroweak and QCD corrections to the
annihilation cross section of a dark matter pair into SM particles. This work will serve as
an initial example of the implementation of next-to-leading order corrections in RelExt for
a specific model, as the goal is to later extend the code in such a way to allow for an easy
implementation of next-to-leading order corrections in RelExt for arbitrary models.

We will present this work as follows. We outline the general idea of the next-to-leading order
calculation in Sec. 14.1. As ultraviolet and infrared divergences can arise at next-to-leading
order calculations, we have to cure these with an appropriate regularisation and renormal-
ization scheme. We provide an overview of the used renormalization schemes in the CxSM
and describe how we treat infrared divergences in our processes in Ch. 15. Furthermore, we
present the in Ch. 16 the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and also the scan
ranges of our example parameter sample. In Ch. 17, we show our obtained results.

Renormalization and the Treatment of Infrared Divergences in the CxSM

In higher-order calculations, ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) divergences may arise. These
must be handled appropriately to obtain physically meaningful and interpretable results.
Ultraviolet divergences are handled by regularization and renormalization schemes. To cure
the IR divergences, a different approach is used; see Sec. 15.5.

Dimensional regularization is a commonly used regularization method. In this approach, the
loop integrals appearing in the calculation are evaluated in D = 4 − 2ϵ dimensions. The
divergences then manifest as poles of inverse powers of ϵ (ϵ−1 for UV divergences and ϵ−1 and
ϵ−2 for IR divergences). To render the physical amplitudes for a calculated process free of
the UV poles, the input parameters must be redefined. The renormalized parameter κ and
the corresponding counterterm δκ are introduced such that the bare parameter κ0, which
emerges in the unrenormalized Lagrangian L0, is defined as

κ0 = κ+ δκ . (15.1)

Furthermore, the bare fields ψ0 are defined by a shift of the wave-function renormalization
constant Zψ such that

photons, and gluons appear in the loop diagrams. These types of diagrams lead to infrared
divergences. According to the Kinoshita-Lee-Nauenberg theorem, IR safety is guaranteed
upon including real corrections [252, 253]. The total UV- and IR-convergent cross section is
then given by

While the Eq. (15.50) is infrared finite, the virtual and real emission cross sections are sepa-

gauge bosons, such as photons or gluons, in loop diagrams. In particular, they enter through
the IR-divergent derivatives of the self-energies, which are used in the wave function renor-
malization constants (cf. Eqs. (15.6), (15.8)), as well as through triangle diagrams with a
massless particle in the loop. In the case of the real corrections, the IR divergences stem
from the divergent phase space of the emitted massless gauge boson in the soft limit, where
the momentum of the emitted particle becomes very small. To obtain a Lorentz-invariant
cancellation of the IR divergences, dimensional regularization should be applied, such that
the integration over phase space must be performed in D = 4−2ϵ dimensions. However, since
it very difficult to analytically extract the IR poles from the 2 → 3 phase-space integral to
cancel them with the corresponding IR poles from the virtual corrections, this method is not
suitable for numerical applications. Hence, we will use the Catani-Seymour dipole subtraction
method [254], which we will discuss in Sec. 15.5.2. In order to use this method, we need to
calculate the real corrections in the full three-body phase space dΠ3. For this purpose, we
will give a brief overview of the derivation of the three-body phase space.

16.2. Experimental Constraints

Electroweak Precision Parameters

Due to the additional scalar particle in the CxSM, additional contributions appear in the
self-energies of the gauge bosons. These lead to deviations from the SM predictions. These
deviations can be parametrized by the oblique parameters S, T , and U [97]. We check via
ScannerS, which uses a fit result, the compatibility of the theoretical and experimental values.

Higgs Searches

The measurements at the LHC of the discovered Higgs boson as well as the searches for
additional scalar particles constrain the parameter space of the CxSM. In order to obtain
valid parameter points, ScannerS is linked to the public code HiggsTools [109], which is a
unification of the modules HiggsSignals [112] and HiggsBounds [260]. Here, we check the
agreement of the signal rates of the SM-like Higgs boson with the experimental data at the 2σ
level by HiggsSignals. The constraints from the searches for the additional scalar particles
in theory are included by HiggsBounds.

Dark Matter Observables

We impose that the parameter points must fulfill at leading-order the relic density constraint
by the PLANCK experiment given in Eq. (3.22). This is checked with our code RelExt [129].
In the CxSM, the direct detection constraint does not affect the parameter space, as the LO
cross section is suppressed by the small DM velocity and therefore negligible.

the CxSM, which we introduced in Sec. 2.2. Within the scope of this project, we extended the
public code RelExt with the calculation of the relic density at next-to-leading order, which
we will extend in future work to automate the implementation of higher-order calculations in
an arbitrary model.

We have presented how the relic density is obtained at next-to-leading order. In Ch. 15, we
demonstrated how we obtain UV- and IR-finite cross sections for our calculation. Afterwards,
we presented the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and the scan ranges of our
parameter sample. Finally, in Ch. 17, we presented the impact of the higher-order corrections
on the dark matter relic abundance. Here, we provided as a proof-of-concept the results
first only with next-to-leading order QCD corrections. Next, we presented the electroweak
and the QCD corrections and the impact of different renormalization schemes. We have
shown that the higher-order corrections can lead to either an increase or a decrease of the
relic density. This has an important phenomenological consequence: higher-order corrections
can invalidate previously valid parameter points by increasing the relic density such that it
exceeds the observed dark matter relic abundance measured by the PLANCK experiment
[3]. Vice versa, due to possibly negative higher-order corrections to the relic density, it can
occur, that previously discarded parameter points, which oversaturated the relic density, can
become valid again. Furthermore, we have shown that the theoretical uncertainty between the
renormalization schemes are small if the variation of the input parameters that are affected
by the change in scheme is small.

Overall, we have shown that the inclusion of higher-order calculations are important to explore
the parameter space of a given dark matter model.

Final Conclusion and Outlook

The success story of the Standard Model of particle physics was further advanced by the
discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012. However, despite its many precise predictions, the
Standard Model still lacks solutions to some unanswered problems. In this thesis, we focused
on understanding the nature of dark matter in the universe by investigating various theories
beyond the Standard Model. A very important observable is the dark matter relic density
Ωch

2, which has been measured by the PLANCK collaboration to be

Ωch
2 = 0.1200± 0.0012 . (19.1)

The computation of the relic density in a theory beyond the Standard Model can become
tedious, in particular for more complex models. This task becomes even more difficult when
the goal is to find the parameter configuration that yields the correct experimental relic
density. To solve this issue, we developed, within the scope of this thesis, the C++ code
RelExt, which automates the computation of the relic density via freeze-out for an arbitrary
model with a dark matter candidate stabilized by a discrete symmetry. Furthermore, we
implemented search algorithms that conveniently provide the parameter configurations which
yield the experimentally observed relic density. Also, due to its modular structure, the code
can easily be extended to implement new features, such as computing the direct-detection
cross section or calculating higher-order corrections to the relic density.

In Part I, we briefly introduced the Standard Model, and the beyond-the-Standard Model
(BSM) theories investigated in this thesis, which are the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model, the Complex Two-Higgs Doublet Model, and the Next-To Minimal Super-
symmetric Standard Model. Afterward, we gave a brief introduction to the Standard Model of
Cosmology. Furthermore, we provided derivations of the Boltzmann equation for calculating
the dark matter relic density and of the direct detection cross section.

To provide precise theoretical predictions, we need a deeper understanding of the experimen-
tal constraints and their interplay within BSM theories. Therefore, in Part II of this thesis,
we studied the interplay of collider and electric dipole constraints by investigating the al-
lowed CP-violation of the coupling between a fermion pair and a Standard Model-like Higgs
boson. We first introduced expressions for calculating the electric dipole moment, including
kite diagrams, which were not included in previous works, followed by a description of the



134 19. Final Conclusion and Outlook

theoretical and experimental constraints used in our parameter scan. In Ch. 6, we presented
the results using traditional scan methods, i.e., using a guided scan method. To potentially
reveal previously overlooked regions in the parameter space, we employed machine learning
algorithms, specifically the CMA-ES algorithm, to explore it. In Ch. 7, we provided a short
description of the machine learning algorithm, as well as the presentation of our results.

Exploring the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model is
a complicated and computationally intensive task. To circumvent this issue, we presented
in Part III our new tool NMSSMScanner, which provides a convenient way to explore the
parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. In Ch. 9, we
presented the theoretical framework necessary for the evaluation of the relic density and
the direct detection cross section in this model. Within the scope of this work, RelExt,
introduced in Ch. 10, was extended to include the calculation of these dark matter observables.
Afterward, we provided an overview of the tool NMSSMScanner, presenting the experimental
and theoretical constraints, as well as the computer codes used in the program chain. As a
proof-of-concept of this tool, we maximized the production cross section of a resonant non-
Standard Model Higgs boson into various final states, as well as investigating the dark matter
observables in the Next-to Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. A detailed description
of our results is given in Ch. 12.

In the final Part IV of this thesis, we computed the dark matter relic abundance at next-to-
leading order electroweak and QCD in the framework of the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model. In order to do so, we implemented the next-to-leading order annihilation
amplitudes squared in RelExt. In Ch. 15, we presented the prescriptions needed in order to
obtain UV- and IR-finite annihilation cross sections. Afterward, we presented the applied
theoretical and experimental constraints, as well as the scan ranges used in the investigated
parameter sample. In Ch. 17, we showed the impact of higher-order corrections on the
relic density, as well as the phenomenological consequences of these, where we saw that the
higher-order corrections can both increase or decrease the computed relic density, making
the higher-order calculation an important contribution to future studies of the validity of
parameter points.

Even though the Standard Model is a success story in itself, the unanswered questions show
us that there is still new physics to be discovered. In order to do so, we need precise cal-
culations within the Standard Model as well as in theories beyond the Standard Model. In
particular, there is a lack of precision in calculations in dark matter models. However, exper-
iments for dark matter searches become increasingly precise. Therefore, the need for precise
theoretical predictions becomes increasingly relevant to solving the mystery of dark matter in
the universe. With this thesis, we provided a contribution to further proceed on this path.

B.1. Mathematica Code

In this section, we provide a more detailed description of the Mathematica code implemented
in RelExt. Here, we will follow the description in Ref. [129].

The implementation of a new model in RelExt is fully automated. Here, the implementation
involves two Mathematica scripts, which are saved in the directory mathematica. The first
script FR_to_CH_FA.m automatically converts the FeynRules model file into FeynArts (FA)
and CalcHep (CH) files. The generated files can then be found in the folders FA_modfiles and
CH_modfiles. These folders are localized in the $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/FR_modfiles/

directory.26 The second Mathematica script, amp2cpp.m, generates and stores all amplitudes
needed to compute the Freeze-Out relic abundance for a DM particle, as well as all information
required to implement a new model. This script can be divided into three different building
blocks: the amplitude generation block, the decay width generation block and the conversion
from Mathematica to C++ code block. In the following, we provide an overview of the most
important functions, lists, and segments for each block.

The most important elements of the amplitude generation block are

• particlelist is a list, where the FA particle identifiers, their masses, the names and
PDG numbers are stored. Here, we also include anti-particles; however, exclude Gold-
stone bosons and ghost particles.

• The function determineDof[pID_] determines the degrees of freedom of the particle,
which is given by the FA identifier pID_.

• The lists dslist(FA particle identifier), dsmass(mass), dsnames(name) and dsDof(degrees
of freedom) store the information of the dark sector particles. The corresponding infor-
mation are given in the brackets.

26
$RelExt denotes the path, where RelExt is installed, and ModelName is a placeholder name for the name of
the user‘s model.

• alldiags provides all tree-level 2 → 2 Feynman diagrams, with two dark sector parti-
cles in the initial states and none in the final state.

• The function removeDuplicate[] is used to remove redundant processes from the di-
agsgrouped list. Here, a new list listofprocs is generated, which is the final list
containing all processes necessary for computing the relic abundance. This includes all
channels with two dark sector particles in the initial state and none in the final state.
In the case of co-annihilation, this leads to redundancy, as channels with the same final
state but with an initial state where the particles are swapped also contribute to the
relic density. The amplitude, however, is analytically the same. Therefore, we compute
only one amplitude, and remove the other one from the list listofprocs. The same
reasoning applies to processes whose initial state is the charge conjugate of a previous
one. To still obtain the correct relic density, we apply a multiplicative factor to the
Boltzmann equation to compensate for the removed channels.

Abstract

In this work, we review 3-dimensional gravity by canonically analyzing the Hilbert-

Palatini action. We apply a time gauge used in 4-dimensional loop quantum grav-

ity [14] to the simpler case of the 3-dimensional loop quantum gravity. By time

gauge fixing this Hilbert-Palatini action it leads to the Gauss constraints, the spa-

tial diffeomorphism constraints, the Hamiltonian constraint and a new constraint

C. The gauge symmetries generated by this new constraints are spacetime diffeo-

morphism and SO(2) gauge transformations. We solve the dynamics of the theory

by providing a regularization of the generalized projector operator in terms of the

Hamiltonian constraint. We provide the definition of the physical scalar product

which can be represented in terms of a sum over finite spinfoam amplitudes. Then

we establish a clear-cut link between the canonical quantization of the new theory

to the spinfoam model (Ponzano-Regge model) defined in terms of the SU(2) spin

networks.

Chapter 1

Introduction and Motivation

1.1 Quantum Gravity

The task of quantizing gravity is one of the outstanding problems of modern

theoretical physics. Attempts to reconcile quantum theory and general relativity

(GR) date back to the early part of the twentieth century. Several decades of

hard work have yielded an abundance of insights into quantum field theory. But

despite this enormous effort, no one has yet succeeded in formulating a complete,

self-consistent quantum theory of gravity [5].

Einstein’s description of gravity as a curvature of spacetime (geometry of curved

spacetime) was seen as a game changer at the time, as this idea totally moved away

from the notion of gravity as a force. The consequence of this was the formulation

of the theory of GR which gave a deep insight into the geometric structure of the

universe at the macroscopic level.

Quantum mechanics (QM), which describes the microscopic world was formulated

based on the laws of probability. It allows for a discrete energy spectrum instead of

a continuous radiation. QM uses the time evolution of quantum states described by

the Schrodinger equation in which the Hamiltonian generates the time evolution.

This means that physical quantities can change only in discrete amounts and not

in a continuous way [27].

Our understanding of physics, and in general nature have been greatly influenced

by QM and GR. Both principles have revolutionized the pivotal structures of New-

tonian physics. The notion of absolute time and space ceases to exist, but rather

space and time and distances between points of the spacetime manifold, that is,

the metric themselves become dynamical objects [27, 28]. Further, the determin-

istic nature of Newton’s equations of motion evaporates at a fundamental level,

1

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



rather dynamics is reigned by probabilities underlying the Heisenberg uncertainty

principle.

A usual phenomenon in fundamental physics is to reconcile two different concep-

tual theories to find a new synthesis, a satisfactory physical theory must therefore

combine both of these fundamental principles, QM and GR, in a consistent way

and which will be called quantum gravity (QG). However, despite the success sto-

ries of both QM and GR, the quantization of the gravitational field has turned

out to be one of the most challenging unsolved problems in theoretical and math-

ematical physics.

The reason for this incompatibility is that, GR requires spacetime to be a dy-

namical field, describing the notion of force as a geometry and also requires an

independent background structure. On the other hand, QM requires a dynamical

field to be quantized, and in addition requires a non-dynamical background space-

time (Hilbert space) for it to take place. In GR, spacetime is dynamical, while

in QM, any dynamical entity is made up of quanta and can be in probabilistic

superposition states.

Not only are there conceptual differences in quantizing gravity, there are techni-

cal obstacles also facing the new synthesis. Einstein’s equations which governs

the theory of gravity are highly non-linear, and hence very difficult to solve. In

addition, conventional field quantization methods which are based on the weak-

field perturbation expansion fail in their application to GR since they yield a

non-renormalizable theory. GR, hence must be replaced by a more fundamental

description that appropriately includes the quantum degrees of freedom of gravity

[24].

However, it is clear that while GR has given a very consistent framework for doing

classical physics, it has not yet been successful in bringing the quantum realm

in its wake [21]. Attempts have been made for decades to formulate a consistent

theory of quantum gravity, but with no success so far.

1.2 Loop Quantum Gravity

The past decades have seen an increase in active research in the field of quantum

theory of gravity, with some claiming to have found a quantum theory of gravity.

Notably among them is string theory, which is based on the physical hypothesis

that elementary objects are extended rather than particle-like [27]. A very rich

unified theory which includes Yang-Mills fields and gravitons, and free of ultravio-

let divergences are a few of string theory’s successful story. However, this comes at

2

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



a cost of additional physics such as supersymmetry, extra dimensions, an infinite

number of fields with an arbitrary masses and spins.

In light of this another active area of research in QG is Loop Quantum Gravity

(LQG) which takes a different approach to string theory. LQG is a canonical

and background independent base approach to the quantization of gravity paying

special attention to the conceptual lessons of GR [9, 23, 27, 28]. It proposes that

spacetime is actually divided into small chucks, when you zoom out it appears

to be a smooth sheet, but when you zoom in, it is a bunch of dots connected by

lines or loops. These small fibres, which are woven together offer an explanation

of gravity.

LQG is based on a Hamiltonian formulation of GR at the classical level. In this

formulation, spacetime is foliated into a family of hypersurfaces of constant time

with coordinates on each slice. LQG is a straightforward quantization procedure

of GR with the physical inputs of the theory been the well-tested physical theories

of QM and GR, there are no major additional physical hypothesis or assumption

made in the construction of the theory [27]. All it tries to do is to merge the

conceptual ideas of GR into QM. In addition, LQG is based on assumption that

even if Einstein’s equations are modified at high energy, the general-relativistic

notion of space and time are assumed to be true.

The theory is formulated in the more physical four dimensional case. It was

initially formulated in terms of the metric variables which was due to Arnowitt,

Deser and Misner [28], hence the name ADM formulation. In this formulation, the

canonical variables are the metric tensor of three dimensional spatial slices qab(x, t)

(here a, b are 3d space indices) and it’s conjugate momentum πab [23, 28] following

an ADM decomposition of the action. The decomposition results in the spatial

diffeomorphism V (qab, π
ab) and Hamiltonian constraints S(qab, π

ab), however the

non-linear dependence on the canonical variables especially by the Hamiltonian

constraint makes it mathematically difficult to promote the constraints into quan-
