abstracts.value: The unique underground location of the Einstein Telescope (ET) is expected to substantially suppress seismic and gravity-gradient noise, providing a favorable environment for gravitational-wave detection at low frequencies compared with surface-based observatories. The baseline ET design aims to achieve broadband sensitivity through a xylophone configuration, in which separate cryogenic and room-temperature interferometers are optimised for low- and high-frequency gravitational-wave detection. However, achieving the target low-frequency sensitivity introduces substantial technical complexity caused by vertical suspension thermal noise, vibrations of the cryocooler, and detuned optical configuration. In this paper, we demonstrate an alternative, entirely room-temperature, fully resonant, single-interferometer architecture that addresses these challenges and achieves broadband sensitivity superior to that of the conventional ET xylophone configuration. Using mature fused-silica suspension technology, recent advances in optical coatings, and novel inertial isolation, we show that 4-m-long fused-silica fibres can meet the required suspension thermal-noise performance. We further demonstrate that vibrations, optical rigidity, and quantum back-action noise can be controlled through appropriate design of the interferometer, test mass suspensions, optical seismometers, and quantum states.

titles.title: A Broadband Room-Temperature Design for the Einstein Telescope

abstracts.value: We study weak field local tests of Schwarzschild-Bertotti-Robinson spacetime, which describes a static black hole embedded in an external magnetic field. Perihelion precession, deflection of light rays and time delay of radar echoes are the phenomena considered in this work to understand the possible effects of this external magnetic field on these observationally important tests. We not only derive weak field analytical results by employing appropriate methods, but also consider an exact approach to directly integrate the relevant geodesic equations, to both confirm those weak field analytical results and to obtain results beyond the weak field approximation.

titles.title: Local tests of Schwarzschild-Bertotti-Robinson spacetime

abstracts.value: Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) amplification enables eV-sub-keV detection thresholds for low-mass dark-matter and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering experiments. We evaluated two University of South Dakota (USD)-grown germanium crystals fabricated as SuperCDMS-style four-channel athermal-phonon detectors and operated near 10 mK. The crystals had electrically active impurity concentrations near $10^10~\mathrm^-3$ and etch-pit densities of $300$-$7000~\mathrm^-2$. Contact-free biasing produced no resolvable amplification. However, after depositing a 600 nm aluminum bias contact, Detector~2 exhibited clear voltage-dependent NTL gain. The reconstructed channel-B energy increased from approximately 3.9 keV at 0 V to 34.9 keV at 40 V, corresponding to an 8.9-fold enhancement. Statistical centroid uncertainties were below 0.3%, while low-bias fits yielded effective prompt- and NTL-phonon response coefficients of $(6.77\pm0.82)%$ and $(4.77\pm0.20)%$, respectively, excluding systematic uncertainties. These results demonstrate the feasibility of USD-grown germanium for SuperCDMS-style high-voltage phonon detectors and highlight the importance of both crystal quality and contact fabrication in achieving NTL amplification.

titles.title: NTL amplification in a SuperCDMS-style detector fabricated from a University of South Dakota-grown germanium crystal

abstracts.value: Primordial tensor non-Gaussianity can probe massive particles present during inflation. We investigate this possibility in an effective field theory where the massless graviton mixes with the helicity-two mode of an additional massive spin-two field $σ_{ij}$ with cubic self-interactions. For constant sound speed, we compute the leading tensor power-spectrum correction and the tree-level bispectrum, finding novel analytical expressions for these quantities. In the $m_σ>3H/2$ regime, we find a nonanalytic squeezed contribution that exhibits logarithmic oscillations with characteristic dependence $(k_L/k_S)^{3/2\pm iμ}$, where $μ=\sqrt{m_σ^2/H^2-9/4}$. The oscillation frequency is set by the mass $m_σ$, while the polarisation contractions determine the relative amplitudes of the different graviton helicity configurations. The same mixing generates corrections to the power spectrum and the bispectrum. We derive the associated quadrupolar modulation of short-scale tensor power spectrum and relate its amplitude to the model parameters. Finally, we explore how a slowly varying sound speed modifies the squeezed signal.~These results connect the two-point, three-point, and quadrupolar tensor signatures of massive spin-two fields in the cosmological gravitational wave collider.

titles.title: Cosmological Gravitational Wave Collider Physics

abstracts.value: Next-generation gravitational-wave detectors, such as LISA, the Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer, will require accurate and efficient models of long-lived, eccentric black-hole binary signals. In previous work, we reduced the cost of evolving nonspinning eccentric effective-one-body dynamics by recasting the equations of motion in terms of osculating orbital elements and applying near-identity averaging transformations to remove the fast orbital-timescale structure during the inspiral. However, the parametrization in terms of the eccentricity and relativistic anomaly becomes singular in the circular-orbit limit, excluding quasicircular binaries and the late stages of eccentric inspirals. Moreover, the cost of generating the waveform from the averaged dynamics limited the overall speed-up to a factor of $1.5-8$. In this work, we replace the eccentricity and relativistic anomaly by the Cartesian components of the eccentricity vector, in which the averaged equations are regular for all eccentricities $0 \leq e < 1$. We also decompose the waveform modes into radial harmonics whose coefficients are tabulated as functions of the averaged variables, so that the waveform is assembled directly on the output time grid at a fixed cost per sample. We validate the method against the full effective-one-body evolution across the parameter space of binaries observable by ground-based detectors, now including circular orbits. At second postadiabatic order, the waveforms reach median mismatches of $\sim 10^{-8}$ with a maximum of $1.1 \times 10^{-5}$, while achieving speed-ups of $3-100 \times$ on a single core or up to $300 \times$ on eight cores against the serial EOB waveform. Given the speed-ups demonstrated here, we plan to apply these techniques to state-of-the-art SEOBNR models in future work.

titles.title: Efficient Eccentric and Quasicircular Effective-One-Body Waveforms via Near-Identity Averaging Transformations

abstracts.value: Two single-ion optical clocks, located in the United Kingdom and in Germany, are compared remotely via a 2220 km long optical fiber link. Both clocks are based on the ${}^2S_{1/2} (F=0)\leftrightarrow {}^2F_{7/2} (F=3)$ electric octupole (E3) transition in $^{171}\text{Yb}^+$. Using more than $10^6$ seconds of measurement data, we determine a fractional frequency difference of $1.0(4.8)\times 10^{-18}$, demonstrating agreement of the independently developed systems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first international clock comparison reaching a fractional uncertainty below $5\times 10^{-18}$, an important milestone towards an anticipated optical redefinition of the SI second. The measurement uncertainty is dominated by that of the relativistic redshift correction between the two sites, which includes time-varying gravity potential differences. We exploit the large baseline between the two clocks to search for violations of Lorentz invariance. In the absence of statistically significant modulations, we improve constraints on the Robertson-Mansouri-Sexl parameter $α$ by approximately a factor of five in the uncertainty, and provide limits on corresponding parameters within the Standard-Model Extension framework.

titles.title: International atomic clock comparison achieving $5\times 10^{-18}$ uncertainty

abstracts.value: We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

titles.title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes

abstracts.value: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

titles.title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

abstracts.value: Impedance matching is a crucial feature of an amplifier used to increase its instantaneous bandwidth and is typically achieved using static LC resonators. Here we show an approach to impedance matching in parametric amplifiers using arrays of unequal Josephson-junction-based elements (rf/dc SQUIDs, SNAILs, etc). The elements act either as small-footprint flux-tunable inductors forming an impedance-matching circuit, or 'active' amplifier elements which result in amplifier gain. We develop an analytical theory describing these systems, predicting a quasi-non-periodic amplifier frequency and gain modulation with applied flux and the broadening of gain bandwidths. We demonstrate this in devices using arrays of flux-focused SNAILs where flux biasing varies across the array. We find instantaneous bandwidths of 200 MHz with $>$17 dB of gain centred at $\sim$5.4 GHz in a device without a static impedance matcher. This broadening of amplifier bandwidth is stable with $>$100 MHz bandwidth at 17 dB gain across $>$1.2 GHz tunable bandwidth. Our analytical model captures flux dependence and qualitatively reproduces gain-bandwidths giving confidence in our understanding of these systems and allowing operational figures of merit to be optimised in future devices.

titles.title: Superconducting parametric amplifiers based on arrays of unequal Josephson junction elements

abstracts.value: POEMMA-Balloon with Radio (PBR) is a hybrid fluorescence and optical Cherenkov telescope that is a pathfinder instrument for a future Probe Of Extreme Multi-Messenger Astrophysics (POEMMA), together with a radio instrument, to be flown on a super pressure balloon in Spring 2028. One of its science objectives is follow up of astrophysical event alerts via signals of tau decays in the atmosphere, sourced by Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. The recent report of the KM3NeT Collaboration's muon event with $ E_μ=120^{+110}_{-60}$ PeV sparked searches for beyond the standard model (BSM) physics explanations. Using a specific, boosted dark matter scenario which together with the KM3NeT observation, sets a scale for the fluence of boosted dark matter in this energy range, we assess the capabilities of PBR to constrain or discover such a source for a boosted dark matter energy spectrum above $\sim 10^8$ GeV. PBR has discovery potential for dark matter energies above $10^9$ GeV, and depending on BSM input parameters, to dark matter energies as low as $1.5\times 10^8$ GeV. While the analysis is focused on one BSM example, the methodology is applicable to any BSM physics that affects tau production in the Earth.

abstracts.value: Carrollian geometry has recently emerged as the proper language to understand the geometry of null hypersurfaces from an intrinsic perspective. In this paper, we demonstrate that the Noether charge associated with the intrinsic conformal symmetry of Carrollian manifolds yields exactly the dynamical entropy formula recently proposed by Hollands, Wald and Zhang. This result follows directly from the requirement that the gravitational phase space induced on a finite distance null hypersurface be anomaly-free, in a covariant phase space sense. We then show that a linearized perturbation of this dynamical entropy charge, sourced by an external matter perturbation falling across the hypersurface, satisfies a physical process first law. Moreover, upon imposing the classical null energy condition, a linearized second law holds for the dynamical entropy. We then turn to a semi-classical generalization of this construction, where we argue that a notion of dynamical generalized entropy follows from considering perturbations sourced by external quantum matter. By imposing the quantum null energy condition (QNEC), we find a generalized second law for a linearized perturbation of the dynamical generalized entropy. Finally, we use our results to speculate on relations to the quantum focusing conjecture.

titles.title: Carrollian Symmetries and Dynamical Entropy

abstracts.value: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

titles.title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods

abstracts.value: Majorana drew a symmetric multiqubit state as points on the Bloch sphere, antipodal to the zeros of its overlap with spin coherent states. Projecting only one qubit of a general state leaves the others in a state that varies with direction. Its entanglement invariants are eigenvalues of a non-Hermitian matrix and form bands over the sphere. Exceptional points appear, without gain or loss, where the entanglement family of the rest changes. Circling one exchanges two bands, so the bands form one Riemann surface. At five qubits it fixes the entanglement class up to finitely many choices.

abstracts.value: At energies above 100 PeV, coherent radio frequency (RF) emission across the 10 -- 1000 MHz band from cosmic particle-induced atmospheric showers becomes increasingly dominant, making radio detection a powerful probe at ultrahigh energies. The Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON) considers mountaintop phased radio arrays to monitor large areas at the horizon for upward-going geomagnetic emission in the 30 -- 80 MHz band produced as a consequence of Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. As part of ongoing efforts to measure the sensitivity of BEACON to such signals, the BEACON prototype identifies cosmic rays through the same emission mechanism. Prior to 2023, BEACON operated a four-antenna prototype, which successfully demonstrated identification of coherent and impulsive sources using a beamforming RF trigger. In 2023, we upgraded the instrument to six newly designed antennas and added an independent scintillator array to cross-validate radio-detectable cosmic rays. This work details the observation of 22 candidate cosmic-ray events in a scintillator-coincidence-triggered dataset using selection cuts based on expected radio characteristics. A simulation of the hybrid-instrument performance verifies this observation rate to within an order of magnitude. We estimate a background of 0.11 events by applying the selection cuts to synthetic datasets of uncorrelated radio-scintillator pairs that are randomly formed using fixed-rate software-triggered data. The reconstructed signal polarization angles are consistent with pure geomagnetic emission compared to various background classes.

titles.title: Cosmic Ray Observations using Coincident Scintillator and Radio Signals with the Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON)

abstracts.value: A two-level emitter chirally coupled to a waveguide imprints a $π$ conditional phase on a two-photon pulse, a key component assumed in quantum photonic neural network architectures, but whether it survives the pure dephasing of a solid-state emitter is unknown, since no two-photon scattering treatment includes it. We derive the dephased two-photon amplitude in closed form and validate it against an independent Fock-state master equation. The conditional phase is pinned at exactly $π$ at every dephasing rate examined: dephasing destroys the amplitude carrying the nonlinear phase rather than rotating it. The one- and two-photon channels are not attenuated equally, so dephasing does not simply scale the node down but reweights it between photon-number sectors---an error no phase setting can train away. The standard factorization of two-photon correlators, exact for arbitrary loss, fails at first order in $γ_ϕ$, discarding $16$--$81\%$ of pairs over $γ_ϕ/γ=0.1$--$1$.

titles.title: Pure dephasing destroys two-photon amplitude, not nonlinear phase

abstracts.value: Studying core-collapse supernovae (SNe) beyond one year after explosion, when ejecta interaction with circumstellar material (CSM) progressively becomes the dominant power source, offers critical insights into the progenitor mass loss history. Using binary progenitors that underwent different levels of H-rich envelope stripping, we present radiative transfer calculations of the ejecta with CSM interaction in Type IIb, II-L and II-P SN scenarios covering epochs of 1.5 to 3-6yr, with a focus on the UV and optical properties. The impact of CSM interaction is evaluated for a cold-dense shell (CDS) of 0.1-2.0Msun (CDS velocity of ~5000-10000km/s) and shock powers of 1e39-1e41erg/s, producing a grid of about 200 models. We find that Lyalpha, MgII2800, and Halpha are typically the strongest individual lines, MgII2800 being the most constant relative to changes in time and in CDS mass. Lyalpha thrives at low CDS mass and is strongly attenuated otherwise. A large fraction of the emerging UV and optical flux is, however, influenced by a forest of Fe lines, which introduces strong optical depth effects. A myriad of other lines, generally forbidden, are predicted that each contain less than a percent of the total flux. N enrichment yield stronger N lines in the UV and optical. A subset of these models roughly match UV and optical observations of SNe 1993J, 1998S, 2013ej, and 2023ixf at 1.5-3yr, although matching the full range consistently is a challenge, in particular when dust must be invoked. Blue-red asymmetry of line profiles is typical of all lines in the UV, the more so at earlier times or higher CDS mass, even in the absence of dust. In our simulations, optical depth effects, associated with the gas or dust or both, quenches the emission of Lyalpha or [OIII]4958-5007A from regions within or below the CDS.

titles.title: The diversity of late-time interaction in Type II supernovae

abstracts.value: Mechanical vibrations are fundamental to a wide range of physical phenomena and technologies, yet their ability to actively shape free-electron dynamics remains largely unexplored. Here we theoretically show how an optomechanical membrane provides a phonon-assisted optical interface for controlling free-electron recoil and sensing localized forces. Transverse membrane motion scatters cavity light into high-momentum evanescent sidebands that enable phase-matched interaction with electrons traveling in vacuum. Beyond supplying momentum for phase matching, the vibration amplitude controls the electron-light interaction strength and redistributes electron populations among recoil orders. External forces that perturb the vibration are thereby encoded in the electron recoil spectrum. Under the modeled conditions, electron readout of localized stochastic forces can yield a higher signal-to-noise ratio than a Gaussian optical homodyne benchmark at equal detected probe rates. These results provide a theoretical basis for mechanically reconfigurable free-electron optics and mode-selective mechanical sensing.

titles.title: Phonon-assisted free-electron recoil control and mechanical sensing

abstracts.value: The waveform left after quasinormal modes filtering of binary gravitational waveforms, often called the direct wave, has recently attracted considerable debate. Analytic models of this residual waveform involve several levels of approximation, while the effects of filtering on the modeling remain unclear. These issues require further investigation. In this paper, we examine the approximation errors, limits of applicability, and role of filtering in these models. We find that the point-particle models examined here show notable discrepancies with the filtered Binary-black-holes waveforms. Analytic particle templates based on the stationary-phase approximation perform reasonably well for the \((\ell,m)=(2,2)\) multipole, but exhibit substantial limitations for the \((4,4)\). Although the filter is all-pass, it substantially affects the modeling results. Our analytic calculations on a Schwarzschild background further show that vacuum perturbations with Gaussian initial data can also exhibit direct-wave-like waveforms after filtering, with their morphology depending on the location of the initial data relative to the light ring.

titles.title: Modeling QNMs-Filtered Gravitational Waveforms: Approximation Limits and Filtering Effects

abstracts.value: SUSY breaking trilinear terms, known as A-terms, play a key role in supersymmetric phenomenology in that 1. large weak scale values help boost the light Higgs boson mass m_h -> 125 GeV and 2. the same large negative values {\it decrease} the top-squark contributions to the weak scale, thus making the theory more natural. Their renormalization group evolution also plays a key role in the string landscape in that large values can drive top-squark soft terms to tachyonic values leading to charge-and-color breaking (CCB) minima in the scalar potential. Adjacent to these CCB regions is where m_h -> 125 GeV and where natural parameter space can be found. This is an example of {\it living dangerously} on the landscape where the draw to large soft terms stops just short of catastrophic minima, but where nature is natural with a Higgs mass near its measured value. In a final panoramic view, we compare the reach of HL-LHC for landscape SUSY via several prominent signatures in the higgsino vs. gaugino mass parameter space for the case of decoupled first/second generation scalars.

titles.title: String phenomenology from the landscape

abstracts.value: Particle production from bubble collisions during First-Order Phase Transitions (FOPTs) has been studied as an efficient mechanism for baryogenesis and dark matter production, but existing semi-analytical treatments assume runaway bubbles with wall velocity $v_w\to 1$. We generalize this treatment to arbitrary $v_w< 1$, relevant for scenarios such as electroweak baryogenesis and transitions with significant wall friction. We first extend the analytical trapping-equation approach to finite-thickness boosted kink profiles for both elastic and inelastic collisions, then go beyond this by numerically solving the full Klein-Gordon equation without assuming $SO(1,1)$ symmetry or thin walls, across a broad grid of $v_w$ and potential shapes. We find the analytical generalization underestimates the true efficiency factor by orders of magnitude away from $v_w\to 1$, and provide new semi-analytic fit functions consisting of a power-law continuum plus a resonance peak, which reproduce the main spectral features of the numerical results across the parameter range studied. Applying these to a toy dark sector model, we show particle production is strongly suppressed as $v_w$ decreases from unity, enhanced for lighter produced particles, and that the relative contribution from the oscillatory peak differs from prior runaway-regime estimates. We also discuss limitations of the trapping equation and the off-shell effective-action truncation underlying this formalism.

titles.title: On Particle Production from Bubble Collisions in the Non-runaway Regime

abstracts.value: A species-resolved anisotropy-response scaling framework is used to investigate heavy-quark dynamics through the elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular ($v_3$) azimuthal anisotropies of $D^0$ mesons. The independently constrained light-flavor response provides a direct null test: the transformed $D^0$ harmonics exhibit approximate inter-harmonic closure but remain systematically displaced from the kaon-anchored scaling function, revealing a charm scaling violation. The common response is recovered through a charm-specific attenuation rescaling, $k_c$, together with a small low-$p_T$ hadronic-rescattering correction, $ζ_{\rm hs}\simeq0.06$, while retaining the established light-flavor prescription. In Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$~TeV, $k_c$ decreases from approximately $2.0$ in central and mid-central collisions to $1.27$ in the 30--50% interval. For $D^0$$v_2$, ultra-central p+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=8.16$~TeV require $k_c\simeq1.5$, whereas Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$~GeV are consistent with $k_c\simeq1$. The transition momentum exhibits a distinct system dependence: $D^0$ and light mesons show comparable $p_{T,\rm tr}\simeq4.5$--$5.0$~GeV/$c$ in Pb+Pb, consistent with the common large-system prescription also used in Au+Au, whereas p+Pb $D^0$ measurements are consistent with the lower light-meson scale of approximately $1.6$~GeV/$c$. These complementary constraints on attenuation strength and transition momentum provide a differential benchmark for heavy-quark transport and medium evolution.

abstracts.value: We propose a random Euclidean CFT description of three-dimensional de Sitter gravity, with fixed central charge and primary spectrum but fluctuating operator product coefficients. Our construction starts from compact regions assembled from generalized hyperbolic tetrahedra. We analytically continue the gravitational amplitudes computed from these triangulations to de Sitter parameters and use them to infer OPE correlations. We recover matching normalized amplitudes from a complex Liouville cosmological wavefunction. A non-Gaussian fourth moment encodes the hyperbolic core volume in an oscillatory semiclassical phase. We construct the associated Lorentzian de Sitter spacetime and show that derivatives of this phase recover its boost holonomies. Its spacelike future boundary carries a positive-definite conformal metric, while the wavefunction obeys Euclidean conformal Ward identities. These relations connect the proposed OPE statistics to both the Euclidean boundary description and the Lorentzian bulk geometry. Integrating the absolute square of the cosmological wavefunction over boundary moduli gives cosmological observables. Their long-collar factorization reproduces the edge measure of the two-matrix model.

abstracts.value: We prove a conjecture of Yu, Lai, and Oh: their rounded family of strengthened quantum Hamming bounds, which interpolates between Hamming-type bounds and the Singleton bound, holds for arbitrary exact quantum subspaces of dimension $K>1$. The result covers every integer local dimension $p\ge2$, every integer $t\ge1$, both distances $2t+1$ and $2t+2$, and every interpolation parameter $e\in\{0,\ldots,t\}$. Yu, Lai, and Oh proved these bounds for pure codes and for general codes of distance three or four; the case $e=0$ contains the ordinary quantum Hamming bound for general codes, recently proved by Zhang and Chen. More generally, for $p\ge3$, we prove the inequality $Kf(0)\le p^n\mathbb{E}f(X)$, where $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,1-p^{-2})$, for every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most $D$, with $2\le D<d$, that is nonnegative on $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ and positive at zero; here $n$ and $d$ are the code length and distance.

abstracts.value: I apply and extend the formalism of osculating orbits of Damour et al. (2004) and Lynch et al. (2026) to eccentric effective one body (EOB) models, in order to obtain an efficient yet accurate description of the inspiral-to-plunge dynamics of tidal, spinning compact binaries, including precessing ones by twisting the otherwise planar motion. The method is recast in terms of equinoctial orbital elements, to circumvent singularities associated with the zero-eccentricity limit. While the formalism is general and can be applied to any EOB model, I focus here on the TEOBResumS-Dalí family and demonstrate how this technique speeds up waveform generation without significantly compromising the accuracy of the model. Over $10^4$ binary neutron stars (BNSs) and as many binary black holes (BBHs) with initial eccentricities up to $0.6$ at $20$ Hz, the median speedup against an optimized version of the model is $\sim 2.6$ for BNSs and $\sim 1.5$ for BBHs, with mismatches against the full numerical solution always below $5 \times 10^{-7}$. The largest speedups, up to $\sim 7$ for individual systems, are obtained for light BBHs ($M \lesssim 8 M_\odot$) with low eccentricities $(e_0 \lesssim 0.1)$. In absolute terms, the median time needed to generate a BNS waveform is $\sim 0.5$ s, with $99.7\%$ of the systems below one second, and for long signals the model is up to $\sim 26$ times faster than a previous version. Applied to the calculation of initial conditions in the $e \rightarrow 0$ limit, the inclusion of radiation-reaction effects allows the model's input eccentricity to agree with the gauge-invariant waveform eccentricity down to initial values of $\sim 7 \times 10^{-8}$. abstracts.value: Tomographic weak gravitational lensing probes cosmic structure growth and geometry, making it a powerful probe of dynamical dark energy. We forecast information beyond the lensing power spectrum from non-Gaussian statistics of tomographic galaxy and CMB lensing convergence maps. Using the $\texttt{DDELenS}$ suite of ray-traced $N$-body simulations, we build Gaussian process emulators for power spectra, Minkowski functionals, moments, peak and minima counts, and the wavelet scattering transform, varying $Ω_m$, $σ_8$, $w_0$, and $w_a$. We consider Rubin-like galaxy lensing and Simons Observatory-like CMB lensing over $15{,}000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$, and validate the analysis using a withheld fiducial cosmology, analytical power-spectrum forecasts, and Gaussian random-field null tests. As an initial step, we neglect baryonic effects and intrinsic alignments and approximate galaxy sources as discrete redshift planes. Using all source redshifts at $z_s=\{0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 1100\}$, combining all five non-Gaussian statistics reduces uncertainties on $w_0$ and $w_a$ by $24.3\%$ and $28.0\%$, and on $Ω_m$ and $σ_8$ by $41.9\%$ and $45.8\%$, relative to the power-spectrum-only baseline. The resulting $w_0$ and $w_a$ uncertainties are $34.7\%$ and $48.7\%$ smaller than current DESI+DES constraints. If the DESI+DES best-fit values remain unchanged, this precision would increase the significance of the departure from $Λ$CDM from $3.0σ$ to $5.2σ$, compared with $3.8σ$ from the power spectrum alone, assuming a Gaussian posterior and unchanged $w_0$--$w_a$ correlation. Minkowski functionals and moments provide comparable constraining power, while combining them with the other summaries gives the strongest constraints. Broad galaxy-lensing redshift coverage is particularly important for dynamical dark energy, while CMB lensing provides complementary information.

abstracts.value: In the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, we provide a simple observable, the imaginary part of the retarded Green's function, which captures the timelike singularity of a charged black brane. Solving wave equations of bulk fields with different spins outside the black brane, we calculate exponentially small contributions to retarded Green's functions in the dual CFT at large real frequency. These contributions admit an interpretation in terms of paths in an analytically continued classical black brane interior via a WKB approximation: they provide the complex time elapsed along null geodesics that reflect off the singularity, and incorporate the corresponding reflection coefficients.

titles.title: A signature of the timelike singularity in holography

abstracts.value: Context: In the context of radio wave propagation through plasma concentrations and for gravitational lensing, the thin screen approximation often provides a suitable approximation for scattering and deflections caused by three-dimensional spatial structures. For scattering of electromagnetic waves from an extended medium, stochastic theories provide analytical bounds on ensemble averaged quantities, such as the scintillation index. If neither the conditions for a stochastic treatment nor the thin screen approximation are fulfilled, fully numerical methods are required. Aims: For an extended structure, the applicability of the thin screen approximation needs to be verified by comparing it with the fully three-dimensional scattering solution. We discuss various exact solutions to simple lensing geometries and provide numerical results for the propagation in the branched-flow regime, which is also of relevance in astrophysical applications. Methods: We transfer several analytical results obtained in quantum mechanical scattering theory to astrophysical settings and complement them with different numerical methods to quantify the deviations of thin screen theories from an extended medium results. Results: We provide the analytical results for spherical waves scattered by a point source and show the emergence of branchef flow in the intermediate regime between thin screen physics and stochastic media results.

titles.title: Extended vs. thin screen approximation in astrophysical settings

abstracts.value: Aims: This study aims to place constraints on the spin of Sgr A* from recent flare observations. It models the flare kinematics in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, evaluates their dependence on black hole spin, and assesses the correlation between the spin of the black hole and the astrometric observations in the Galactic center. Methods: Our study extends the work of Antonopoulou et al. 2025 to a range of black hole spins. A prominent flux eruption is identified in the simulation, and the evolution of the active region on the equatorial plane is tracked during the event. The flare model consists of a spherical hot spot ejected along the flux tube with a relativistic velocity. Results: In MAD simulations, the flux tube wraps around the jet funnel in the opposite direction to the black hole's spin. This dependence is imprinted on the flare trajectory and provides a strong correlation between the spin of the black and the flare kinematics. This analysis favors Kerr black holes, with a preference towards larger spin magnitude. Although prograde simulations show a consistent clockwise motion in the sky regardless of disk rotation, retrograde models require a clockwise accretion disk to account for the observations of July 22, 2018. Conclusions: A maximally rotating Kerr black hole is the most promising candidate for reproducing the observed flare trajectory in the vicinity of Sgr A*, illustrating a pass faction surpassing $90\%$ among the investigated flare models. In particular, determining spin orientation within this model is linked to the rotation of the accretion disk. Assuming a counterclockwise accretion disk, a prograde black hole with $a\geq1/2$ is able to reproduce the observed flare kinematics in the Galactic center. Conversely, assuming a clockwise rotation for the disk, the observations support both prograde and retrograde Kerr black holes with a large spin.

titles.title: Modeling MAD Sgr A* flares and their dependence on spin

abstracts.value: Solutions of the Bohr-Mottelson Hamiltonian with a sixth-order anharmonic oscillator potential, for both axially-symmetric and $γ$-unstable deformations, are applied to investigate the lowest states of the $^{94}$Zr nucleus. The experimentally observed $B_{4/2}$ anomaly is explained, within the present approach, by the presence of a coexistence between an approximately spherical shape ($2_{1}^{+}$) and an axially-symmetric deformed one ($4_{1}^{+}$). On the other hand, the energies of the $0_{2}^{+}$ and $2_{2}^{+}$ states and their associated electromagnetic transitions fit better a dynamical triaxial deformation configuration ($γ$-unstable). This overall picture of the lowest states in $^{94}$Zr corresponds to a triple shape coexistence scenario.

titles.title: B$_{4/2}$ anomaly related to the shape coexistence in $^{94}$Zr

abstracts.value: Quantum computing represents a fundamental shift in computation, promising to solve problems currently intractable for classical computers. However, misconceptions persist; quantum computers are not universally faster, nor do they replace classical systems. Current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices face significant challenges, including decoherence, high error rates, and limited scalability. Additionally, leveraging quantum systems requires rethinking traditional computing principles, adopting different programming models, and addressing the complexities of integrating quantum and classical workflows, making their practical use in computer science both demanding and non-trivial. This article provides a system-level perspective on quantum computing for computer scientists, software engineers, and IT professionals, examining its current capabilities, key architectural and software challenges, and potential paths toward quantum advantage in real-world applications within hybrid quantum-classical environments.

titles.title: Entangled Futures: Quantum Computing's Potential and Challenges in Computer Science

abstracts.value: Testing quantum software is challenging because quantum states cannot be directly inspected. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are a particularly important target as they are among the most promising approaches for near-term noisy quantum hardware. Many testing methods rely on classically computed results, which conflicts with the regime where quantum advantage is expected. Although prior studies mitigate this oracle problem, the core difficulty remains that existing approaches do not verify whether the execution deviates from the intended problem or whether the obtained solution is physically plausible. We propose a symmetry-oriented testing framework for VQAs that addresses this gap by using operators commuting with the target Hamiltonian as test specifications. The framework provides two complementary diagnostics: a commutator-based health check that monitors whether each execution step during optimization remains consistent with the symmetry of the target Hamiltonian, and a variance-based acceptance check that assesses the converged solution by examining whether the state is an eigenstate of the symmetry operators. Both diagnostics derive from the problem structure and do not require the exact solution. We evaluate the framework on representative user- and system-side faults, across multiple target systems, and under injected noise. Results show that the two diagnostics detect faulty behavior, provide informative signals of solution quality, and remain useful under noisy execution.

titles.title: Symmetry-Oriented Testing Framework for Variational Quantum Algorithms

abstracts.value: Optically addressable electron spin qubits that function at room temperature and under ambient conditions are essential for advancing quantum sensing. Solid state defect platforms offer robust spin-photon interfaces but lack precise defect positioning and electronic tunability. Molecular spin qubits enable bottom up chemical design yet suffer from limited photostability. Here, we introduce para-halophenyl (-Cl, -Br and -I) quantum defects in (6,5) single wall carbon nanotubes that trap triplet excitons with a spin-photon interface that is operable under ambient, room temperature conditions. These defects were shown to emit in the near infrared within the biological transparency window, and their placement on the nanotube surface provides nanoscale proximity to target environments. The deep optical traps formed by the defects yield exceptional photostability. Here, we demonstrate optical initialization and readout of these triplet states at room temperature, provide proof of principle sensing of paramagnetic molecules, and highlight potential for on chip detection. Together, these results establish SWCNT defects as a promising new platform for future quantum sensing.

titles.title: Room-temperature near-infrared optical readout of triplet spin states integrated in carbon nanotubes towards quantum sensing

abstracts.value: Quantum entropies based on the eigenspectrum characterize spectral mixedness, whereas diagonal entropies describe basis-dependent measurement uncertainty but neglect off-diagonal structure. Here, we introduce quantum association entropy (QAE), which combines the Shannon entropy of the diagonal probability distribution with the quantum Tanimoto coefficient fidelity between a quantum state and its dephased counterpart. QAE reduces to the Shannon, diagonal, and von Neumann entropies for incoherent states, remains nonzero for coherent pure states, and distinguishes states with identical diagonal statistics but different off-diagonal structures. The complementary fidelity deviation defines a QAE-based coherence-related quantity, which equals the QAE difference between the dephased and original states and quantifies the off-diagonal contribution weighted by measurement uncertainty. The same state–reference construction is extended to entanglement-related correlations using a marginal-constrained separable reference state obtained through relative-entropy optimization. For bipartite pure states in the Schmidt product basis, the resulting QAE difference is non-increasing under deterministic LOCC transformations. These results provide a common state–reference entropy-difference framework for characterizing coherence-related structure and entanglement-related correlations. •Introduces quantum association entropy via fidelity-based framework.•Captures quantum uncertainty without full eigendecomposition.•Characterizes coherence-related structure through dephased-state deviation.•Extends entropy-difference analysis to entanglement-related correlations.

titles.title: Quantum association entropy for characterizing coherence and entanglement-related quantum correlations

abstracts.value: Characterizing the unknown Hamiltonian of a quantum many-body system is essential for exploring fundamental physical phenomena and advancing frontier quantum technologies. However, the complexity of many-body interactions and limited control capabilities in realistic experimental systems render this task formidable. Here, we experimentally demonstrate efficient Hamiltonian tomography in a solid-state nuclear spin system by exploiting high-temperature thermalization. In an interacting spin network subject to periodic driving, we extract the dominant interaction structures of the engineered effective Hamiltonian using a sequence in which a tunable global rotation is sandwiched between two identical thermalization processes governed by the target Hamiltonian. By performing an SO(3) Fourier transform and principal component analysis on the response signals sampled across rotation angles, we successfully reconstruct the relative coefficients of all two-body terms, as well as selected three- and four-body interactions. Our protocol scales polynomially with the number of Hamiltonian parameters, providing an efficient and practical tool for investigating complex quantum many-body systems.

titles.title: Experimental Tomography of Quantum Many-Body Hamiltonians in Solids via Thermalization

abstracts.value: The performance of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) critically depends on the architecture of parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), yet manually designing effective circuits remains challenging due to the exponentially large design space. Conventional quantum architecture search methods address this challenge but are fundamentally constrained by predefined search spaces and expensive evaluate-and-select loops, limiting both the efficiency and novelty of discovered circuits. We propose quantum architecture diffusion (QADiff), a predictor-guided, score-based diffusion framework that shifts from searching fixed catalogs to learning generative priors over PQC structures. By representing quantum circuits as directed acyclic graphs, we train an unconditional diffusion model to capture circuit distributions alongside a graph-based performance predictor that estimates task-specific performance directly from structure. During generation, predictor gradients guide the reverse diffusion process toward high-performing regions, eliminating exhaustive candidate screening while enabling generations of architectures beyond the training distribution. We evaluate QADiff on four benchmarks: binary classification on the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) and Fashion-MNIST datasets using variational quantum classifiers, and ground-state energy estimation for the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) and Heisenberg model using variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) under IBM hardware topologies. QADiff achieves a mean accuracy of 92.44% across the top-30 discovered architectures on WDBC, with even its worst-performing selected circuit (91.01%) exceeding the mean accuracy of every baseline, and discovers VQE circuits achieving mean energies of −8.257 on the seven-qubit TFIM and −8.381 on the five-qubit Heisenberg model, outperforming all baselines with statistical significance across all tasks. On WDBC, at equal predictor-training budget, QADiff requires fewer than 1% of the query-time circuit evaluations needed by search-based methods, and maintains substantial efficiency advantages across all four benchmarks. Physical analysis of Heisenberg circuits reveals that predictor guidance discovers shallower architectures with fewer two-qubit gates while maintaining comparable global entanglement, suggesting that the guidance signal promotes efficient gate arrangement rather than simply maximizing circuit complexity. Generated circuits exhibit 100% novelty on WDBC, containing structural motifs entirely absent from the circuit pool. These results suggest that predictor-guided diffusion is a promising direction for sample-efficient, generative PQC design across VQAs.

titles.title: Quantum architecture generation via predictor-guided diffusion models

abstracts.value: We propose a theoretical protocol for reconstructing the density matrix of a single-electron spin qubit using spin-polarized transport. The system consists of a quantum dot coupled to ferromagnetic reservoirs and subject to a magnetic field lying in the <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> plane of the Bloch sphere. Spin-dependent tunneling events measured along the <math><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>±</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>±</mo></mrow></math>, and <math><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>±</mo></mrow></math> quantization axes give rise to probability distributions that encode the quantum state of the qubit. The open-system dynamics are described using a Lindblad master equation, which captures the time evolution of the spin under continuous coupling to the reservoirs. By counting tunneling events for four different magnetic alignments, we formulate a scheme for reconstructing the full density matrix of the qubit. The resulting simulation data are analyzed using Gaussian process regression as a supervised machine-learning postprocessing tool to reconstruct smooth time-dependent density-matrix elements from the measured probability distributions. The proposed model enables complete access to the open-system density matrix, including both population probabilities and relative phase information. Successful state reconstruction demonstrates the validity and robustness of the approach, highlighting its applicability to experimentally accessible spin-transport platforms.

titles.title: Spin-polarized transport tomography of a quantum-dot spin qubit via ferromagnetic leads

1.1 Why Dark Matter?

Nowadays, one of the most important challenges in cosmology and particle physics
is the understanding of the dark matter (DM) nature. Many astrophysical and cos-
mological observations [1–9] support the existence of a great amount of non-baryonic
DM which constitutes the most abundant type of the matter in the presently ac-
cepted cosmological model for our Universe (the ΛCDM model [10]). Its density is
experimentally well-determined by recent analysis of the Planck Collaboration [11],
ΩCDMh2 = 0.120± 0.001. They have also specified the value of the baryonic density,
Ωbh2 = 0.0224± 0.0001, and that of the total matter density, Ωmh2 = 0.1430± 0.0011.
Despite this fact, its true identity remains still an open question, see for example a
discussion in [12]. The current theoretical efforts are aimed at finding extensions of
the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics looking for dark candidates since under
its present form it cannot explain the DM nature.

1.1.1 Evidence for DM

As early as the 1930s, F. Zwicky came to the conclusion that it was required a bigger
amount of matter than the visible one so that galaxies in the Coma Cluster remained
joined [1, 2]. Therefore, it was necessary the existence of another type of matter with
negligible or no electromagnetic but gravitational interaction.

However, it was not until 1977, year in which Vera Cooper Rubin measured the
rotation curves of spiral galaxies, when the most convincing and direct evidence
for DM was achieved. Observed rotational curves exhibited a flat behavior at large
distances against what was expected [3]. In other words, if it is considered that the
galaxy mass distribution is gathered in the visible part of the galaxy, far from the
galactic disk the gravitational field is that created by a point-like mass. In this way,
the velocity of the stars will have to decrease at large distances as v(r) ∝ 1√

r . On
the contrary, it was obtained that v(r) ∼ constant, see Figure 1.1. This fact implies a
mass halo M(r) ∝ r. Hence, galaxies should be inside an enormous halo of dark and
unknown matter.

Since then, a big amount of proofs have been exhibited. The General Relativity
(GR) theory postulates that masses distort the space-time and, consequently, a pho-
ton passing close to a massive object will deviate its otherwise straight trajectory.
Thus, some clusters and elliptical galaxies act like gravitational lenses curving the
light trajectory, see Figure 1.2. Using this method, masses of clusters and galaxies
can be measured and what is obtained is that only ∼ 20% of the mass deduced by
gravitational lenses can be observed (luminous matter).

Another striking DM evidence is that provided by the Bullet Cluster [4–6]. This
cluster is part of two colliding clusters of galaxies, being the smaller subcluster mov-
ing away from the larger one. It has been demonstrated that this cluster pair is
mainly compound by three different types of matter. One of them is DM, whose
abundance can be measured using gravitational lensing. On the other hand, the
stars of the galaxies are observable in visible light and it can be seen that they are
not greatly affected by the collision although gravitationally slowed. Another com-
ponent of the Bullet Cluster is the hot gas, emitting X-rays, which constitutes most
of the baryonic matter in the cluster pair and moves much slower than the stars
due to the electromagnetic interaction. The key point here is that, during collision,
these three components behave differently and can be studied separately. It can be
observed that, whereas both gases collide creating a shock wave, the centers of grav-
itational masses of the subclusters do not collide. See Figure 1.3. This fact cannot be
explained in theories involving a pure gravitational effect such as Modified Newto-
nian Dynamics (MOND) [14, 15] since, in this case, the centers of masses would be
expected to follow the baryonic matter.

Besides these indications of the DM existence, there are other ones at cosmolog-
ical scales. One powerful window into the early Universe is the Cosmic Microwave
Background (CMB) [7–9]. This background radiation was originated at the time in
which radiation and matter decoupled, when the age of the Universe was ∼ 380000
years and baryonic matter started to collapse and to generate structures. Nowadays,
CMB is observed to follow an almost perfect black body spectrum, isotropic at 10−5

level, corresponding to a temperature T = 2.725K [16]. Its small anisotropies are in-
timately related with the structure formation and, from their analysis, it is possible
to test cosmological models and get information about the cosmological parameters.
In this way, assuming the ΛCMD model for our Universe, both the abundance of
baryons and total matter are determined [11] obtaining that ∼ 85% of the total mat-
ter content does not possess a baryonic nature. Besides, it can be concluded that
baryonic matter has not been able alone to create the present Universe. DM would



1.1. Why Dark Matter? 3

have to decouple from radiation before than ordinary matter to prompt the big struc-
tures that we detect.

1.1.2 Candidates

As it has been previously reviewed, the evidence for DM is mainly based on gravi-
tational effects and it can not be explained only by baryonic matter. At the moment,
the problem has been circumvented by postulating a new type of matter which inter-
acts gravitationally but negligibly electromagnetically [12]. As another explanation,
modifications of gravity have also been suggested as the answer for the total miss-
ing gravitational matter. Nevertheless, apart from the problem for some modified
gravity (MG) theories like MOND to explain the dynamics of the Bullet Cluster [6],
the impossibility to reproduce large-scale structure formation and the anisotropies
in the CMB rules out most of them [18–20]. Despite this, newer MG theories aim
to match ΛCDM model on cosmological scales solving the before mentioned prob-
lems [21, 22]. However, a recent paper [23] concludes that internal motions of Dwarf
Galaxies can only be understood by adding cold DM (CDM). They postulate that if
two galaxies with the same mass profiles exist, then, they will have to exhibit the
same internal dynamics as one another since the law of gravity is the same for both
of them. In their study they find that there are at least two galaxies with almost the
same mass profiles but largely different gravitational effects.

In this context, the new dark particles that we are looking for have to fulfill
some requirements. First of all, DM particles have to be stable against decay or
be long lasting, having a lifetime comparable or longer than the age of the Universe,
τU ∼ 1017 s. They should be non-relativistic (as proposed by the paradigm of CDM)
at the epoch of structure formation to allow the rise of big structures. In addition, if
our candidate is a leading DM constituent, its density has to be consistent with the
relic density deduced from the CMB fluctuations [11]. One possibility for its identity
is that it is a thermal relic from the early Universe. This points to a weakly interacting
particle with a thermally averaged annihilation cross section 〈σav〉 ∼ 3 10−26 cm3/s
[24]. As another condition, DM should be mostly collisionless in order to be com-
patible with constraints on structure formation and observations of galaxy cluster
systems [25]. However, this could be also satisfied for strongly self interacting DM
created thermally via 2 to 3 or 2 to 4 processes (providing the correct relic density)
as long as its mass is in the appropriate range, see [26–29]. Finally, it is generally



4 Chapter 1. Thesis report

argued that DM particles must be electrically neutral or slightly charged [30]. Oth-
erwise they would scatter off photons and thus not be dark.

One of the best motivated candidates are the WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Mas-
sive Particles) [24] which interact with SM particles through weak interaction. This
can be understood as an interaction given by the Fermi theory, with a coupling
GF ∼ 10−5 GeV−2 [31], or just a (sub)weak but non negligible coupling. The motiva-
tion for them comes from the assumption that DM particles were created thermally
in the early Universe providing the known relic abundance, although other WIMP
production mechanisms exist, see [24, 32]. In addition, these requirements can be
fulfilled by strongly interacting massive particles (SIMPs) as long as they provide
〈σav〉 ∼ 3 10−26 cm3/s. These candidates with interaction cross sections with SM
particles significantly larger than those of the weak interactions have been studied
in the literature by many authors [33–35]. On the other hand, apart from this re-
quirement, values for both DM mass and cross sections with baryonic matter have
to be in concordance with constraints coming from the so-called direct, indirect and
collider searches. This will be discussed later.

A vast amount of well motivated models can be used to describe the phenomenol-
ogy of these WIMP and SIMP candidates (Supersymmetric DM [36], Scalar DM [37],
secluded DM [38]...). It is out of the scope of this work to discuss the details of all of
them. We will restrict our discussion to the models considered during the research
presented in this thesis dissertation.

An useful approach is describing the interactions of DM with SM particles by
effective operators making minimal assumptions on the DM particle nature and its
couplings with SM particles [39, 40]. In their validity range (low momentum trans-
ferred) these Effective Field Theories (EFTs) have demonstrated to successfully de-
scribe the main features of generic WIMP candidates, having predictive power for
direct and collider experiments.

On the other hand, some theories propose a DM particle which interacts with
SM particles through metastable mediators providing an almost negligible rate for
direct detection (DD) and collider production due to the reduction of its couplings to
SM particles by this intermediate state. This scenario is known as secluded DM. In
the context of these theories there is a vast amount of models described by different
lagrangians, see Tables I and II from [41].

One of the motivations for studying this scenario is the fact that, although di-
rect and collider searches could be not sensitive to these candidates, indirect signals



1.1. Why Dark Matter? 5

from their annihilation may be observed. Besides, if the annihilation of DM into SM
particles via metastable mediators happens inside stellar objects, the indirect signal
coming from this reaction may be enhanced. This would happen due to the fact
that the finite lifetime of these mediators may decrease the attenuation of the SM
final products passing through the interstellar medium [42–44]. There are also other
authors studying the possibility that these candidates annihilate into long lived par-
ticles in the galactic center providing an excess of SM particles (coming from the
decay of these mediators) far away from the point in which the annihilation takes
place [45]. Short lived mediators are also taken into account in the context of indirect
detection (ID) [46] demonstrating that the signal is highly dependent not only on the
DM annihilation cross section and annihilation final states, but also on the mediator
mass.

1.1.3 DM searches and current constraints

In this context, it is necessary to talk about experimental searches and current con-
straints for our DM candidates.

It is likely that if our galaxy resides inside an enormous DM halo, these par-
ticles may be crossing the Earth continuously making possible their detection via
interaction with a terrestial target provided a non-zero cross section exists. DD ex-
periments search for a scattering signal due to the interaction between DM particles
and SM ones. In particular, most of these settings try to detect particles with masses
mχ & 1 GeV by measuring an energy of recoiling nuclei Er ∼ keV in the detector
[60]. Other types of direct searches that are starting to be increasingly significant
are those which look for DM in the sub-GeV mass range. Such light masses are un-
reachable for nuclear recoil DD experiments, but may be detected through the small
ionization signals caused by DM-electron scattering [61].

Another method of search is attempting to detect DM particles indirectly, via
their annihilation or decay into SM products, such as neutrinos [63, 64], gamma
rays [65] or antiprotons and positrons [66] above those present in the astrophysical
background. An excess of their annihilation products is trying to be observed in
regions of increased DM density such as the galactic center and dwarf spheroidal
galaxies.

Yet as another strategy, DM is searched as final product in annihilation of SM
particles at colliders, see [67] for a review. These experiments alone are not be able
to detect DM, they would detect the existence of an invisible particle providing clues
for direct and indirect detection experiments. However, they can put constraints on
certain models, see Figures 7 and 8 from [67]. Besides, existing models from super-
symmetric theories predict favoured regions in the space of parameters which can be
complemented by DD and ID bounds, see Figure 8 from [68]. If DM can be produced
in particle accelerators, it would be a powerful tool to understand the connection of
ordinary matter to DM and to comprehend how the two sectors interacted shortly
after the Big Bang.

So far, despite direct and indirect search experiments are increasingly more sensi-
tive and colliders such as the LHC [69] are running at energies close to 13 TeV center-
of-mass energies, no signal coming from DM particles has been detected. However,
exclusion limits have been established both for nucleon-DM [62] and electron-DM
[70] cross sections versus DM mass values. In Figure 1.4 from [71] contraints on
DM-nucleon SI cross section versus DM mass are shown.

1.2 Dark Matter inside compact objects

In spite of the variety of detection experiments, some popular candidates are yet
difficult to test and they may be well suited to be studied indirectly in astrophysical
scenarios. To illustrate, LDM particles with masses smaller than that of the nucleon
can only provide kinematical recoil energies at the Er ∼eV range, below the Er ∼keV
threshold for current conventional terrestrial searches in DD experiments. Never-
theless, they could yet have an impact on the properties of astrophysical objects and
provide new indirect signals.

On the other hand, there are many DM candidates displaying interactions with
ordinary matter which are momentum suppressed, i.e. their scattering cross sections
with normal matter σχ,N ∼ O(q2) or σχ,N ∼ O(q4), see [72, 73]. This fact makes them
almost impossible to test via DD experiments due to the fact that in this context
q → 0. On the contrary, these interactions can be important inside dense objects,
such as neutron stars (NSs) or white dwarfs (WDs), in which transferred momentum
could be higher due to typical temperatures, 10−4 MeV . T . 1 MeV (setting the
Boltzmann constant kB = 1), since it is likely that DM particles gain energy from
the medium during the interaction. Besides, collisions will not be much coherent
because of the boost of DM particles provided by these compact stars.

Yet as another motivation to test DM in these compact scenarios, velocity sup-
pressed annihilation channels, i.e those in which σv ∼ O(v2), in vacuum or inside
the Earth or the Sun, where v2 ∼ 10−6, arise from some particular type of DM-
SM couplings, see tables I and II of [41] for some examples. These channels could
be important if happen inside compact objects in which once DM has thermalized

1.2.1 Neutron Stars and White Dwarfs

Both NSs and WDs are formed at the end of the life of a luminous star. The fate of a
star with a mass 0.4M� . M . 8M� is a WD with a degenerate core of Carbon (C)
and Oxygen (O), whereas stars with masses M & 8 M� will end their lives becoming
NSs or black holes depending on the remnant mass.

NSs are the smallest and densest stars known, with a radius of R ∼ 10 km and
being ∼ 1014 times denser than the Earth. Into such a small object there is an en-
closed mass of M ∼ 1.5M�.

The notion of NSs as the remnants of supernova (SN) explosions [75], very en-
ergetic events in which the previous star releases its outer layers producing electro-
magnetic emissions, neutrinos and gravitational waves, was suggested for the first
time by Baade and Zwicky in 1934. They proposed that the source of these explo-
sions, some of which are visible in daylight for weeks, was the gravitational binding
energy of the NS progenitor. On the other hand, NSs can acquire high angular ve-
locities due to the angular momentum conservation of the progenitor and strong
magnetic fields through magnetic flux conservation during the collapse of luminous
stars. These two features were those which made these objects suitable to be detected
for the first time in 1967 due to the beamed periodic signal of pulsars [76].

These compact stars are mostly constituted by nucleons (∼ 90% of the star),
which support the star against collapse due to the Fermi pressure, forming a cen-
tral core at a density in excess of nuclear saturation density, ρ0 = 2.4 1014 g/cm3

[77]. The rest of the star is composed by an outer and an inner crust [78]. The



1.2. Dark Matter inside compact objects 9

outer crust is formed by periodically arranged nuclei, with increasing baryonic num-
ber, A, from Iron (Fe) to Krypton (Kr), with typical densities ranging from ρB ∼
2 106 − 4 1011 g/cm3. At these high densities, electrons form a degenerate Fermi
sea and very neutron rich nuclei are immersed in a gas of dripped neutrons. This
∼ 1 km thick layer forms the inner crust. See Figure 1.5 from [74] where the section
of a NS is shown.

In addition, NSs are born hot in SN explosions, achieving internal temperatures
around T ∼ 1011 K. During the first minute after its birth the star becomes transpar-
ent for neutrinos generated in its interior [79, 80]. In the following stage NSs cool by
emitting neutrinos from their body (mainly from the core) and by heating transport
through the envelope to the surface, where electromagnetic emission takes place. In
a hundred of years the NS crust and core become thermally adjusted and the NS
interior can be considered isothermal. Emission of neutrinos mainly cools the star
over the next million years making the star to reach temperatures T ∼ 107 K.

A less dense star example is that of a WD. WDs are the core remnants of medium
and low-mass stars after a thermal expansion of their envelope. They are constituted
by nuclei immersed in a degenerate electron gas, which supports the star against
gravitational collapse due to the degeneracy pressure of electrons. Because of the
Pauli exclusion principle, which postulates that two fermions with same quantum
numbers cannot occupy the same state, collapse of a WD will increase the kinetic
energy of the electrons and, accordingly, the pressure. Densities of these objects are
ranging ρB ∼ 105 − 109 g/cm3, with masses between M ∼ 0.4M� and M ∼ 1.2M�
and an average mass of M ∼ 0.6M� compacted in radii of ∼ 1% of the solar radius.

WDs show a layered structure: in most cases it consists of a C and O degenerate
and nearly isothermal core surrounded by a very thin almost pure Hydrogen (H)
layer on top of a Helium (He) one, both non-degenerate [81]. These outer layers
constitute ∼ 1% of the total radius of the star and, although thin, they determine its
thermal evolution. Whereas most of the WD mass is at almost the same tempera-
ture, T ∼ 106 − 107 K, the surface temperature drops significantly reaching values
between T ∼ 103 − 104 K [82, 83].

With respect to the equation of state (EoS), for NSs microscopic theories of dense
matter are model dependent and provide a large list of possibilities [84], ranging
from stiff to soft ones, with different compositions of inner NS cores. A stiff EoS is
understood as one in which pressure increases fast when density increases, being the
matter described by this equation hard to compress. Conversely, a soft EoS provides
a smaller increase of pressure for the same change in density.

On the other hand, for WDs it can be a good estimation to use a polytropic EoS,
which relates pressure and density through an equation of the form P = Kρ1+ 1

n ,
with K a constant with appropriate units and n the index of the equation. It can be
easily demonstrated that a non-relativistic Fermi gas of degenerate electrons can be
described by an EoS with n = 3

2 , whereas for the relativistic case the correspondent
index is n = 3. Thus, a WD with non-relativistic electrons could be described by a
polytropic EoS of index n = 3

2 . Above a certain density, electrons will become rel-
ativistic as they are pushed up to higher momenta by the Pauli exclusion principle.
In this case, the index needed will be n = 3. See [85–88] for more details.

Memoria de la tesis

1.1 ¿Por qué Materia Oscura?

Hoy en día, uno de los retos más importantes en el ámbito de la cosmología y la
física de partículas es la comprensión de la naturaleza de la materia oscura (DM, por
sus siglas en inglés). Multitud de observaciones cosmológicas y astrofísicas [1–9]
evidencian la existencia de una gran cantidad de DM no bariónica que constituye
la mayor parte de la materia en el modelo cosmológico actualmente aceptado para
nuestro Universo (modelo ΛCDM [10]). Su densidad está determinada experimen-
talmente con gran exactitud por análisis recientes de la colaboración Planck [11],
ΩCDMh2 = 0.120± 0.001, así como la densidad bariónica, Ωbh2 = 0.0224± 0.0001,
y la total, Ωmh2 = 0.1430± 0.0011. A pesar de este hecho, su verdadera identidad
continúa siendo una cuestión no resuelta, ver por ejemplo una discusión sobre esto
en [12]. Desde un punto de vista teórico, actualmente, los esfuerzos se centran en
encontrar extensiones del Modelo Estándar (SM, por sus siglas en inglés) de física
de partículas buscando nuevos candidatos, ya que éste en su forma actual no puede
explicar la naturaleza de la DM.

1.1.1 Algunas evidencias

Ya en 1933, F. Zwicky llegó a la conclusión de que, para que las galaxias del Cú-
mulo de Coma permanecieran unidas, se requería una cantidad de materia mayor
que la que se observada debido a la emisión electromagnética (materia luminosa)
[1, 2]. Por lo tanto, era necesaria la existencia de otro tipo de materia cuya inter-
acción electromagnética fuera despreciable o inexistente pero que sí interaccionara
gravitacionalmente.

Sin embargo, no fue hasta 1977, año en el que Vera Cooper Rubin midió las cur-
vas de rotación de galaxias espirales, que se logró la evidencia más directa y con-
vincente. Las curvas de rotación observadas mostraban un comportamiento plano a
grandes distancias del centro galáctico, contrariamente a lo que se esperaba [3]. En
otras palabras, si se considera que la distribución de masa de la galaxia está agru-
pada en la parte visible de ésta, lejos del disco galáctico el campo gravitacional puede
ser descrito por el de una masa puntual. De esta forma, la velocidad de las estrellas
tendrá que disminuir a grandes distancias de la forma v(r) ∝ 1√

r . Por el contrario, lo
que se obtuvo fue que v(r) ∼ constante, ver Figura 1.1. Este hecho implica que debe
haber un halo cuya masa M(r) ∝ r. Es decir, las galaxias deben estar dentro de un
halo enorme de materia oscura y desconocida.

Desde entonces, se han obtenido una gran cantidad de evidencias. La teoría de la
Relatividad General (GR, por sus siglas en inglés) postula que las masas deforman el
espacio-tiempo y, como consecuencia, un fotón pasando cerca de un objeto masivo
desviará su trayectoria, que en otro caso seguiría una línea recta. De esta forma,

Otra evidencia importante es aquella que proviene del Cúmulo de Bala [4–6].
Este cúmulo es parte de dos cúmulos de galaxias que están en colisión, estando el
subcúmulo menor alejándose del mayor. La cantidad de DM del cúmulo puede
medirse usando el método de lente gravitacional. Por otro lado, las estrellas de las
galaxias, que no se ven muy afectadas por la colisión a pesar de que su movimiento
es algo decelerado gravitacionalmente, son observadas en el visible. Otro compo-

mayor parte de la materia bariónica del sistema de cúmulos y se desplaza mucho
más lentamente que las estrellas debido a la interacción electromagnética. El punto
importante aquí es que, durante la colisión, estos tres componentes se comportan de
forma diferente, pudiendo estudiarse por separado. Se puede observar que, mien-
tras que los gases colisionan creando una onda de choque, los centros de las masas
gravitacionales, que no se encuentran donde están los gases de rayos X sino en dos
regiones separadas cerca de las galaxias visibles, no se ven afectados por la colisión.
Ver Figura 1.3. Este hecho no puede ser explicado mediante teorías que involu-
cran efectos puramente gravitacionales como la Dinámica Newtoniana Modificada
(MOND, por sus siglas en inglés) [14, 15] puesto que, en ese caso se esperaría que la
lente gravitacional ocurriera gracias a la materia bariónica.

Además de estas evidencias, existen otras a escalas cosmológicas. Una potente
ventana hacia el Universo primitivo es el Fondo Cósmico de Microondas (CMB, por
sus siglas en inglés) [8, 9]. Esta radiación de fondo fue originada en el momento en
el que se desacoplaron la materia bariónica y la radiación, cuando el Universo tenía
∼ 380000 años y la materia bariónica empezó a colapsar y a dar lugar a estructuras.
Hoy en día observamos que el CMB sigue un espectro de cuerpo negro práctica-
mente perfecto, isótropo a un nivel de 10−5, con una temperatura T = 2.725K. Sus

1.1.2 Candidatos

Como hemos visto en la sección anterior, estas evidencias están basadas principal-
mente en efectos gravitacionales que no pueden ser explicados únicamente por la
materia bariónica. Hasta el momento, el problema se ha sorteado postulando la ex-
istencia de un nuevo tipo de materia que interacciona gravitacionalmente pero cuya
interacción electromagnética es despreciable [12]. Como otra alternativa, se ha sug-
erido que la explicación a la materia que falta podría venir dada por modificaciones
de la gravedad. Sin embargo, aparte del problema que presentan algunas teorías
de gravedad modificada (MG, por sus siglas en inglés) como MOND a la hora de
explicar la dinámica del Cúmulo de Coma [6], la imposibilidad para reproducir la
formación de estructuras a grandes escalas y las anisotropías del CMB descarta la
mayor parte de estas teorías [18–20]. A pesar de ello, es cierto que teorías más mod-
ernas logran coincidir con el modelo ΛCDM a escalas cosmológicas, resolviendo
estos dos problemas [21, 22]. Sin embargo, un paper reciente [23] llega a la con-
clusión de que los movimientos internos de galaxias enanas solo pueden entenderse
añadiendo materia oscura fría (CDM, por sus siglas en inglés). Su planteamiento
es que si existen dos galaxias con el mismo perfil de materia, entonces, ambas ten-
drán que presentar la misma dinámica interna, debido a que la ley de la gravedad es
la misma para ambas. En su estudio encuentran que hay al menos dos galaxias con
prácticamente el mismo perfil de materia pero con efectos gravitacionales diferentes.

En este contexto, las nuevas partículas que buscamos tienen que satisfacer ciertas
condiciones. Primero, la DM tiene que ser estable, en el sentido de que no debe de-
caer en otras partículas, o de larga vida, siendo ésta comparable o mayor que la edad
del Universo, τU ∼ 1017 s. Debe ser no relativista (como propone el paradigma de
