6.3.2 Two-Stage Reconstruction Pipeline

Overview

The query-based mask-prediction formulation defined in Eq. 6.5 is realised through a
two-stage architecture consisting of a hit-filtering model followed by a MaskFormer-
based track-reconstruction network.

The first stage predicts whether each detector hit is relevant to the chosen reconstructable-
particle target. Applying a high-e!ciency filtering threshold substantially reduces
the number of input tokens while retaining nearly all hits that can contribute to
the downstream reconstruction task. The filtered hit collection therefore allows the
subsequent Transformer model to operate within a computationally tractable regime.

The second stage performs hit-to-track assignment and track-level prediction. Given the
filtered hit set, the model predicts a fixed collection of candidate objects, each comprising
a track-validity score, a soft hit-assignment mask, and a set of continuous particle-
property predictions. This stage implements the object-centric tracking representation
introduced in Section 6.3.1.

Hit-Filtering Model

The hit-filtering stage is a lightweight Transformer encoder operating at the level
of individual detector hits. Each hit is first mapped to a learned embedding using
a multilayer perceptron and augmented with positional encodings of the cylindrical
coordinates (r,↽, z). Since ↽ is periodic, its positional encoding is constructed from
sine and cosine functions at multiple frequencies, ensuring that the encoding is periodic
under ↽ ↑ ↽+2↩ and continuous across the ↔↩/↩ boundary. The Transformer encoder
then updates the hit embeddings through self-attention, producing a contextualised
representation of each hit that incorporates information from other hits in the event.

The encoder output is passed to a binary classification head trained with a binary
cross-entropy loss to predict whether each hit should be retained for downstream
track reconstruction. The targets are derived from the same reconstructable-particle
definition used for the MaskFormer tracking stage, as specified in Section 6.4.2. The
filter therefore acts as a target-conditioned preprocessing stage, reducing the input

phase space.

6.3.3 E!cient Attention and Geometric Locality

The large hit multiplicities present in TrackML events make dense self-attention over
the complete hit collection computationally impractical. Standard self-attention has
quadratic computational and memory scaling in the number of hit tokens, so applying
it directly to all detector hits would be poorly suited to high-occupancy tracking
environments.

Although attention is in general permutation equivariant, track reconstruction depends
critically on detector geometry [117]. The model is therefore expected to benefit from
spatial priors. In particular, detector geometry can be used as an inductive bias for
sparse attention.

In a solenoidal tracking detector, charged-particle trajectories have coherent structure
in cylindrical coordinates, so the interactions most relevant to local trajectory recon-
struction are not uniformly distributed over the full hit collection. In the architecture
used here, this structure is exploited by ordering hits in ↽ and applying sliding-window
self-attention in the resulting sequence.

Each hit attends only to a fixed neighbourhood of w nearby hits in the ↽-ordered
sequence. This windowed-attention pattern is used in both Transformer encoders in the
pipeline, the hit-filtering encoder, which operates on the full input hit collection, and

6.3.4 Decoder Architecture and Outputs

Each decoder layer updates the query representations through query self-attention,
query–hit cross-attention, and feed-forward transformations. The query self-attention
allows candidate tracks to exchange information, while the query–hit cross-attention
allows each query to aggregate information from the encoded detector-hit collection.
In addition to conventional query-to-hit cross-attention, the architecture includes hit-
to-query cross-attention, allowing the encoded hit representations to be updated using
information from the evolving query states. This bidirectional exchange couples the
candidate-track and detector-hit representations throughout the decoder. It increases
the computational cost of each layer, but was found to improve the consistency of the
predicted hit–track associations.

A central feature of the decoder is the use of masked attention, following the Mask2Former
formulation [94]. In Mask2Former, intermediate mask predictions are used to constrain



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 106

later cross-attention layers to the predicted foreground pixel region of each object query.
The analogous mechanism is used here for track reconstruction. After each decoder
layer, the current track–hit assignment predictions are converted into query-dependent
attention masks, which are then used by the following decoder layer. Hits with low
predicted compatibility for a given query are suppressed in that query’s subsequent
cross-attention update, while hits with su!ciently high compatibility remain available.

This mask-feedback mechanism is important for the tracking task. The decoder is
not required to repeatedly search the full filtered hit collection from scratch at every
layer. Instead, each query progressively refines a candidate trajectory by concentrating
attention on the subset of hits currently associated with that query. This encourages
the decoder to resolve the hit-assignment problem iteratively, reducing interference
from unrelated hits and from competing trajectory hypotheses.

The role of masked attention should be distinguished from the fixed-width local attention
used in the encoder. The encoder window changes the permitted hit–hit interaction
pattern and reduces the asymptotic scaling of encoder self-attention. By contrast, the
masked attention used in the decoder is primarily a learned focusing mechanism. In
the architecture studied in this chapter, it does not a"ect the asymptotic memory
scaling of the decoder cross-attention. Its purpose is instead to improve the quality
and stability of the query–hit associations by allowing intermediate mask predictions
to guide subsequent decoder updates.

The final query representations are passed to task heads that predict the track-validity
score sj , the soft hit-assignment mask mj , and the continuous particle-property vector
ŷj for each query j.

The hit-assignment masks are constructed by projecting the query and hit representa-
tions into a common embedding space and evaluating their pairwise similarity, followed
by a sigmoid activation. The continuous particle properties are predicted from the final
query representations using dedicated regression heads.

6.3.5 Matching and Training Objective

Training follows the set-prediction paradigm introduced in Section 6.3.1. The decoder
produces a fixed collection of Nquery candidate predictions, while the target for each
event is an unordered set of truth trajectories whose multiplicity varies between events.
Since there is no predefined correspondence between a particular decoder query and
a particular truth track, the predicted objects are matched to the truth trajectories
before evaluating the loss.

The loss contains separate terms for the track-validity classification, the hit-assignment
mask, and the continuous particle-property regression. The classification term LCE is
a cross-entropy loss over the physical-track and null classes, and supervises whether
each query corresponds to a reconstructed trajectory. The hit-assignment mask is
supervised using a combination of Focal [119] loss and Dice loss [120]. The Focal loss
LFocal is used to handle the strong imbalance between hits assigned to a given trajectory
and the much larger number of hits not belonging to that trajectory. The Dice loss
LDice directly compares the overlap between the predicted and truth masks, making
it well suited to supervising the quality of the complete hit set assigned to a track.



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 108

The regression term Lreg uses a Smooth L1 loss [121, 122] on the predicted particle
properties, providing a robust penalty for continuous track-level quantities, such as
particle momentum.

Auxiliary losses are applied to the track-validity and hit-assignment predictions pro-
duced after each decoder layer, rather than only to the final decoder output. This
provides direct supervision for the intermediate predictions used by the masked-attention
mechanism, encouraging the decoder to refine candidate trajectories progressively across
layers. In contrast, the particle-property regression loss is evaluated only from the
predictions obtained after the final decoder layer. The full training objective therefore
combines the auxiliary classification and mask losses from the intermediate decoder
layers with the final classification, mask, and regression losses.

The assignment is performed using the Hungarian algorithm [116], which identifies the
one-to-one matching between predicted queries and truth tracks that minimises the
total matching cost over the event. For predicted query j and truth trajectory k, the
pairwise matching cost is

6.4.2 Target Definitions and Dataset Splits

Hit-Filtering Targets

The hit-filtering model is trained as a binary classifier at the level of individual detector
hits. A hit is labelled as signal if it is associated with a reconstructable particle under the
target definition of the corresponding model configuration, and as background otherwise.
The background class therefore includes simulated detector noise, hits from particles
outside the fiducial acceptance, hits from particles below the selected p

min

and hits from particles that leave fewer than three selected pixel measurements.

The filter performs target-conditioned preprocessing. It reduces the hit multiplicity
presented to the track-reconstruction model while retaining nearly all hits relevant to
the selected reconstruction phase space. The inference threshold is therefore chosen
to favour high signal-hit e!ciency rather than maximum output purity. Residual

background hits are passed to the downstream MaskFormer model, where they may be

Training, Validation, and Test Splits

The labelled TrackML sample is divided into mutually exclusive training, validation,
and test sets at the event level. A total of 100 events are reserved for validation and a
further 100 events are reserved for final testing, with all 8650 remaining labelled events
used for training. The validation sample is used to monitor optimisation, select model
checkpoints, and determine inference operating points. The test sample is used only
for the final performance evaluation.

Duplicate suppression is relevant for fixed-query set-prediction models because several

6.5 Results

This section presents the performance of the MaskFormer configurations defined in
Section 6.4. Their reconstructable-particle selections and principal architectural pa-
rameters are summarised in Tables 6.2 and 6.3, respectively. All results are evaluated
on the common held-out test sample of 100 TrackML events.

The MF-0.6 target definition gives the larger reconstructable-particle multiplicity and
includes a greater proportion of strongly curved low-pT trajectories. The MF-1.0
target population extends to |▷| ′ 4 at a higher transverse-momentum threshold and
correspondingly lower multiplicity. In both configurations, the models receive hits
from the full available TrackML pixel subsystem. The two configurations therefore
probe complementary operating points, a lower-pT central reconstruction task and a
higher-threshold full-acceptance task.

6.5.1 Hit-Filtering Performance

The hit-filtering performance is summarised in Table 6.4 and Fig. 6.7. Before filtering,
only 13–16% of the selected pixel hits are associated with reconstructable particles
under the corresponding target definition. The hit-filtering model assigns each hit a
score representing its predicted probability of belonging to a reconstructable particle.
Hits with a score greater than 0.1 are retained and passed to the track-reconstruction
model, while those below this threshold are discarded. This selection increases the
signal-hit purity to approximately 64–73%, while retaining close to 99.5% of signal
hits. The low threshold is deliberately conservative: it reduces the input multiplicity
substantially while prioritising the retention of measurements that may contribute to
target trajectories.

A central requirement of the filtering stage is that particles remain reconstructable after
hit selection. As shown in Fig. 6.7, more than 98% of reconstructable particles retain at
least three selected pixel hits after filtering in both configurations. The filtering stage
therefore contributes only a small upper bound on the attainable downstream tracking
e!ciency. At the same time, the average hit multiplicity is reduced from approximately
60 000 hits per event to approximately 10 000 retained hits, allowing the subsequent
MaskFormer reconstruction model to operate in a computationally tractable regime.

6.5.4 Inference Time and Scalability

The inference times for both configurations are listed in Table 6.6 and demonstrate
sub-second inference for the TrackML configurations and hardware setup studied. These
timings were measured on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with a batch size of 1.

Over the range of occupancies studied, the measured inference time exhibits an approxi-
mately linear dependence on hit multiplicity, as shown in Fig. 6.10. For the hit-filtering
and encoder stages, this behaviour follows from fixed-width local attention, whose
cost scales as O(Nhitw) for fixed window size w. Within a given trained configuration,
the number of decoder queries is fixed and is the same for every event. The dense

Comparison with classical tracking

For context, the Run-2 ATLAS Inner Detector reconstruction requires approximately
1–4 s per event over the typical pile-up range ⇐µ⇒ ⇔ 20–60 on the CPU hardware used
for o#ine reconstruction [126]. The quoted ATLAS timings describe Run-2 operating
conditions and should not be interpreted as estimates of the cost of tracking at the
HL-LHC. Conventional track reconstruction becomes increasingly expensive as the
detector occupancy rises. In particular, higher hit multiplicities increase the number of
compatible combinations considered during seeding and cause track-building algorithms
to branch when several measurements are compatible with a candidate trajectory. The
resulting computational cost is expected to grow super-linearly with occupancy. This
presents a significant challenge for the HL-LHC, where up to approximately ⇐µ⇒ = 200

interactions per bunch crossing are expected.

A more closely related classical reference is provided by the ACTS study [58], which
evaluates a seed finder followed by combinatorial Kalman-filter track finding and fitting
using the TrackML detector geometry. The simulated detector response includes both
pixel and strip measurements for particles with pT > 0.4 GeV and |▷| ′ 2.5.

The ACTS study timing measurements were performed on a 2.3 GHz Cori–Haswell
CPU node. At ⇐µ⇒ = 200, seed finding requires approximately 0.11 s per event, while
the subsequent combined CKF track finding and fitting requires approximately 3.97 s

per event; only seeds with pT > 0.5 GeV are included in this measurement. The
combined reported time of approximately 4.08 s per event is more than an order of
magnitude larger than the 99–123 ms measured for the MaskFormer pipeline. This
di"erence is notable because both studies use high-occupancy events and the TrackML
detector geometry, but it should not be interpreted as a controlled measurement of
speedup. ACTS uses CPU hardware, processes both pixel and strip measurements,
and performs precision track fitting, while MaskFormer is evaluated on an NVIDIA
A100 GPU, uses only pixel hits, and does not include an equivalent fitting stage.

For reconstructed seeds in simulated tt̄ events with ⇐µ⇒ = 200, the ACTS study shows
an e!ciency of approximately 93–94.5% over much of the central pseudorapidity region,
with local reductions to approximately 78% in the forward region. The fake-rate
values remain below approximately 0.05%. These values are approximate readings from
individual bins of the published distributions rather than results integrated over the full
fiducial region. For the reported e!ciency measurement, truth particles are required



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 122

to have pT > 1 GeV and at least nine detector measurements, while reconstructed
tracks must have pT > 1 GeV and at least six measurements. A reconstructed track is
associated with a truth particle when that particle provides the largest fraction of its
measurements and this fraction is at least 50%. This di"ers from the double-majority
criterion used for the MaskFormer results, which also requires the reconstructed track
to recover at least half of the truth particle’s measurements.

The approximately linear event-level scaling observed for MaskFormer over the range
studied, together with its low measured latency, therefore motivates further investigation
of attention-based reconstruction for high-occupancy tracking. A direct comparison
with conventional reconstruction would require both approaches to be evaluated using
the same detector inputs, event sample, target-particle definition, output requirements,
hardware, and timing convention. Evaluation using a realistic ITk simulation and a
complete precision track-fitting stage is consequently required before conclusions can
be drawn about deployment in ATLAS reconstruction.

6.6 Architectural and Training Optimisations for the
Tracking Model

The preceding results establish the initial fixed-query MaskFormer tracking model
reported in Ref. [107]. The following studies introduce targeted architectural and
training modifications, subsequently reported as part of the scale-up study in Ref. [127],
that improve reconstruction performance and define the strengthened fixed-query
reference configuration used in Chapter 7.

The most important physics-level change is the introduction of an explicit mask-quality
prediction task, which separates the question of whether a query corresponds to a
charged particle from the question of whether its predicted hit assignment is complete
and uncontaminated. The remaining changes stabilise optimisation, simplify the
decoder heads, and reduce training overhead.



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 123

6.6.1 Mask-IoU Prediction

In the baseline tracking model, the object-validity score serves two related but distinct
functions. It identifies whether a decoder query corresponds to a reconstructable
charged particle, and it also implicitly determines whether the associated hit mask is
of su!cient quality to be retained. These quantities are not identical. A query may
correspond to a genuine particle while producing an incomplete or contaminated mask,
while a spurious query may produce a spatially coherent mask that does not correspond
to a reconstructable trajectory. Applying a single threshold to the object-validity score
therefore imposes an unnecessary trade-o" between e!ciency and fake-rate suppression.

To separate these e"ects, an auxiliary mask-quality prediction task is introduced, as
reported in Ref. [127]. A regression head acting on the final decoder embedding is
trained to estimate the intersection over union (IoU) between the predicted hit mask
and the corresponding ground-truth track mask, independently of the object-validity
score. For each matched query i, the target is the soft IoU between the predicted
assignment probabilities pij and the binary truth mask tij , where j indexes the detector
hits,

The task-specific heads are also simplified. The nonlinear hit and query projections

The auxiliary losses are adjusted to reflect the iterative refinement structure of the

the queries have not yet formed stable track hypotheses. The mask-IoU objective is
applied only to the final decoder output, so that it supervises the final reconstructed
mask quality rather than intermediate refinement states.

6.7 Conclusion

This chapter has presented a MaskFormer-based formulation of charged-particle track
reconstruction in which a fixed set of decoder queries predicts track-validity scores,
hit-assignment masks, and approximate particle properties directly from detector
hits. One-to-one cost-based matching enables these predictions to be trained against
an unordered, variable-multiplicity set of truth trajectories without explicit graph
construction or edge classification.

The approach was evaluated using the TrackML dataset. A Transformer-based filtering
stage reduced the average input multiplicity from approximately 60 000 hits per event
to 10 000 while retaining more than 99% of signal hits. For truth particles with
pT > 1 GeV, MF-0.6 achieved double-majority and perfect-match e!ciencies of 97.1%
and 93.2% within |▷| ′ 2.5, with a fake rate of 1.2%. The corresponding MF-1.0
values were 94.1%, 90.4%, and 0.7% over the full TrackML pixel acceptance of |▷| ′ 4.
The complete filtering and tracking pipeline required only 123± 14 ms and 99 ± 11 ms

per event for the two configurations, respectively, on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with
batch size one.

Architectural and training optimisations strengthened the full-acceptance fixed-query
model. In particular, an auxiliary mask-quality prediction separated track-validity
confidence from hit-assignment quality. Together with changes to the decoder, predic-
tion heads, auxiliary losses, and training implementation, this increased the MF-1.0
double-majority e!ciency from 94.1% to 96.6%, increased the perfect-match e!ciency
from 90.4% to 94.0%, and reduced the fake rate from 0.7% to 0.4%.

These results establish mask-based set prediction as a viable approach to charged-
particle pattern recognition in a simplified high-occupancy environment. The study
nevertheless remains a pixel-only proof of concept. The fixed query count must
accommodate the largest track multiplicity in each configuration, while dense decoder
cross-attention scales as O(NqueryNhit). Extending the model to lower transverse
momentum, wider acceptance, and heterogeneous detector measurements therefore



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 127

requires improved model scaling. This motivates the dynamic-query and sparse-
attention methods developed in Chapter 7.



Chapter 7

E!cient and Scalable Query-Based

Track Reconstruction

Chapter 6 establishes a proof of principle for Transformer-based charged-particle track
reconstruction. The track-reconstruction architecture introduced there is summarised
schematically in Fig. 6.1. Filtered detector hits are first mapped to contextualised repre-
sentations by the input encoder, while a fixed bank of learned queries provides candidate
track representations. The Transformer decoder updates these queries through inter-
actions with the encoded hits, after which task-specific heads predict a track-validity
score, a hit-assignment mask, and continuous track parameters for each query. The
present chapter extends this work by addressing the computational scalability of this
architecture, reducing its latency and memory footprint while preserving reconstruction
performance.

As discussed in Chapter 6, the fixed-query model could not be extended simultaneously
to lower transverse-momentum thresholds and the full pixel-detector acceptance within
the available GPU-memory budget. Lowering the transverse-momentum threshold
increases both the number of reconstructable particles and the number of hits retained
after filtering, while extending the detector input beyond pixel measurements to include
strip measurements further increases the hit multiplicity and introduces heterogeneity
between detector technologies.

A principal source of this computational cost is the decoder cross-attention, which
scales as O(NqNh), where Nq and Nh denote the numbers of queries and detector hits,
respectively. Candidate tracks are represented by a fixed bank of learned queries that
must be large enough to accommodate the highest reconstructable-particle multiplicity

128



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 129

expected in the training sample. Many queries therefore remain inactive in lower-
occupancy events while still participating in the decoder computation. As both the hit
and target particle multiplicities increase, this combination of query–hit attention and
a fixed query cardinality becomes increasingly restrictive.

Charged-particle trajectories exhibit approximate geometric locality in azimuth. As a
result, when detector hits and truth particles are ordered in azimuth, the truth-level
hit–particle association matrix is approximately band diagonal, suggesting that dense
decoder cross-attention could be replaced by a local interaction pattern. Fixed learned
queries, however, do not possess a stable event-dependent ordering and therefore do
not define a su!ciently consistent coordinate system on which to impose such locality.

The approach developed in this chapter addresses these limitations through event-
dependent query construction and geometrically local decoder cross-attention, as
summarised schematically in Fig. 7.1. The ↽-ordered encoded hit representation is
retained, while the construction of the decoder queries and the manner in which they
interact with the encoded hits are modified. In the fixed-query baseline, shown in
the left-hand panel, candidate tracks are represented by an event-independent bank
of learned queries and query–hit cross-attention is restricted using the dynamically
generated MaskAttention masks. The first modification, shown in the central panel,
replaces this fixed query bank with an event-dependent set of dynamic queries. A
lightweight classifier applied to the encoder-level hit representations identifies candidate
first measurements of reconstructable trajectories, and the corresponding hit embeddings

7.1 Experimental Setup and Metrics

All studies in this chapter use the TrackML dataset described in Section 6.2. Pixel-only
studies use the detector-hit representation introduced in Chapter 6, while Section 7.6.2
extends the input to include strip measurements.

Unless stated otherwise, results are reported for the Pix1.0 configuration, which
uses pixel-only inputs and defines reconstructable particles by pT > 1 GeV, |▷| ′ 4,
and at least three associated pixel hits. Two additional reconstruction regimes are
considered. The Pix0.6 configuration lowers the transverse-momentum threshold
to pT → 0.6 GeV while retaining pixel-only inputs, providing a controlled test of
increased event complexity. The PixStrip1.0 configuration additionally includes strip
measurements and is treated as an exploratory detector-extension study.

The reconstruction-quality metrics follow the definitions introduced in Chapter 6.
Since this chapter focuses on hit assignment and reconstruction quality, the kinematic-
regression head is omitted from the models considered.

Computational performance is evaluated using the per-event inference latency and the
peak GPU memory during training and inference. Peak allocated memory corresponds
to CUDA [132] memory actively occupied by tensors and therefore provides the
clearest measure of the intrinsic memory cost of the workload. Peak reserved memory
additionally includes memory retained by the CUDA caching allocator and is therefore
more directly related to whether the workload fits within the available GPU capacity.

All timing and memory measurements are performed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU

7.2.1 Reducing Hit-Filter Latency

The hit-filtering stage constitutes a significant fraction of the total inference cost of the

7.2.2 E!cient Attention Mechanisms

The scalability of Transformer architectures is strongly influenced by the cost of the
attention operation. For a sequence of N input elements, dense self-attention forms
the score matrix QK

T ∈ RN↔N , where Q and K denote the query and key matrices,
respectively. In standard implementations, this gives memory and computational
costs that scale as O(N

2
), as discussed in Chapter 4. This scaling is problematic for

charged-particle tracking, where the number of detector-hit tokens can be large.

A substantial body of work has addressed the quadratic scaling of Transformer atten-
tion [133]. One class of approaches uses sparse attention, in which attention scores are
computed for only a subset of the possible query–key pairs, rather than for every pair of
input elements. Examples include local and other structured sparse-attention patterns,
in which the permitted pairs follow a predefined regular topology, such as fixed win-
dows, dilated connections, or block-sparse layouts [95, 96, 134]. Alternative approaches
approximate dense attention using hashing, low-rank projections, or kernel feature
maps [135–137], or improve the implementation of exact attention through IO-aware
GPU kernels [97, 118]. The approach developed in this chapter is closest to structured
sparse attention combined with hardware-aware exact kernels. Detector geometry is
used to define a regular subset of query–key interactions that can be exploited by the
implementation, while e!cient attention kernels realise the corresponding reductions
in memory use and latency.

As described in Section 6.3.3, the tracking encoders exploit the approximate locality
of charged-particle trajectories in azimuth by ordering hits in ↽ and applying sliding-
window self-attention. For a fixed window width w, this reduces the encoder attention
cost from O(N

2

h) to O(Nhw), where Nh is the number of input hits. The permitted
interactions are evaluated using FlashAttention [97, 118], which implements exact
attention using tiled GPU kernels and avoids materialising the full attention matrix.
The reduction in encoder complexity therefore arises from the imposed local attention
pattern, while FlashAttention provides an e!cient implementation of that pattern.

Decoder cross-attention, however, does not naturally exhibit the same regular sparse
structure. It is important to distinguish structured sparsity from the learned masked-
attention mechanism used in the MaskFormer decoder. At each decoder layer, the
hit and query representations are used to predict track–hit association masks, which
suppress the contribution of hits that are unlikely to belong to a given candidate



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 135

trajectory in the subsequent cross-attention operation. This focuses each query update
on hits that are more compatible with the corresponding track hypothesis and improves
the quality of the learned hit assignment.

However, suppressing individual query–hit pairs does not by itself guarantee a reduction
in computational cost. FlashAttention-style kernels evaluate attention in blocks of track
queries and detector hits. Unless the predicted mask excludes complete blocks in a
regular pattern, the kernel must still process essentially all query–hit blocks. The mask
therefore changes which hits contribute to each track update, but does not substantially
reduce the number of blocks that must be evaluated, the corresponding arithmetic
operations, or the intermediate memory required by the attention kernel.

Structured sparsity instead defines the support of the attention operation in a form
that can be exploited by the implementation. The permitted interactions are organised
so that entire regions of the query–hit interaction matrix are known to be inactive
before the attention computation is launched. These regions can then be represented
as masked blocks and skipped by the kernel, rather than evaluated and subsequently
suppressed.

The aim of the sparse decoder studies in this chapter is therefore not merely to suppress
irrelevant query–hit interactions, but to define a physically motivated structured
sparsity pattern that can be leveraged through block-sparse attention kernels to reduce
computational complexity.

In addition to structured sparsity, the decoder presents a distinct scaling opportunity
through the query representation itself. The fixed-query formulation requires the
number of decoder queries to be chosen large enough to accommodate the highest-
multiplicity events encountered in the validation sample. Many query slots are therefore
inactive in typical events, but still contribute to decoder computation. Dense decoder
cross-attention consequently scales as O(NqNh), even when only a subset of the query
slots ultimately correspond to physical trajectories.

The following sections therefore explore two complementary routes to more scalable
decoding. The first is to search for a physically meaningful sparse cross-attention
pattern, so that the query–hit interaction space can be reduced while retaining the
associations needed for track reconstruction. The second is to replace the fixed query
budget with an event-dependent query representation, allowing decoder capacity to scale



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 136

with the trajectory content of the event rather than with the worst-case multiplicity of
the training sample.

7.3 Towards Physically Aligned Local Cross-Attention

The first step towards sparse decoder cross-attention is to determine whether structured
sparsity can be enforced in a physically meaningful way. In its standard form, the
learned query bank has no intrinsic spatial ordering. Query indices correspond to
latent output slots rather than detector regions or trajectory seeds. This section tests
whether an externally imposed azimuthal topology can align the fixed learned queries
in such a way that decoder cross-attention becomes approximately local. The study is
diagnostic rather than the final sparse-attention architecture.

7.3.1 Locality in the Ordered Hit–Particle Association

A physically motivated sparse attention pattern requires an ordering in which the
relevant query–hit interactions are approximately local. In a tracking detector immersed
in a solenoidal magnetic field, charged particles follow approximately helical trajectories.
Their motion in the transverse plane is approximately circular, with curvature inversely
related to pT. Over the transverse-momentum range considered in this work, the
curvature is small, and therefore the azimuthal displacement between successive detector
layers is typically local relative to the full detector occupancy, so hits produced by a
given charged particle remain confined to a limited and smoothly varying region in ↽.

In addition, the azimuthal coordinate is well suited to fixed-size local neighbourhoods
because the hit density is approximately uniform in ↽. Locality in the polar direction
is less robust. The pseudorapidity ▷ = ↔ ln tan(↼/2) is naturally defined relative to the
production vertex, which is not known from the detector hits alone. Hit-level values of
▷ computed relative to the detector origin can therefore di"er substantially from those
computed relative to the true longitudinal production point. The particle density is
also non-uniform in ▷, so fixed-size windows in an ▷-ordered sequence correspond to
variable detector occupancies.

Truth-level locality does not, however, imply that the learned query–hit interaction

The central challenge is therefore to induce an ordering of the learned query repre-

acquire an approximately band-diagonal form, with queries representing trajectories
at a given azimuth attending primarily to the corresponding local support of hits.

Imposing query topology through azimuthal positional priors

To attempt to induce band-diagonal form in decoder cross-attention, each decoder
query is assigned an external azimuthal coordinate,

of the query lattice. This defines a uniform partition of the detector coverage in ↽,
giving the otherwise unordered query bank a fixed one-dimensional topology shared
across events and decoder layers. Detector hits are ordered by their measured azimuth
↽h, so that a geometrically aligned query–hit interaction would appear as a diagonal
structure in the ordered query–hit plane.

The azimuthal prior is introduced using a positional-encoding-at-attention strategy
inspired by segmentation architectures [139–141]. In this approach, positional encodings
are added only to the query and key representations used to compute the cross-attention
logits, rather than to the query and hit embeddings that are propagated between decoder
layers. The positional information therefore influences which hits receive large attention
weights, while the evolving hidden representations remain free to encode non-geometric
information. In e"ect, the prior biases each query towards hits in a nearby azimuthal
region without forcing the query embedding itself to remain a purely geometric object.

Repeated exposure to a restricted azimuthal region can encourage each learned query
to specialise towards trajectories passing through that region. Over training, the fixed
query bank can therefore acquire an approximate one-dimensional topology, in which
neighbouring query indices correspond to neighbouring regions in ↽. When the hits are
also ordered in ↽h, this induced topology can manifest as a near-diagonal structure in
the query–hit interaction tensor.

Following optimisation studies, sinusoidal ↽ encodings, uniformly assigned query coordi-
nates, and cross-attention-only PE injection are used. These choices define a fixed-query
decoder in which the query axis is given a soft azimuthal topology without replacing
the learned query bank itself. This construction tests whether an externally imposed
query coordinate is su!cient to make the fixed-query decoder locally ordered. The



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 140

key question is not only whether a diagonal structure can be induced on average, but
whether the resulting query–hit alignment is stable enough on an event-by-event basis
to support a hard local attention mask.

Emergent Diagonal Sparsity in Query–Hit Attention

The ↽-aware positional priors bias the cross-attention logits to favour hit–query pairs
that are nearby in azimuth. When both queries and hits are ordered by ↽q and ↽h,
respectively, this induces a near-diagonal structure in the resulting query–hit interaction
maps, with the dominant predicted associations concentrated in a band around the
main diagonal.

This e"ect is illustrated schematically in Fig. 7.4. In the absence of azimuthal query
ordering and local positional priors, the cross-attention tensor remains dense and
unstructured, with no exploitable sparsity pattern. By contrast, the introduction of
a consistent ↽-ordered query topology concentrates the high-weight interactions into
a band whose width reflects the e"ective angular support of a track hypothesis. The
learned interaction pattern is nevertheless only approximately diagonal. It remains
broader and less stable than the truth-level association structure.

The positional prior can therefore organise the fixed-query decoder into an approximately
local representation, but this does not by itself establish a usable sparse-attention
pattern. To provide a practical computational benefit, the sparsity must be expressible
in a form that can be exploited by a block-sparse attention implementation. Although
an adaptive learned support could in principle be converted into a block-sparse mask,
rebuilding and lowering a new mask at each decoder layer would introduce additional
overhead and remove much of the latency advantage. A more useful sparse decoder
therefore requires a support pattern that is su!ciently stable to be reused across layers,
or defined by a simple fixed rule. This motivates the stricter local-attention test in
Section 7.3.3, where the learned adaptive support is replaced by a fixed local-attention
window.

The performance of the local cross-attention mask was found to depend strongly on
the number of fixed object queries. This behaviour is expected. In the fixed-query
formulation, the number of learned queries must be chosen to accommodate the largest
expected track multiplicity events in the validation sample. Most events therefore
contain more query slots than reconstructable trajectories, and many queries correspond
to null or unmatched predictions. Since the imposed azimuthal coordinates are assigned
uniformly across the query bank, these inactive queries occupy positions in the ↽-ordered
query lattice between queries associated with real tracks. They therefore interrupt the
relationship between neighbouring query indices and neighbouring physical trajectories.

In addition, null queries occupy positions in the imposed ↽ lattice. Since azimuthal
coordinates are assigned uniformly across all fixed query slots, a query that is ultimately
classified as null still consumes a position in the ordered query sequence. That position
is therefore unavailable to a query representing a physical trajectory. The queries
matched to real tracks are consequently interleaved with inactive slots, so their assigned
↽ coordinates need not align with the true azimuthal positions of the trajectories they
represent. This broadens the induced diagonal and makes its position less stable from
event to event. Fluctuations in the true track multiplicity and local ↽ density further
aggravate this e"ect. Although tracks are approximately uniform in ↽ on average,
their number and locations vary between events, while the fixed query lattice remains
unchanged. Alternative query-coordinate assignments, including schemes based on the
event-level hit ↽ distribution, were tested but did not recover the adaptive masked-
attention performance, and the induced diagonal remained too broad to support an
e!cient hard local window.

The failure of fixed-query local attention is therefore not evidence against azimuthal
locality itself. With a su!ciently large fixed query bank, queries whose assigned
azimuthal coordinates lie near real trajectories can still develop into valid track hy-
potheses, while the remaining queries are classified as null. The di!culty is that the
correspondence between a query’s imposed coordinate and the trajectory it ultimately
represents is not fixed by the event geometry.

Adaptive masked attention can compensate for this mismatch by updating the query-
specific hit support after each decoder layer. The fixed local window, by contrast,
assumes from the outset that the externally assigned query coordinate is already aligned
with the represented trajectory. When this alignment is inaccurate, relevant hits fall
outside the permitted window and unrelated local hits remain available, degrading hit



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 144

assignment quality. Sparse decoder cross-attention therefore requires a query sequence
that is more strongly aligned with the event before the local constraint is imposed. This
motivates the dynamic-query construction introduced in Section 7.4.1, where queries
are initialised from selected encoder-level hit representations and therefore inherit both
event-dependent content and the ↽ ordering of the detector-hit sequence.

7.4 Dynamic Queries

7.4.1 Dynamic-Query Construction

The fixed-query studies in Section 7.3 demonstrate that the obstacle to sparse decoder
attention is not the absence of azimuthal locality, but the lack of an event-aligned query
coordinate system. Fixed learned queries are input independent, and their number
must be chosen to cover the largest expected track multiplicities. Even when azimuthal
positional priors encourage them to develop an approximately diagonal interaction
pattern, their ordering is only indirectly related to the physical trajectories present in
a particular event. Null or unmatched query slots can interrupt this ordering, while
the queries associated with real trajectories need not remain su!ciently aligned with
their assigned ↽ coordinates. A hard local mask applied in this coordinate system can
therefore exclude valid associations or admit unrelated local hits, with the balance
between these failure modes determined by the window width.

This suggests that sparse decoder attention requires the query sequence itself to
be constructed in an event-aligned coordinate system, rather than imposing such
a coordinate system on a fixed bank of learned embeddings. The dynamic-query
construction introduced in Ref. [127] implements this idea by forming the decoder query
set from encoder-level hit representations. The resulting query set is event dependent
in three respects; its cardinality is determined by the selected seed hits, its content
is inherited from encoder representations of detector measurements, and its ordering
follows the ↽ ordering of the input hit sequence.

Figure 7.6 supports the use of an event-dependent query set. The number of recon-
structable charged particles scales approximately linearly with the number of detector
hits, and this correlation remains strong after hit filtering. The required decoder
capacity is therefore itself event dependent, motivating a query construction whose



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 145

cardinality can scale with the observed hit content rather than being fixed by the
highest-multiplicity events in the sample.

The computational improvements arise from two related changes to the decoder. First,
the query set is no longer fixed by a conservative worst-case query budget, but is

bidirectional cross-attention is removed, while improving reconstruction performance.

problem itself, rather than acting only as a systems optimisation.

As described in Section 7.4.1, dynamic queries are initialised from selected encoder-

As discussed in Section 7.3.3, the local LSCA mask provides a computational benefit only
if the kernel is not required to evaluate the full query–hit tile space. The LSCA decoder
is therefore implemented using PyTorch FlexAttention [98, 138], which constructs a
block-sparse attention representation from the binary support rule in Eq. 7.11.

FlexAttention represents the sparse attention support using a BlockMask, which records
the query–hit blocks that contain at least one permitted interaction, rather than



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 156

materialising a mask over all individual query–hit pairs. Blocks for which every
interaction is masked are omitted from the active block representation and can therefore
be skipped by the attention kernel. Partially masked blocks remain active, with the
element-level support rule applied within each block. The event-level BlockMask
is constructed once after dynamic-query selection and reused across decoder layers,
avoiding repeated mask construction.

This programmable block-sparse interface is well suited to LSCA because its support
is defined by a strided cross-attention pattern over query and hit sequences of di"erent
lengths. The pattern does not correspond to the standard dense, causal, or sliding-
window self-attention masks supported by conventional FlashAttention interfaces.

Summary

This study, performed in the Pix1.0 configuration, separates the e"ects of the two
architectural changes introduced in this part of the chapter. Replacing the fixed learned
query bank with dynamic queries improves both reconstruction quality and compu-
tational e!ciency, because the decoder is initialised with an event-dependent set of
track-like hypotheses rather than an overcomplete set of abstract latent slots. Retaining
adaptive MaskAttention in this setting gives the best reconstruction performance, with
DQ+MA achieving the highest double-majority and perfect-match e!ciencies and the
lowest fake rate among the Pix1.0 models considered.

Replacing adaptive MaskAttention with LSCA introduces a controlled loss in recon-
struction quality but reduces the decoder memory and latency. The loss is most visible
in the perfect-match e!ciency, indicating that the fixed local window preserves most
of the trajectory-finding capability but is less selective than the learned, query-specific
MaskAttention support for exact hit assignment. LSCA should therefore be inter-
preted as a systems-oriented variant of the dynamic-query model, suited to deployment
scenarios in which memory capacity, latency, or computational throughput impose
stronger constraints than the small loss in reconstruction quality. Such trade-o"s may
be relevant, for example, in resource-constrained online reconstruction environments
such as the trigger.

Summary

The Pix0.6 results demonstrate that the dynamic-query architecture not only reduces de-
coder memory su!ciently to make the previously inaccessible lower-pT , full-acceptance
regime computationally tractable, but also maintains strong reconstruction perfor-
mance in this setting. The architecture can be extended over the full pixel-detector
acceptance while lowering the target threshold to pT → 0.6 GeV, thereby covering the
full topological and kinematic range considered in the pixel-only studies and extending
reconstruction below the standard 1 GeV HL-LHC tracking threshold while retaining
low inference latency. Despite the more than twofold increase in both retained-hit
and reconstructable-particle multiplicity associated with the lower threshold, DQ+MA
and DQ+LSCA retain combined double-majority e!ciencies of 98.0% and 97.6%,
respectively, with fake rates below 0.5%.

Consistent with the pT → 1.0 GeV regime, LSCA provides a further reduction in decoder
cost within the dynamic-query architecture, reducing both inference latency and memory
while preserving most of the reconstruction performance. Although DQ+LSCA gives
slightly lower e!ciency and exact hit-assignment fidelity than DQ+MA, its substantial



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 166

computational advantages make it particularly well suited to use cases in which memory,
latency, or throughput constraints are more restrictive.

7.6.2 Extending to Strip Measurements

The previous section showed that dynamic queries allow the MaskFormer tracking
architecture to scale from the Pix1.0 benchmark to the lower-pT , full-acceptance Pix0.6
regime. We now ask whether the model can be extended beyond the pixel-only setting
to a heterogeneous pixel–strip detector input.

Motivation

The architectural modifications introduced in Sections 7.4 and 7.5 substantially reduce
the memory and runtime cost of the tracking architecture, particularly within the
decoder where global query–hit interactions previously dominated resource usage. This
recovered computational capacity enables the model to be extended beyond the pixel-
only setting studied thus far to a more realistic inner-detector reconstruction task that
additionally includes silicon strip measurements.

As introduced in Section 3.2.1, the silicon strip detector surrounds the inner pixel layers
and provides measurements at larger radii. In classical reconstruction pipelines, pixel
hits are primarily used to form initial track seeds, which are then extended outward
through the strip detector using combinatorial Kalman filtering. The additional outer-
layer measurements provide more measurements per trajectory and extend the radial
lever arm. In a complete reconstruction pipeline, these properties are expected to
improve robustness against local ambiguities and sensitivity to trajectory curvature,
although the present study does not evaluate these potential physics gains directly, since
the model is assessed through hit-association metrics rather than fitted track-parameter
resolution.

Reconstructability definition

The inclusion of strip measurements changes the supervised reconstruction task, rather
than simply adding detector information to the pixel-only benchmarks. In the earlier
pixel-only studies, a charged particle was considered reconstructable if it satisfied

This criterion is naturally aligned with a learned seeding task, since three spatial
measurements provide the minimum information required to define a short trajectory
segment. For the strip-inclusive studies, the target definition is extended to require
both a pixel seed and a longer trajectory through the combined pixel–strip detector.

Detector heterogeneity and input representation

Extending the reconstruction to strip measurements introduces detector heterogeneity
in addition to the increase in hit multiplicity. The pixel-only representation introduced
in Section 6.3.1 combines global geometric variables with charge-sharing and cluster-
morphology observables derived from the two-dimensional pixel readout.

These pixel-specific observables are not directly transferable to strip measurements. As
described in Chapter 3, strip sensors provide e"ectively one-dimensional measurements,
with stereo geometry used to recover higher-dimensional space-point information. The
local two-dimensional cluster morphology and charge-sharing variables used for pixel
hits are therefore not naturally defined for the strip space-points considered here.

Strip hits consequently retain the geometric variables common to both detector tech-
nologies, namely (x, y, z), (r, ▷,↽), and the conformal coordinates (u, v), while the
charge fraction and pixel-cluster variables (lς, lφ), (lx, ly, lz), and (gς, gφ) are omitted.
Pixel and strip measurements are processed by separate detector-specific input networks,
allowing their di"erent input feature spaces to be mapped into a common embedding
dimension before the resulting representations are passed to the shared Transformer
encoder.



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 169

Pixel-seeded strip-inclusive architecture

After detector-specific input embedding, the pixel and strip embeddings are concate-
nated into a single sequence and sorted globally in increasing azimuthal angle ↽. This
shared ordering preserves the locality prior used in the pixel-only architecture. Pixel and
strip measurements from the same trajectory remain approximately local in sequence
space, allowing windowed self-attention in the shared encoder to exchange information
between detector technologies.

The strip-inclusive decoder is then constructed as a pixel-seeded architecture. Dynamic
queries are initialised exclusively from encoded pixel-hit embeddings, and decoder
cross-attention is applied only to the encoded pixel-hit sequence. The pixel detector is
therefore treated as a learned seeding system, in which the high-resolution inner-detector
measurements define the candidate trajectory queries and provide the information used
for iterative query refinement.

The refined query embeddings are subsequently used to predict hit associations in both
detector subsystems. Rather than predicting a single mask over the union of pixel and
strip hits, the model uses separate association heads for pixel and strip measurements.
The query representation is shared between the two heads, but the output masks are
detector specific.

This design separates trajectory-hypothesis formation from strip-hit association. Pixel
hits determine the dynamic-query set and drive decoder refinement, while strip hits
enter through the final association task. The structure mirrors the seeding–extension
logic of conventional tracking, in which precise inner-detector measurements define
initial track candidates that are extended into the outer strip detector. It also prevents
decoder cross-attention from scaling with the full pixel-plus-strip hit sequence. The
cross-attention cost is controlled by the number of retained pixel hits, while strip
information is incorporated through the detector-specific association head.

Several more symmetric strip-inclusive variants were considered, including query initial-
isation from both pixel and strip hits and decoder cross-attention over the combined
pixel–strip sequence. These variants did not yield stable or competitive performance in
the present study. Other alternatives remain possible, including a unified association
head that predicts a single query–hit mask over the combined pixel–strip hit sequence,
rather than separate detector-specific masks. The configurations studied here should
therefore be interpreted as exploratory extensions of the dynamic-query architecture to



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 170

heterogeneous detector inputs, rather than as optimised strip-inclusive reconstruction
models.

Discussion

The strip-inclusive models presented here should be interpreted as proof-of-principle
configurations. The PixStrip0.6 results demonstrate that the pixel-seeded dynamic-
query architecture remains computationally tractable in a substantially more demanding
lower-threshold pixel–strip regime. However, neither the reconstruction architecture nor
its computational implementation was systematically optimised for this operating point.
The results therefore establish the feasibility of heterogeneous pixel–strip reconstruction,
rather than defining an optimal strip-inclusive strategy.

The reduction in reconstruction e!ciency relative to PixStrip1.0 may reflect the
increased target and hit multiplicities, the longer heterogeneous hit masks, or limitations
of the present model capacity and pixel-seeded association strategy. A dedicated
optimisation would be required to separate these e"ects and determine the best
achievable trade-o" between reconstruction quality and computational cost.

The present study also evaluates hit association only. It therefore does not establish
whether the increased radial lever arm provided by strip measurements improves
track-parameter resolution after fitting. This remains an important requirement for a
complete strip-inclusive reconstruction model.

7.7 Future Work

The scaling improvements introduced in this chapter make several previously inaccessible
tracking regimes computationally tractable. Future work should therefore move in
two complementary directions. The first is to test whether the reconstruction quality
demonstrated on TrackML persists in more realistic detector conditions and with
more complete tracking objectives. The second is to further optimise the architecture
and its implementation, improving reconstruction performance while reducing the
computational cost needed for large-throughput evaluation and deployment.



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 176

Migration to realistic ITk simulation. The next step is migration from the
TrackML-style detector geometry to realistic ITk simulation. Although TrackML
includes several important tracking e"ects, including high pile-up, material interactions,
and noise, it remains a simplified benchmark rather than a full experiment-specific de-
tector simulation. Realistic ITk simulation would provide the detailed ATLAS geometry,
material description, sensor response, detector conditions, and reconstruction interfaces
needed to assess the robustness and deployment potential of the architecture. It would
also enable direct comparison with traditional reconstruction strategies developed for
the Phase-II ATLAS Inner Tracker.

Full strip-inclusive reconstruction. The strip-inclusive study in this chapter
should be regarded as an initial proof of principle. Future work should jointly optimise
the dynamic-query budget, LSCA window width, model depth, first-hit threshold, and
detector-specific association heads for the heterogeneous reconstruction task. The
broader architecture design space should also be explored, including improved strip-hit
representations, unified pixel–strip association heads, separate encoder streams with
late fusion, and sequential pixel-to-strip extension stages.

The present pixel-seeded formulation is physically motivated by conventional track
seeding, but is not unique. Alternative query definitions could allow strip information
to contribute more directly to trajectory-hypothesis formation, for example through
joint prediction of an inner pixel seed and an outer strip anchor, or through explicit
prediction of the first and final measurements associated with each trajectory. These
studies would clarify whether the observed performance limitations arise primarily from
model capacity and optimisation or from the present strip-integration strategy.

Improved regression and track-fitting objectives. The present work focuses
primarily on hit association. A complete tracking model must also estimate track
parameters with su!cient resolution for downstream physics analyses. This becomes
particularly important once strip measurements are included, since their increased
radial lever arm should improve sensitivity to trajectory curvature and transverse-
momentum resolution. Future studies should therefore revisit helix-parameter or
momentum-regression objectives and evaluate the resulting parameter resolution after
track fitting.



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 177

Scalable matching and evaluation. As the decoder becomes more e!cient, non-
decoder components of the training and evaluation pipeline become increasingly impor-
tant. The bipartite matching stage is a natural target for further optimisation. The
same ↽-locality that motivates LSCA could be used to restrict candidate query–target
comparisons in the matcher, reducing the cost of assignment by avoiding geometrically
implausible pairs. Explicit batched-inference studies should also be performed, since
the reduced inference-memory footprint reported in this chapter should permit larger
batch sizes and therefore improved throughput.

Sparse-attention kernel development. The current LSCA implementation uses
FlexAttention because it supports user-defined strided sparse masks with unequal query
and key/value sequence lengths. This makes it well suited to diagonal query–hit cross-
attention, but it is less specialised than highly optimised FlashAttention-style kernels
in settings where standard aligned windowing is available. Future FlashAttention
backends may support the strided structure needed for LSCA while reducing overhead.
Re-evaluating the locality-aware decoder under future FlashAttention developments is
therefore an important systems direction.

Low-precision deployment. Finally, the reduced memory footprint of the dynamic-
query and LSCA models opens the possibility of more aggressive deployment optimisa-
tion. Quantisation to FP8 or other mixed-precision formats, particularly on H100-class
and later hardware, may reduce memory-bandwidth pressure and increase throughput
with limited degradation in tracking quality. This should be studied together with
batched inference, since the practical deployment target is not only low single-event
latency but also high sustained event throughput.

7.8 Conclusion

This chapter developed a scalable query-based Transformer architecture for high-
occupancy charged-particle reconstruction. Its central contribution is the replacement
of the overcomplete fixed query bank with an event-dependent set of dynamic queries
initialised from encoder-level detector-hit representations. This provides the decoder
with physically meaningful trajectory hypotheses whose number and ordering adapt
to the event. In the Pix1.0 configuration, dynamic queries improve the combined



E!cient and Scalable Query-Based Track Reconstruction 178

hit-filter plus tracking double-majority e!ciency from 96.6% to 98.1%, increase the
perfect-match e!ciency from 94.0% to 95.8%, and reduce the fake rate from 0.4% to
0.3%. These reconstruction gains are obtained together with a reduction in tracking
latency from 76.0±9.0 ms to 48.0±2.9 ms and in peak allocated training memory from
23.8 GB to 3.9 GB. Dynamic queries therefore improve both the physical reconstruction
problem and its computational implementation.

The event-aligned ordering inherited by the dynamic queries also exposes a stable
local structure in the query–hit interaction space. Local Strided Cross-Attention
exploits this structure through block-sparse execution, providing a further reduction in
decoder cost while preserving high reconstruction performance. In Pix1.0, DQ+LSCA
retains a double-majority e!ciency of 97.1% while reducing the full pipeline latency to
52.8 ± 15.2 ms and the peak allocated inference memory to 0.2 GB. LSCA therefore
provides a systems-oriented operating point for environments in which memory capacity,
latency, or throughput requirements are particularly stringent.

Together, these developments extend the MaskFormer tracking framework into regimes
that were inaccessible with the fixed-query formulation under the available memory
budget. The dynamic-query models reconstruct particles with pT → 0.6 GeV over the
full |▷| ′ 4 pixel-detector acceptance, despite more than doubling both the retained-hit
and reconstructable-particle multiplicities relative to Pix1.0. DQ+MA and DQ+LSCA
achieve double-majority e!ciencies of 98.0% and 97.6%, respectively, with fake rates
below 0.5%; the latter requires only 43.7 ± 5.4 ms for the complete filtering and
tracking pipeline. Exploratory pixel–strip studies further demonstrate the feasibility of
applying the architecture to longer, heterogeneous hit-association masks. The chapter
therefore establishes that physically structured query initialisation and sparse attention
can simultaneously deliver high reconstruction performance and tight computational
requirements in increasingly demanding tracking regimes.

8.1 Analysis Overview

As discussed in Chapter 2, Higgs-boson pair production provides the principal direct
collider probe of the trilinear Higgs self-coupling. The production rate and kinematic
properties of the Higgs-boson pair are sensitive to this coupling and to possible deviations
from the Standard Model Higgs potential [5]. This chapter describes the development
of a search for non-resonant Higgs-boson pair production in the HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ final state
using proton–proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS detector during Run 2 and
the early part of Run 3. Since H ↑ bb̄ has a branching fraction of approximately
58%, the HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ decay mode accounts for approximately 34% of Higgs-boson

channels [21,142]. Although this decay mode provides the largest expected signal yield,
the fully hadronic final state is dominated by a large background from QCD multijet
production and therefore requires data-driven background modelling.

requirement. A smaller contribution arises from top-quark production. This QCD

prediction is therefore derived from collision data, as discussed in Section 8.5.

The resulting year-specific predictions are then combined, with the 2016–2018 estimates
forming the Run 2 prediction and the 2022–2023 estimates forming the partial Run 3
prediction. These combined predictions are used in the validation plots and summary
results shown in Section 8.6.4.

8.5 Background Estimation

Three data-driven strategies are considered for predicting the multijet background in a
2Pass target region. The first two methods use the observed 1Pass events as a source
sample and construct the 2Pass prediction by applying a 1Pass-to-2Pass transfer. The
baseline method uses a single inclusive transfer factor, while the classifier-reweighting
method replaces this scalar factor with an event-dependent correction learned from
1Pass and 2Pass events in the control region.

The Gaussian-process plus conditional-normalising-flow method uses a di"erent fac-
torisation of the target distribution. A Gaussian process models the smooth variation
of the 1Pass-to-2Pass transfer across the Higgs-candidate mass plane, while a condi-
tional normalising flow models the remaining event kinematics given the mass-plane
coordinates, pass category, and data-taking year. This method therefore combines a
mass-plane transfer with conditional density estimation, rather than assigning only
deterministic weights to the observed 1Pass events.

The assumptions, use of the available data, and uncertainty constructions of the three
methods are described separately in the following sections. Although the methods
di"er in how they construct the 2Pass prediction, they are compared using the same
validation observables, the inclusive 2Pass yield and the binned mHH distribution, in
the nominal validation region.

8.5.1 Background Composition and the 1Pass-to-2Pass Transfer

As discussed in Section 8.1, the selected sample is dominated by QCD multijet pro-
duction, with a smaller contribution from tt̄ production. The rate and kinematic
composition of the QCD background cannot be predicted with su!cient precision using
simulated samples alone, and the background estimate is therefore constructed from
collision data.

The data-driven prediction is derived in control regions and applied to the signal or
validation region of interest, with the region definitions given in Section 8.4. This
procedure assumes that the background behaviour constrained outside the target region
provides a reliable prediction within it. Since this extrapolation cannot be guaranteed
from smoothness alone, its validity is tested empirically in validation regions close to
the blinded signal region, as described in Section 8.4.2.

The estimate exploits the relationship between the 1Pass and 2Pass categories defined

contains substantially more events than the 2Pass sample, its kinematic distributions

8.5.5 Uncertainty and Goodness-of-Fit Prescription

The uncertainty prescription used in this validation study separates two contributions to
the predicted background uncertainty. The first is the statistical uncertainty associated
with the finite 1Pass source samples used to populate the predicted mHH template.
The second is a method-dependent model uncertainty, which probes the stability of
the procedure used to determine the 1Pass-to-2Pass transfer. These uncertainties do
not constitute a final-fit systematic uncertainty model; they are used only to provide a
more complete comparison of the fixed background predictions in the validation studies.
No additional non-closure uncertainty is assigned. Instead, any residual normalisation
or shape disagreement between the prediction and observed 2Pass data is reported
explicitly.

an event-dependent transfer through classifier reweighting substantially improves the
partial Run 3 closure while maintaining good agreement in Run 2.

8.7 Conclusion

This chapter has presented the development and validation of data-driven multijet
background-modelling methods for a boosted search for non-resonant HH ↑ bb̄bb̄

production using ATLAS Run 2 and 2022–2023 partial Run 3 data. At the time of
writing, this analysis is ongoing and the signal region remains blinded. The results pre-
sented here therefore concern the selection and validation of the background-modelling
strategy rather than a final statistical interpretation.

Three background-modelling methods were studied: an inclusive baseline rescaling,
a classifier-based density-ratio reweighting method, and a Gaussian-process-plus-flow
method. All three methods give good closure in Run 2 under the validation-study
diagnostics. In partial Run 3, the methods are more clearly distinguished by their
inclusive normalisation. The baseline-rescaling method overpredicts the observed yield
by approximately 20%, corresponding to φnorm = +3.24. The classifier-reweighting
method reduces this di"erence to approximately 11%, with φnorm = +1.08. The GP-
plus-flow method instead underpredicts the observed yield by approximately 6%, giving
the smallest fractional di"erence between prediction and observation, although its
comparatively small assigned validation uncertainty results in a normalisation residual
of φnorm = ↔1.80.

At the level of the retained partial Run 3 mHH distribution over 600 < mHH <

1450 GeV, all three methods remain compatible with the observed data within the
assigned validation uncertainties. The learned methods give more favourable binned
closure diagnostics than the baseline rescaling, with the GP-plus-flow method providing
the lowest ◁

2
/Nbin and highest corresponding pseudo-experiment p-value among the

three methods. The classifier-reweighting method, however, gives the smaller inclusive
normalisation residual. The validation therefore does not identify a single method as
uniformly superior according to every closure metric.

Taken together, the results support the use of a learned transfer model over the
single-factor baseline for the partial Run 3 dataset. Of the approaches studied, the
GP-plus-flow method provides a particularly useful framework because it combines
competitive inclusive and binned closure with a generative description of the target-
region kinematics. It therefore provides the most suitable basis for further development
towards the final background model, while the classifier-reweighting result provides an
important independent comparison.



Development of a Boosted Non-Resonant HH → 4b Search 224

The validation studies do not, however, establish the GP-plus-flow prediction as a fully
validated background estimate for a final statistical interpretation. The uncertainty
treatment used here is intended as a validation diagnostic and does not retain the full
bin-to-bin correlation structure of the ensemble variations. A final signal-region fit
would require a covariance-based treatment of the GP-plus-flow uncertainty, together
with an appropriate treatment of residual non-closure derived from validation data.



Chapter 9

Conclusions

This thesis has explored how machine-learning methods can be designed and adapted
to extract physical information from the complex, high-dimensional data produced
by the ATLAS experiment. Methods originating in computer vision, modern deep
learning, and probabilistic density estimation were applied to charged-particle tracking
and data-driven background modelling, with the model design in each case guided by
the structure of the underlying detector or physics problem.

The principal focus of this thesis is charged-particle reconstruction in dense detector
environments, motivated by the conditions expected for the upgraded ATLAS Inner
Tracker at the High-Luminosity LHC. Studies of high-pT b-hadron decays showed that
the e!ciency loss is driven primarily by the surrounding dense jet environment and
is distributed across track finding and ambiguity resolution. Targeted ablations did
not recover the lost tracks, motivating approaches that learn hit-to-track associations
directly from detector measurements.

A Transformer-based tracking framework was then explored to reconstruct charged-
particle trajectories directly from hits in the pixel detector. In this formulation, decoder
queries represent candidate tracks and predict hit-assignment masks, allowing tracking
to be treated as an object-level set-prediction problem. In the TrackML setting,
the optimised fixed-query model achieved a double-majority e!ciency of 96.6%, a
perfect-match e!ciency of 94.0%, and a fake rate of 0.4%, with a mean end-to-end
inference time of 99.0 ± 11.0 ms per event on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. However,
the computational cost of dense decoder cross-attention limited scaling to tracks below
1 GeV.

225



Conclusions 226

Architectural modifications informed by the event topology were introduced to address
these computational constraints. Dynamic queries replace the fixed learned query bank
with event-dependent trajectory hypotheses derived from detector-hit representations.
Relative to the optimised fixed-query MaskAttention baseline, this reduced the event-
processing latency by approximately 36%, from 99.0 ± 11.0 ms to 63.7 ± 6.6 ms, and
the allocated training memory by approximately 84%, from 23.8 GB to 3.9 GB, while
increasing the combined hit-filter and tracking e!ciency from 96.6% to 98.1% and
the perfect-match e!ciency from 94.0% to 95.8%, and reducing the fake rate from
0.4% to 0.3%. Structured sparse attention was then introduced to exploit the ordered
query–hit association and reduce the cross-attention interaction space. This reduced
the allocated inference memory by approximately 82% relative to the dynamic-query
MaskAttention model and further reduced the full processing time to 52.8±15.2 ms, with
a controlled reduction in reconstruction performance. These developments provided
the computational headroom required to extend the model to lower-pT particles over
the full fiducial acceptance and to heterogeneous pixel–strip detector inputs.

Machine-learning approaches were also applied at the analysis level to data-driven
multijet background estimation in a boosted non-resonant HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ search using
Run 2 and partial Run 3 data. Three approaches were implemented and compared:
baseline rescaling, classifier-based kinematic reweighting, and a probabilistic model
combining Gaussian processes with conditional normalising flows. Validation studies
showed that the GP-plus-flow model provided the most favourable overall combination
of inclusive and binned agreement among the methods considered, although no single
method was uniformly superior across all diagnostics. The signal region remained
blinded, and no final statistical interpretation was presented.

Together, these studies demonstrate how physically informed machine-learning methods
can address challenges at multiple stages of collider-data analysis, from charged-particle
reconstruction to data-driven background estimation. By exploiting the geometry
and structure of the underlying problems, such methods provide a route towards
accurate and computationally scalable reconstruction and flexible modelling of complex
backgrounds in increasingly challenging experimental environments.
